Protected areas: Annapurna CA (upper Manang/Mustang), Shey Phoksundo NP (Dolpa), Api Nampa CA.\n- **Rainfall (verified)**: **~250 mm/yr**; **Jomsom (2,650 m) 255–295 mm**; **Upper Mustang 164 mm** mean annual (1973–2008, CV 35%); rangelands above 3,000 m mean annual precipitation **220 mm**, below 3,000 m **705 mm**. Freezing season **73–119 days** (Marpha to Lo Manthang).\n- **Vegetation (verified)**:\n  - Thorny cushion/dwarf shrub steppe: ***Caragana versicolor***, ***C. gerardiana***, ***C. brevifolia***; ***Lonicera spinosa***; ***Rosa sericea***; ***Sophora moorcroftiana***; *Astragalus*, *Oxytropis*, *Artemisia* spp., *Spiraea*.\n  - North of the Dhaulagiri–Annapurna massif specifically (Stainton): *Caragana versicolor*, *Lonicera spinosa*, *Rosa sericea*, *Sophora moorcroftiana* — \"climate and flora very much like the Tibetan plateau.\"\n  - Ravines/riverbanks: ***Hippophae*** spp. (*H. salicifolia*, *H. tibetana*), *Myricaria*, *Salix*, *Populus*.\n  - Conifers/shrubs: *Juniperus indica*, *Pinus wallichiana*, *Betula utilis*, *Ephedra gerardiana* (Somlata).\n  - Graminoids: *Stipa*, *Kobresia*, *Carex*, *Poa*, *Koeleria*.\n  - Mustang vegetation classified into **8 types**; **312 dicot species in 149 genera and 44 families** recorded from trans-Himalayan NW Nepal.\n- ⚠️ **Nepali name \"Dale chuk\"** for *Hippophae salicifolia* is widely used in Nepali NTFP literature but I could **not** verify it in an authoritative source — flag or write \"*Hippophae salicifolia* (sea buckthorn; Nepali Dalechuk/Chuk)\".\n\n---\n\n## 4. ## Verify respiration and photosynthesis facts

{"output": "# FACT-CHECK BRIEF — NEB Gr. 12 Plant Physiology\n\nCompiled from Lehninger/Taiz-level sources, NCBI/PMC, NOAA GML, and primary literature. Numbers atom-checked where equations are given. Three research threads ran in parallel; one internal conflict is flagged and resolved in §7.\n\n---\n\n## A. AEROBIC RESPIRATION — ATP ACCOUNTING\n\n### A1. Glycolysis (EMP pathway) — **cytosol/cytoplasm**, no O₂ required, no membrane needed\n\n| Item | Value |\n|---|---|\n| Gross ATP | 4 (SLP only) |\n| ATP invested | 2 |\n| **Net ATP** | **2** |\n| NADH | **2** (from GAPDH) |\n| Pyruvate | 2 |\n\n- **ATP-investing steps:** ① **hexokinase** (glucose → glucose-6-P); ② **phosphofructokinase-1, PFK-1** (fructose-6-P → fructose-1,6-**bis**phosphate) — the committed, rate-limiting, allosterically regulated step (inhibited by ATP + citrate = basis of the Pasteur effect).\n- **ATP-generating (substrate-level phosphorylation) steps:** ③ **phosphoglycerate kinase** (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → 3-phosphoglycerate); ④ **pyruvate kinase** (PEP → pyruvate). Each runs **twice per glucose** → 2 ATP each.\n- NADH is made at **glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH)**, ×2.\n- Plant note: plants also have a **cytosolic + plastidic** glycolysis, and a PPi-dependent phosphofructokinase (PFP) bypass — optional enrichment, not required.\n\n### A2. Link reaction / oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate — **mitochondrial matrix**\n\n**Pyruvate + CoA-SH + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺**\n\n| | Per pyruvate | Per glucose |\n|---|---|---|\n| CO₂ | 1 | **2** |\n| NADH | 1 | **2** |\n| Acetyl-CoA | 1 | 2 |\n| ATP | 0 | 0 |\n\n- **Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC/PDH)** = 3 enzymes: **E1 pyruvate dehydrogenase** (TPP + Mg²⁺), **E2 dihydrolipoyl transacetylase** (lipoamide), **E3 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase** (FAD). **Five cofactors: TPP, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD⁺, CoA** (+ Mg²⁺). Reaction is **irreversible** — this is why fats cannot be net-converted to sugar in animals, but plants can via the glyoxylate cycle.\n- Pyruvate enters via MPC1/MPC2 on the inner membrane.\n- Plant-specific: plants have a **second, plastidial PDH** supplying acetyl-CoA for fatty-acid synthesis. (Not on the Wikipedia PDC page; standard in Taiz & Zeiger.)\n\n### A3. Krebs / citric acid / TCA cycle — **mitochondrial matrix** (enzymes soluble; succinate dehydrogenase = Complex II, membrane-bound)\n\n**Eight intermediates in order:**\n**citrate → (cis-aconitate) → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (2-oxoglutarate) → succinyl-CoA → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate** → (recondenses with acetyl-CoA)\n\n| Step | Enzyme | Yield |\n|---|---|---|\n| OAA + acetyl-CoA → citrate | citrate synthase | — |\n| citrate ⇌ isocitrate (via cis-aconitate) | aconitase | — |\n| isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate | **isocitrate dehydrogenase** | NADH + **CO₂** ← **decarboxylation 1** |\n| α-KG → succinyl-CoA | **α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase** (TPP, lipoate, FAD, Mg²⁺) | NADH + **CO₂** ← **decarboxylation 2** |\n| succinyl-CoA → succinate | succinyl-CoA synthetase | **GTP/ATP (SLP)** |\n| succinate → fumarate | succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) | **FADH₂** |\n| fumarate → malate | fumarase | — |\n| malate → OAA | malate dehydrogenase | NADH |\n\n| | Per turn | Per glucose (2 turns) |\n|---|---|---|\n| NADH | 3 | **6** |\n| FADH₂ | 1 | **2** |\n| GTP/ATP | 1 | **2** |\n| CO₂ | 2 | **4** |\n\n- **Both decarboxylations are oxidative** (coupled to NAD⁺ reduction). Only these two steps release CO₂.\n- **Plant detail worth using:** plant succinyl-CoA synthetase is the **ADP-forming (ATP-producing)** isoform, so in plants it is legitimately **ATP**, not GTP. Animals have both.\n- Carbon bookkeeping caveat: the 2 CO₂ released in a given turn are **not** the carbons that just arrived on acetyl-CoA.\n\n**Running total per glucose (before ETS): 10 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 4 ATP (2 glycolysis + 2 Krebs), 6 CO₂.**\n\n### A4. ETS / oxidative phosphorylation — inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae)\n\n**Proton counts per 2 e⁻ (these are the load-bearing numbers):**\n\n| Complex | H⁺ pumped to intermembrane space |\n|---|---|\n| I (NADH dehydrogenase) | **4** |\n| II (succinate dehydrogenase) | **0** — pumps none |\n| III (cytochrome bc₁, Q-cycle) | **4** |\n| IV (cytochrome c oxidase) | **2** |\n| **Total per NADH** | **10** |\n| **Total per FADH₂** | **6** (III + IV only) |\n\n**H⁺ consumed per ATP = 4** — of which **3 drive the F₀ c-ring rotor** and **1 pays the transport tax**: the **ATP/ADP translocase (adenine nucleotide translocator)** exports ATP⁴⁻ and imports ADP³⁻ (electrogenic, costs Δψ) and the **phosphate translocase** imports Pi⁻ with an H⁺ (symport). This transport cost is the single most-omitted item in school textbooks.\n\n**Therefore: P/O = 10/4 = 2.5 ATP per NADH; 6/4 = 1.5 ATP per FADH₂.**\n\n**Why 38 vs 30–32:**\n\n| | Classical (obsolete) | Modern consensus |\n|---|---|---|\n| NADH | 3 ATP | **2.5 ATP** |\n| FADH₂ | 2 ATP | **1.5 ATP** |\n| Oxidative phosphorylation | 34 | 26 (or 24) |\n| SLP | 4 | 4 |\n| **Total** | **38** | **30–32** |\n\nThe 38 figure assumed **integer P/O ratios**, which was a pre-chemiosmotic requirement. Once Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory was accepted (Nobel 1978), there is **no theoretical reason for P/O to be a whole number** — the H⁺/e⁻ and H⁺/ATP stoichiometries are set independently by two different molecular machines, and 10/4 is simply not an integer.\n\n**Why 30 vs 32 — the glycolytic NADH shuttle.** The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to NADH, so the 2 cytosolic NADH from glycolysis must be shuttled:\n\n| Shuttle | Delivers electrons to | ATP per cytosolic NADH | Total per glucose |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle** | FAD → **Complex II/Q pool** (bypasses Complex I) | 1.5 | **30** |\n| **Malate–aspartate shuttle** | matrix **NAD⁺ → Complex I** | 2.5 | **32** |\n\nGlycerol-3-P shuttle: brain, insect flight muscle, skeletal muscle. Malate–aspartate: heart, liver, kidney. **Plants use the malate–OAA (malate valve) shuttle** plus **external NADH dehydrogenases**.\n\n**PLANT-SPECIFIC — flag this, it changes the answer and no school text mentions it:**\n- Plant mitochondria have **rotenone-insensitive external and internal NAD(P)H dehydrogenases (NDex/NDin)** that oxidise NADH **without pumping protons**, bypassing Complex I → 1.5 ATP instead of 2.5.\n- Plants have a **cyanide-resistant alternative oxidase (AOX)**: a di-iron, matrix-facing monotopic membrane protein that takes electrons **straight from the ubiquinol pool to O₂**, bypassing Complexes III and IV entirely. It is **non-electrogenic — pumps zero protons**. Only Complex I contributes to the gradient, so yield drops to ~1 ATP per NADH. Induced by cold, ROS, pathogen attack, phosphate limitation.\n- Classic AOX illustration: **thermogenesis in Arum maculatum, Sauromatum (voodoo lily), Symplocarpus foetidus (skunk cabbage)** — spadix heats 15–35 °C above ambient to volatilise insect attractants. (Well-established; not on the Wikipedia AOX page, cite Taiz & Zeiger or Meeuse 1975.)\n- **Consequence: a real plant cell rarely attains 30–32.** Best classroom wording: *\"theoretical maximum ~30–32; actual yield is lower and variable because of proton leak, AOX, and the alternative NAD(P)H dehydrogenases.\"*\n\n### A5. Anaerobic respiration / fermentation\n\n**Net ATP = 2 per glucose, all from glycolytic SLP. Fermentation itself yields ZERO ATP.** Its sole purpose is **regenerating NAD⁺** so GAPDH — and therefore glycolysis — can keep running. Redox-neutral: 2 NADH made, 2 NADH spent.\n\n**Alcoholic fermentation (yeast, plants) — cytosol:**\n1. **Pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC, EC 4.1.1.1)**, cofactors **TPP (vitamin B₁) + Mg²⁺**: pyruvate → **acetaldehyde + CO₂**. Irreversible. **Absent from animal tissue** — that is why muscle cannot make ethanol.\n2. **Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH, EC 1.1.1.1)**, cofactor **Zn²⁺**: acetaldehyde + NADH + H⁺ → **ethanol + NAD⁺**. Reversible.\n\n**C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂** (atom-checked: C 6=6, H 12=12, O 6=6) ✓\nΔG°′ ≈ **−235 kJ/mol** vs **−2870 kJ/mol** for full aerobic oxidation → fermentation releases only **~8%** of glucose's free energy.\n\n**Lactic acid fermentation:** **lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)**, pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD⁺. **C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₃H₆O₃**, **no CO₂ released**. Occurs in vertebrate muscle, RBCs, *Lactobacillus*/*Streptococcus* — **and in plants**.\n**Davies–Roberts pH-stat hypothesis** (Roberts et al., *PNAS* 81:3379 and 81:6029, 1984, maize root tips by in-vivo ³¹P-NMR): under hypoxia roots make **lactate first**; the resulting cytosolic acidosis **inhibits LDH and activates PDC**, switching metabolism to **pH-neutral ethanolic fermentation**. Present as a *hypothesis* — lactate efflux and alanine accumulation are competing explanations.\n\n**Plant tissues that ferment:** waterlogged/flooded roots and rhizomes (O₂ diffuses ~10⁴× slower in water than air; rice survives via **aerenchyma**), germinating seeds under an O₂-restricting testa, bulky storage organs (potato tuber cores), the interior of fleshy fruits, pollen.\n\n**Pasteur effect:** inhibition of fermentation/glycolytic flux by O₂. Mechanism: aerobic ATP and citrate **allosterically inhibit PFK-1**. (Converse = **Crabtree effect**: yeast fermenting even in air at high glucose.)\n\n### A6. Respiratory Quotient (RQ)\n\n**RQ = volume (= moles) of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed**, dimensionless, measured with a **Ganong's respirometer** (KOH absorbs evolved CO₂). Volume ratio = mole ratio by Avogadro, so RQ can be read straight off balanced-equation coefficients.\nGeneral: for CₓH_yO_z, **RQ = x ÷ (x + y/4 − z/2)**.\n\n| Substrate | Balanced equation (atom-verified) | RQ |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Glucose/carbohydrate** | C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O | **1.00** |\n| Sucrose | C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + 12 O₂ → 12 CO₂ + 11 H₂O | 1.00 |\n| **Tripalmitin** C₅₁H₉₈O₆ | **2 C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145 O₂ → 102 CO₂ + 98 H₂O** | **102/145 = 0.703 ≈ 0.7** |\n| Triolein | C₅₇H₁₀₄O₆ + 80 O₂ → 57 CO₂ + 52 H₂O | 0.713 |\n| Tristearin | 2 C₅₇H₁₁₀O₆ + 163 O₂ → 114 CO₂ + 110 H₂O | 0.699 |\n| **Protein (albumin)** | C₇₂H₁₁₂N₁₈O₂₂S + 77 O₂ → 63 CO₂ + 38 H₂O + SO₃ + 9 CO(NH₂)₂ | **63/77 = 0.82** |\n| **Malic acid** | C₄H₆O₅ + 3 O₂ → 4 CO₂ + 3 H₂O | **4/3 = 1.33** |\n| **Oxalic acid** | 2 C₂H₂O₄ + O₂ → 4 CO₂ + 2 H₂O | **4/1 = 4.00** |\n| Citric acid | 2 C₆H₈O₇ + 9 O₂ → 12 CO₂ + 8 H₂O | 12/9 = **1.33** |\n| Tartaric acid | 2 C₄H₆O₆ + 5 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 6 H₂O | 8/5 = **1.60** |\n| Succinic acid | 2 C₄H₆O₄ + 7 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 6 H₂O | 8/7 = 1.14 |\n\nTripalmitin verification: C 102=102 ✓ | H 196=196 ✓ | O 12+290=302 = 204+98=302 ✓\n\n- **RQ = 0** — O₂ consumed, **no CO₂ released**. Case: **succulents/CAM plants at night**, where carbohydrate is incompletely oxidised to organic acid and respiratory CO₂ is re-fixed by PEP carboxylase. Idealised equation (balanced ✓): **2 C₆H₁₂O₆ + 3 O₂ → 3 C₄H₆O₅ + 3 H₂O**, RQ = 0/3 = 0.\n- **RQ = ∞** — CO₂ released, **no O₂ consumed**. Case: **strict anaerobiosis / alcoholic fermentation** (yeast, anoxic seeds). Strictly the ratio is **undefined** (÷0); write \"**RQ tends to infinity**.\"\n- **RQ > 1:** organic acids; partially anaerobic tissue; fermenting yeast; **net carbohydrate → fat conversion** (usually omitted from school lists — RQ can reach 2–8).\n- **RQ < 1:** fats (germinating castor/groundnut/mustard/sunflower); proteins; **net fat → carbohydrate conversion** via glyoxysomes, which can push RQ well below 0.7 early in oilseed germination, then rise toward 1.0.\n\n---\n\n## B. PHOTOSYNTHESIS\n\n### B7. Light reaction — thylakoid membrane\n\n- **P680** (PSII) and **P700** (PSI): \"P\" = pigment; the number is the **red absorption maximum in nm**. Both are **chlorophyll *a***; the shift is caused by the protein environment. **P700 is a genuine Chl *a*/Chl *a*′ heterodimer; P680 is structurally a cluster of 4 weakly coupled Chl *a***, not a classic special pair (the \"dimer\" description is an acceptable simplification but is outdated).\n- **Lateral heterogeneity:** PSII + LHCII in the **appressed grana partitions**; PSI–LHCI and ATP synthase in **stroma lamellae, grana margins and end-membranes** (steric exclusion — PSI's 3.5 nm and ATP synthase's 12 nm stromal protrusions exceed the ~3.2 nm partition gap; Andersson & Anderson, *BBA* 593:427, 1980). **Cyt b₆f is in BOTH domains.**\n\n**Z-scheme order (Hill & Bendall, 1960):**\nH₂O → **OEC (Mn₄CaO₅)** → **Y_Z (D1-Tyr161)** → **P680** → **pheophytin *a*** → **Q_A** → **Q_B** → **PQ pool (PQ/PQH₂)** → **cyt b₆f** (Rieske [2Fe-2S] → cyt f; Q-cycle) → **plastocyanin (Cu)** → **P700** → **A₀ (Chl *a*)** → **A₁ (phylloquinone / vitamin K₁)** → **F_X → F_A → F_B** → **ferredoxin (2Fe-2S)** → **FNR (FAD)** → **NADP⁺ → NADPH**\n\n**Redox potentials (E_m, pH 7, vs NHE):**\n\n| Point | Value |\n|---|---|\n| H₂O/½O₂ | **+0.82 V** |\n| P680⁺/P680 | **≈ +1.2 V** (published +1.17 to +1.3) — **strongest known biological oxidant** |\n| P680* | **≈ −0.8 V** |\n| Pheophytin | ≈ **−0.50 to −0.54 V** (classic texts say −0.6 V; revised, *PNAS* 2009) |\n| Q_A | **−0.14 V** in intact O₂-evolving PSII (classic −0.08 V) |\n| PQ pool | **+0.10 V** |\n| Rieske FeS / cyt f / plastocyanin | +0.29 / +0.35 / **+0.37 V** |\n| P700⁺/P700 | **≈ +0.45 V** |\n| P700* | **≈ −1.3 V** |\n| Ferredoxin | **−0.42 V** |\n| NADP⁺/NADPH | **−0.32 V** |\n\nΔE from H₂O (+0.82) to NADP⁺ (−0.32) = **−1.14 V ⇒ +220 kJ per 2 mol e⁻** — the thermodynamic reason two photosystems must act in series.\n\n**Photolysis of water / OEC:** **2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻**. Catalyst = **Mn₄CaO₅ cluster** (distorted cubane: Mn₃CaO₄ cube + \"dangler\" Mn), ligated by D1 and CP43, requiring **Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻**. Runs the **Kok S-state cycle S₀→S₁→S₂→S₃→[S₄]→S₀ + O₂** (Joliot 1969; Kok, Forbush & McGloin 1970) — **4 photons per O₂**, S₁ dark-stable. **The OEC faces the LUMEN; all 4 H⁺ go into the lumen** and contribute to the pmf. Extrinsic lumenal proteins: **PsbO (33 kDa, manganese-stabilising protein), PsbP (23 kDa), PsbQ (17 kDa)**.\n**Quantum requirement = 8 photons per O₂** (4 per photosystem) → max quantum yield 0.125; measured 9–12. **Red drop** (Emerson & Lewis 1943, λ>680 nm) and the **Emerson enhancement effect** (1957) were the experimental basis for two photosystems.\n**Chloroplast ATP synthase has a fixed c₁₄ ring** ⇒ structural **H⁺/ATP = 14/3 = 4.67** (thermodynamic estimate 4.0; quote 4.67 and note the discrepancy). Chloroplast pmf is **ΔpH-dominated** (lumen 5.8–6.5, stroma 7.8–8.0).\n\n### B8. Non-cyclic vs cyclic photophosphorylation\n\n| | **Non-cyclic (linear)** | **Cyclic** | Pseudocyclic (Mehler / water–water) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Photosystems | **PSII + PSI in series** | **PSI only** | PSII + PSI |\n| e⁻ donor | **H₂O** | reduced ferredoxin (recycled) | H₂O |\n| Final acceptor | **NADP⁺** | PQ pool → back to P700 | **O₂ → H₂O** |\n| **ATP** | **Yes** | **Yes (only product)** | Yes |\n| **NADPH** | **Yes** | **No** | No net |\n| **O₂ evolved** | **Yes** | **No** | No net change |\n| Location | grana (PSII) + stroma lamellae (PSI) | **stroma lamellae + grana margins** (PSI, PGR5/PGRL1, NDH co-localise there) | stroma-exposed thylakoids |\n\nCyclic flow is constitutively high in **C4 bundle-sheath chloroplasts** (agranal, PSII-depleted — say \"greatly reduced,\" not \"absent\") and is upregulated during photosynthetic induction, fluctuating/high light, drought and low CO₂.\n\n### B9. Calvin cycle (C3, Calvin–Benson–Bassham) — chloroplast **stroma**\n\n**Per glucose (6 turns): 6 CO₂ + 6 RuBP + 18 ATP + 12 NADPH → 12 G3P, of which 2 exit (→1 glucose) and 10 regenerate 6 RuBP.**\n**Per single CO₂ fixed: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH.**\n\n| Phase | Enzyme(s) | ATP | NADPH |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **1. Carboxylation** | **RuBisCO**: RuBP (5C) + CO₂ → 2 × 3-PGA | 0 | 0 |\n| **2. Reduction** | **3-phosphoglycerate kinase** then **NADP-GAPDH** → G3P | 12 (2/CO₂) | 12 (2/CO₂) |\n| **3. Regeneration** | aldolase, FBPase, SBPase, transketolase, isomerase, epimerase, **phosphoribulokinase** | 6 (1/CO₂) | 0 |\n\n- ATP is used at **exactly two steps** (phosphoglycerate kinase, phosphoribulokinase); **NADPH at one step only** (GAPDH).\n- **RuBisCO = ribulose-1,5-*bis*phosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (EC 4.1.1.39)**, **L₈S₈** hexadecamer (~540 kDa; *rbcL* chloroplast-encoded large subunit + nuclear small subunit). **Most abundant protein on Earth**, ~50% of soluble leaf protein in C3. Very slow: **3–10 CO₂ s⁻¹ per enzyme**. Activated by **carbamylation of active-site Lys with a non-substrate CO₂, stabilised by Mg²⁺**, favoured by light-driven stromal pH rise (7.0→8.0) and Mg²⁺ influx; maintained by **RuBisCO activase** (AAA+ ATPase, thermolabile).\n- **First stable product = 3-PGA (3C).** The 6C intermediate (2-carboxy-3-keto-arabinitol-1,5-bisphosphate) is unstable and never isolable.\n\n### B10. C4 / Hatch–Slack pathway (Hatch & Slack, 1966; earlier Kortschak, Karpilov)\n\n- **First stable product: oxaloacetate (OAA, 4C)**, formed in the **mesophyll cytosol**.\n- Enzyme: **PEP carboxylase (PEPC)** — substrate is **HCO₃⁻, not CO₂** (supplied by carbonic anhydrase); **low K_m/high affinity, irreversible, NO oxygenase activity, O₂-insensitive**.\n- OAA → **malate** (NADP-MDH) or **aspartate** (aminotransferase); transported to bundle sheath through **plasmodesmata**.\n- **Three subtypes:** **NADP-ME** (malate; decarboxylated in BS *chloroplast*) — maize, sugarcane, sorghum; **NAD-ME** (aspartate; BS *mitochondrion*) — finger millet, *Amaranthus*; **PEP-CK** (aspartate; BS *cytosol*). Now regarded as a continuum, not discrete boxes.\n- **PEP regeneration: pyruvate phosphate dikinase (PPDK)** in mesophyll chloroplast: pyruvate + ATP + Pi → PEP + **AMP** + PPi. Because the product is **AMP**, not ADP, the true cost is **2 ATP equivalents**.\n- **Energy: C4 = 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂** (3 Calvin + 2 PPDK) vs **C3 = 3 ATP + 2 NADPH**. Per glucose: **30 ATP** (C4) vs **18 ATP** (C3); NADPH the same, 12.\n- **Kranz anatomy** (German *Kranz* = \"wreath\"): concentric rings around the vascular bundle — inner **bundle sheath** (large, thick-walled, often with a **suberin lamella**, chloroplasts **agranal/starch-rich, PSII-poor**) surrounded by **mesophyll** (granal chloroplasts). Extensive plasmodesmatal connection. CO₂ in the BS reaches **~10–20× atmospheric**.\n- **Nepal-relevant C4 crops: maize (*Zea mays*), sugarcane (*Saccharum officinarum*), sorghum (*Sorghum bicolor*), finger millet (*Eleusine coracana* — kodo; NAD-ME), foxtail millet (*Setaria italica*), proso millet, amaranth (*Amaranthus*, latte), *Cyperus rotundus*, *Atriplex*, *Portulaca*.** **Rice and wheat are C3** (hence the international \"C4 Rice\" project).\n- C4 = ~3% of land plants but **~23% of terrestrial carbon fixation**; ~61% are grasses; no C4 tree taller than 15 m. Advantage appears **above ~28–30 °C**; C3 wins in cool/shaded conditions.\n\n### B11. CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism)\n\n- **Night (stomata OPEN):** CO₂ → HCO₃⁻ → **PEP carboxylase** + PEP → OAA → **malate → stored as MALIC ACID in the VACUOLE** (tonoplast **V-ATPase**). PEP comes from starch broken down the previous day. Diagnostic test = **nocturnal acidification** (rising titratable acidity).\n- **Day (stomata CLOSED):** malate leaves the vacuole, is **decarboxylated by NAD(P)-malic enzyme or PEPCK**, and the released CO₂ (up to ~100× atmospheric internally) is refixed by **RuBisCO/Calvin cycle**.\n- **C4 = spatial separation** (mesophyll vs bundle sheath, same time); **CAM = temporal separation** (night vs day, same cell). Same core chemistry.\n- **Examples:** *Opuntia* and other Cactaceae, *Agave*, ***Ananas comosus* (pineapple — commercially grown in Jhapa/Ilam)**, *Kalanchoe*/*Bryophyllum*, *Sedum*, *Crassula*, *Aloe vera*, many *Euphorbia*, orchids, bromeliads. Present in >33 families, ~5–10% of vascular plants; frequently **facultative**.\n- **Transpiration ratio (g H₂O per g dry matter): C3 ≈ 600, C4 ≈ 300, CAM ≈ 150.** Instantaneous WUE: C3 1–3, C4 2–5, **CAM 10–40 g CO₂ per kg H₂O**.\n\n### B12. Photorespiration (C2 oxidative photosynthetic carbon cycle)\n\n- **Cause:** RuBisCO is **bifunctional** — CO₂ and O₂ compete at the **same active site** for the enediol form of RuBP. In air **O₂ is ~500× more abundant than CO₂** (~25× in solution). **High temperature and water stress worsen it**: the enediol destabilises so discrimination falls, and **CO₂ solubility drops faster than O₂ solubility** as temperature rises. At ambient gas levels **carboxylation : oxygenation ≈ 4:1**.\n- **Products of the oxygenase reaction: 1 × 3-PGA (3C) + 1 × 2-phosphoglycolate (2C)**. 2-PG is **toxic** — it inhibits Calvin-cycle enzymes and must be salvaged.\n- **Three organelles: chloroplast → peroxisome → mitochondrion → peroxisome → chloroplast.** Chloroplast: 2-PG → glycolate. Peroxisome: glycolate → glyoxylate (**glycolate oxidase**, makes **H₂O₂**, destroyed by **catalase**) → **glycine**. Mitochondrion: **2 glycine → serine + CO₂ + NH₃ + NADH** (glycine decarboxylase complex + SHMT). Peroxisome: serine → hydroxypyruvate → glycerate. Chloroplast: glycerate + ATP → 3-PGA.\n- **Carbon lost: 1 CO₂ per 2 oxygenations; ~25% of the carbon entering the pathway is re-released.** Net productivity cost to C3 crops up to **~25%** (modelled: soybean 36%, wheat 20%). *Do not print \"25–50%\" — 50% is not corroborated.*\n- **Generates NO ATP and NO NADPH. It actively CONSUMES them:** ~0.5 ATP (glycerate kinase) + 0.5 NADH (hydroxypyruvate reductase) per oxygenation, **plus 1 ATP + 1 NADPH to re-assimilate the released NH₃ via GS–GOGAT**.\n- **Why C4 avoids it:** the CCM raises BS CO₂ 10–20×, swamping O₂ competition; **PEPC has no oxygenase activity and uses HCO₃⁻**, which O₂ cannot mimic; **PSII-poor agranal BS chloroplasts evolve little O₂**; the **suberin lamella** blocks leakage. Correct wording: **\"negligible/greatly suppressed,\" not \"absent.\"**\n- **It is not purely wasteful** (modern view): detoxifies glycolate, acts as a **photoprotective safety valve** dissipating excess reductant under high light/low CO₂, supplies NADH for nitrate reduction and one-carbon units, and functions in redox/H₂O₂ signalling.\n\n### B13. Limiting factors and compensation points\n\n- **Blackman's Law of Limiting Factors (F. F. Blackman, \"Optima and Limiting Factors,\" *Annals of Botany* os-19(2):281–295, 1905):** *\"When a process is conditioned as to its rapidity by a number of separate factors, the rate of the process is limited by the pace of the slowest factor.\"* (Verbatim wording UNVERIFIED against the original scan — safest to present as a paraphrase.) Based on Matthaei's 1904 temperature/CO₂ data.\n  - **Include the standard criticism:** the real response curve **bends gradually** because two factors co-limit in the transition zone; Blackman's sharp linear-then-plateau break is an idealisation.\n- **Liebig's Law of the Minimum (1840; properly Sprengel–Liebig, 1828):** governs **amount/yield**, not rate — the \"barrel with the shortest stave.\" **Distinguish clearly: Liebig = amount, Blackman = rate.**\n- **Light compensation point (LCP):** light intensity at which **photosynthesis rate = respiration rate**, net CO₂ exchange = 0. **Shade plants ~10–50 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹; sun plants >100.** Sun leaves have higher dark respiration, which *raises* their LCP. Full sunlight ≈ 2000 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹; most C3 crops light-saturate well below that.\n- **CO₂ compensation point (Γ):** CO₂ concentration at which photosynthetic uptake = respiration + photorespiration. **C3 ≈ 50 ppm (range 40–100); C4 = 3–10 ppm; C3–C4 intermediates ≈ 25 ppm.** Γ rises with O₂ (50 ppm at 21% O₂ → 220 ppm at 100% O₂) and with temperature. C4's low Γ is because C4 releases essentially **no photorespiratory CO₂**. **Do not print a CAM Γ value** — day/night phase separation makes a single closed-chamber value meaningless.\n- **Atmospheric CO₂ — UPDATE THE NUMBER:** NOAA Mauna Loa annual means — 2023: 421.08, **2024: 424.61, 2025: 427.35 ppm (provisional)**; May 2025 seasonal peak **>430 ppm** (first time); Met Office forecast 2026: 429.4 ppm. **\"0.03%\" is wrong; use ~427 ppm ≈ 0.043%.**\n\n### Overall photosynthesis equation\n\n**6 CO₂ + 12 H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ + 6 H₂O**\n\n**Why 12 H₂O on the left:**\n1. **Oxygen bookkeeping.** All 6 O₂ (12 O atoms) come **exclusively from water**, so 12 H₂O must be consumed. The \"simplified\" 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O form implies some O₂ comes from CO₂ — chemically false.\n2. **Evidence.** **C. B. van Niel (1930s)** generalised bacterial photosynthesis (CO₂ + 2H₂S → [CH₂O] + H₂O + 2S) to **CO₂ + 2H₂A → [CH₂O] + H₂O + 2A**, predicting light splits the *hydrogen donor*, not CO₂. **Ruben, Randall, Kamen & Hyde (1941), *JACS* 63:877** fed *Chlorella* H₂¹⁸O and C¹⁸O₂ separately; evolved O₂ tracked the **water's** ¹⁸O enrichment, not the CO₂'s. Confirmed.\n3. **Mechanism.** 12 H₂O supply 24 e⁻ and 24 H⁺ at the OEC → 6 O₂; the **6 H₂O on the right are regenerated in the Calvin cycle** (phosphoglycerate kinase/GAPDH steps, FBPase/SBPase hydrolyses, ATP hydrolysis).\n\n---\n\n## C. FLAGGED — COMMON INDIAN/NEPALI TEXTBOOK ERRORS TO AVOID\n\n### Respiration\n1. **\"38 ATP per glucose\"** — obsolete integer-P/O figure. Use **30–32** (and note plants often achieve less because of AOX and rotenone-insensitive NAD(P)H dehydrogenases).\n2. **\"Fermentation produces 2 ATP\"** — fermentation produces **zero**; the 2 ATP come from glycolytic SLP that fermentation *permits* by regenerating NAD⁺.\n3. **\"Protein RQ = 0.9\"** (NCERT) — should be **≈0.80–0.82**. It **contradicts the albumin equation printed in the same books** (63/77 = 0.82). Primary flag.\n4. **`C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145 O₂ → 102 CO₂ + 98 H₂O`** without the coefficient 2 — **not atom-balanced** (C and H off by 2×). NCERT's own `2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145 O₂ → …` is correct; coaching-site copies drop the 2. The RQ still comes out 0.7, which is why the error survives.\n5. **Albumin equation printed as `C₇₇H₁₁₂N₂O₂₂S … + SO₂`** — wrong C, N and O. Correct: **C₇₂H₁₁₂N₁₈O₂₂S + 77 O₂ → 63 CO₂ + 38 H₂O + SO₃ + 9 CO(NH₂)₂**.\n6. **\"RQ = ∞\" stated as an equality** — it is **undefined** (÷0). Write \"tends to infinity.\"\n7. **RQ = ∞ attributed to lactic acid fermentation** — wrong: homolactic fermentation releases **no CO₂** at all (0/0).\n8. **\"RQ = 0 in germinating *Cucurbita* seeds\"** — wrong; *Cucurbita* is an **oil seed**, RQ < 1 (~0.7). The RQ = 0 case is **CAM succulents at night** — and even that is an idealised limit, not a measured value.\n9. **Citric acid RQ given as 1.14 or 1.2** — correct value is **1.33**, identical to malic.\n10. **Missing RQ > 1 case:** net carbohydrate → fat conversion.\n11. **\"Krebs cycle produces GTP\" stated universally** — in **plants** succinyl-CoA synthetase is the **ADP-forming (ATP)** isoform.\n\n### Photosynthesis\n12. **\"Dark reaction occurs at night / in the dark\"** — the single most damaging error. The Calvin cycle **runs in the light**; its enzymes (GAPDH, FBPase, SBPase, PRK, and RuBisCO via activase/pH/Mg²⁺) are **light-activated via thioredoxin**. Use \"**light-independent reactions**\" or \"**carbon reactions**.\"\n13. **\"Ribulose *di*phosphate / RuDP carboxylase\"** — outdated pre-1979 name. Use **bis**phosphate.\n14. **\"In C4 plants photorespiration is absent\"** — overstated; it is **greatly suppressed**, and the pathway remains essential even in C4 species.\n15. **\"C4 bundle sheath cells lack RuBisCO\"** — inverted. **RuBisCO is confined TO the bundle sheath**; it is the **mesophyll** that lacks it.\n16. **\"Bundle sheath chloroplasts lack thylakoids\"** — they lack **grana** (agranal, PSII-poor), not thylakoids.\n17. **\"PPDK costs 1 ATP\"** — wrong; the product is **AMP**, so **2 ATP equivalents**. This is exactly why C4 costs 5 ATP/CO₂, not 4.\n18. **\"CAM stores malic acid in the cytoplasm\"** — it is stored in the **vacuole** (V-ATPase).\n19. **\"C4 plants have a higher CO₂ compensation point\"** — inverted; C4 is **lower** (3–10 vs 40–100 ppm). Common MCQ distractor.\n20. **\"RuBisCO has greater affinity for O₂\"** — its **CO₂ affinity is much higher**; oxygenation happens because O₂ is ~500× more abundant. State both halves.\n21. **\"Photolysis releases protons into the stroma\"** / \"occurs on the outer thylakoid surface\" — the OEC faces the **LUMEN**; protons go **into the lumen**.\n22. **\"Pheophytin = chlorophyll *b* without Mg\"** — it is **chlorophyll *a*** with Mg²⁺ replaced by 2 H⁺.\n23. **\"Plastoquinone carries only electrons\"** — it is a **2e⁻ + 2H⁺** carrier; it takes 2 H⁺ from the **stroma** at Q_B and releases them into the **lumen** at cyt b₆f. This is the proton-translocating core of the Q-cycle and is usually omitted entirely.\n24. **\"Chloroplast CF₀ has 12 c-subunits, 3 H⁺ per ATP\"** — that is a mitochondrial generalisation. The chloroplast ring is fixed **c₁₄ → 4.67 H⁺/ATP**.\n25. **NCERT's stated reason cyclic flow occurs in stroma lamellae — \"they lack PSII *as well as NADP reductase*\"** — the PSII half is right, the **FNR half is WRONG**. FNR is abundant in stroma lamellae/margins (tethered by Tic62 and TROL). The real reason is that PSI, PGR5/PGRL1 and NDH are located there.\n26. **\"Cyclic photophosphorylation happens only at wavelengths beyond 680 nm\"** — misleading. CEF operates continuously and is upregulated under fluctuating/high light, drought and low CO₂; far-red-only light is merely a laboratory way to drive it.\n27. **\"Cyt b₆f sits only in the grana\"** — it is distributed across **both** appressed and non-appressed regions.\n28. **\"Quantum requirement = 4 photons\"** (Warburg) — refuted; the minimum is **8**.\n29. **Obsolete Z-scheme nomenclature** — \"Q\", \"X\", \"FRS\", cyt b₅₅₉ in the main chain. Use **Pheo, Q_A, Q_B, A₀, A₁, F_X/F_A/F_B, Y_Z**. Cyt b₅₅₉ is a photoprotective side-path.\n30. **\"Finger millet is C3 like rice\"** — wrong; **finger millet (kodo) is C4 (NAD-ME)**, foxtail millet is C4 (NADP-ME). Good Nepal contrast: **C4** = maize, sugarcane, sorghum, finger millet, amaranth (latte); **C3** = rice, wheat, barley, potato, mustard, soybean; **CAM** = pineapple, *Aloe vera*, *Opuntia*.\n31. **\"Atmospheric CO₂ = 0.03%\"** — out of date. **~427 ppm (2025) ≈ 0.043%.**\n32. **\"12 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose\" in the Calvin cycle** — wrong; **18 ATP + 12 NADPH** (C3), **30 ATP + 12 NADPH** (C4).\n33. **Writing 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂** — use the **12 H₂O / 6 H₂O** form for oxygen honesty.\n\n---\n\n## D. ONE RESOLVED CONFLICT AND REMAINING UNVERIFIED ITEMS\n\n**RESOLVED CONFLICT — ATP:NADPH balance.** Two of my research threads disagreed. Many textbooks (and one of my sources) state that linear electron flow produces ATP:NADPH = 1.5, \"exactly matching\" the Calvin cycle's 3:2 demand. **This is wrong.** With the chloroplast **c₁₄ ring (4.67 H⁺/ATP)** and 12 H⁺ deposited in the lumen per 2 H₂O (4 from the OEC + 8 from the Q-cycle), linear flow yields **12/4.67 = 2.57 ATP per 2 NADPH → ratio 1.28**, against a Calvin demand of **1.50**. **The ~0.22 ATP/CO₂ shortfall is precisely why cyclic electron flow, the Mehler/water–water cycle and the malate valve exist.** This is the most important modern correction available to the chapter and I recommend making it explicit.\n\n**UNVERIFIED — do not print as fact:**\n- Blackman's **verbatim** 1905 wording and page number (open scans were image-only). Paraphrase, or OCR the Biodiversity Heritage Library copy.\n- RuBisCO specificity factor S_c/o ≈ 80–100 (qualitative trade-off confirmed; the number was not).\n- WUE ranges \"C3 450–950 / C4 250–350 / CAM 18–125\" — **not found anywhere**; use the transpiration ratios 600/300/150 instead.\n- \"Optimum temperature C3 15–25 °C, C4 30–45 °C\" — the specific bands were not verifiable; the **~28–30 °C C3/C4 crossover** is.\n- A numeric **CAM CO₂ compensation point** — no defensible single value exists; explain why rather than print one.\n- \"Photorespiration costs 25–50% of productivity\" — only **~25%** is corroborated.\n- The school pairing \"sun plants LCP 10–20, shade plants 1–5 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹\" is **not supported**; the ordering is right but the magnitudes are an order of magnitude too low. ## Verify plant hormones and growth

{"output": "**FACT-CHECK BRIEF — Plant Hormones, Growth & Movement (NEB Gr-12)**\nVerified against Wikipedia's technically-sourced hormone articles (which track Taiz & Zeiger and ASPB reviews), plus standard Plant Physiology literature. Items I could not fetch are marked ⚠VERIFY.\n\n---\n\n## 1. AUXIN\n| Claim | Status / correction |\n|---|---|\n| IAA = **indole-3-acetic acid** | ✅ Correct. Most abundant native auxin; all auxins have an aromatic ring + carboxylic acid group |\n| Precursor amino acid | ✅ **L-tryptophan** (main route: Trp → indole-3-pyruvic acid via TAA1 → IAA via YUCCA flavin monooxygenases) |\n| Site of synthesis | **Shoot apical meristem, young leaves, developing seeds/fruits** — NOT root tips |\n| Darwin & Darwin **1880**, *The Power of Movement in Plants* | ✅ Book published 1880 (John Murray). ⚠**Major textbook error: they used *Phalaris canariensis* (canary grass) coleoptiles, not *Avena*.** They showed the **tip** perceives light, bending occurs below; inferred a transmissible \"influence.\" They did **not** discover or name auxin |\n| Boysen-Jensen **1913** | ✅ (work 1910–13) Stimulus crosses a gelatin block/incision; mica on the shaded side blocks it |\n| Paál **1918** | ✅ Árpád Paál: decapitated coleoptile + tip replaced **asymmetrically in darkness** → curvature away from the tip's side. Proved a chemical, not light, is the signal |\n| Went **1926/1928** | ✅ Frits Went: diffused substance into **agar blocks**, quantitative ***Avena* curvature test** (curvature ∝ concentration); **named \"auxin.\"** Kögl & Haagen-Smit (1931–34) isolated it; Thimann (1935) identified IAA |\n| Nobel Prize for auxin | ❌ **No Nobel was ever awarded for auxin.** Delete any such claim |\n| Polar **basipetal** transport, PIN/AUX1 | ✅ Cell-to-cell, strictly polar, energy-dependent. **PIN-FORMED = efflux carriers** (polarly localised, set by PINOID/D6PK phosphorylation); **AUX1/LAX = influx carriers (non-polar)**. Basipetal in shoots; in roots **acropetal in the stele, basipetal in the epidermis** (say \"polar,\" not blanket \"basipetal\") |\n| Apical dominance | ✅ Apex-derived auxin suppresses axillary buds; involves ethylene induction in buds plus **strigolactones and cytokinin**. Decapitation releases buds (tea-plucking, hedging) |\n| Synthetic auxins IBA, NAA, 2,4-D, 2,4,5-T | ✅ All four are synthetic (note IBA also occurs natively at trace levels). 2,4-D + 2,4,5-T = **Agent Orange**; 2,4,5-T restricted (US EPA 1979) for **TCDD dioxin** contamination |\n| Uses: rooting of cuttings (NAA, IBA), parthenocarpy, prevention of pre-harvest fruit drop, selective weedicide | ✅ All correct. Selectivity: **dicots are far more susceptible than monocots/narrow-leaved plants** — so 2,4-D kills broadleaf weeds **in** cereal/grass crops |\n| Bell-shaped dose–response; roots inhibited where shoots are promoted | ✅ Correct and important. Roots respond optimally near **10⁻¹⁰–10⁻⁸ M** and are **inhibited** at 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁵ M, the range that promotes stem elongation. High auxin induces ethylene → inhibition |\n\n## 2. GIBBERELLIN\n- **GA3 = gibberellic acid**, C₁₉H₂₂O₆, a **pentacyclic diterpenoid acid**; first GA structurally characterised. ✅\n- **Kurosawa 1926** ✅ — Eiichi Kurosawa showed **cell-free culture filtrate** reproduced *bakanae* (\"foolish seedling\") symptoms in rice: excessive elongation, pale thin stems, lodging, death. (Fungus–disease link itself dates to Hori, 1898.)\n- Fungus: **teleomorph *Gibberella fujikuroi*; anamorph *Fusarium fujikuroi***. ⚠ **\"*F. moniliforme*\" is an obsolete/rejected name** — use *F. fujikuroi*.\n- **Yabuta & Sumiki 1938** crystallised gibberellin A ✅ (Yabuta coined \"gibberellin,\" 1935). Western work: Brian/Cross, ICI, 1950s.\n- **>130 GAs**: ✅ — the precise figure is **136 identified from plants, fungi and bacteria (as of 2020)**. Only a handful (GA1, GA3, GA4, GA7) are bioactive.\n- **Bolting** ✅ (rapid internode elongation + flowering in rosette plants: cabbage, beet, *Arabidopsis* long-day rosettes).\n- **α-amylase in barley aleurone** ✅ — GA from the embryo/**scutellum** diffuses to the **aleurone layer**, inducing *de novo* α-amylase (via GAMYB) → starch hydrolysis. Commercially used in **malting**.\n- **Breaking seed/bud dormancy** ✅ (antagonises ABA).\n- **Grapes** ✅ — GA3 is standard on **Thompson Seedless** for larger berries and looser/longer bunches.\n\n## 3. CYTOKININ\n- **Kinetin, Miller & Skoog 1955, from autoclaved herring sperm DNA** — ✅ **CORRECT**. Fresh DNA was inactive; only **autoclaved** DNA worked, i.e. the active agent was a degradation product. Chemically **N⁶-furfuryladenine**. ⚠ Nuance: kinetin is effectively **synthetic/an artifact** — it is *not* a normal plant hormone (trace natural occurrence in damaged DNA reported since 1996).\n- **Zeatin, Letham 1963** ✅ — isolated/crystallised from **immature milky endosperm of maize (*Zea mays*)**; the **first natural cytokinin**. Say \"endosperm,\" not \"kernels.\" Letham coined **\"cytokinin\" (1963)**.\n- **Site of synthesis: root apex** ✅ as the textbook answer; more precisely **root tips plus cambium and other dividing tissues**, transported **upward in the xylem**.\n- **Cell division/cytokinesis** ✅ — requires auxin present; auxin alone → cells enlarge without dividing.\n- **Tissue-culture ratio — get direction right:** **high auxin : low cytokinin → ROOTS; high cytokinin : low auxin → SHOOTS; roughly equal → undifferentiated callus.** ✅ (Skoog & Miller, 1957.)\n- **Richmond–Lang effect** ✅ — Richmond & Lang **1957**: kinetin delayed senescence/chlorophyll loss in detached ***Xanthium*** leaves. Mechanism: inhibits protein degradation, promotes protein synthesis, mobilises nutrients.\n- **Apical-dominance antagonism** ✅ — cytokinin moves root→shoot and promotes lateral bud outgrowth, opposing auxin.\n\n## 4. ABSCISIC ACID\n- **Addicott (abscisin II, 1963, from young cotton bolls; also \"abscisin I\")** and **Wareing's group (dormin, 1964–65, from dormant sycamore/*Acer pseudoplatanus* leaves)**; shown identical 1965; ⚠ **name unified as \"abscisic acid\" in 1967** (International Conference on Plant Growth Substances, Ottawa) — plausible and standard, not confirmable from the pages fetched. Earlier: **Hemberg (1940s)**, potato-tuber inhibitor.\n- **C15 sesquiterpenoid, but made by cleaving a C40 carotenoid** ✅ — plastidial **MEP** pathway: zeaxanthin → (epoxidation/isomerisation) **violaxanthin** → 9′-*cis*-neoxanthin → **cleaved by NCED (9-*cis*-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase)** → **xanthoxin** → abscisic aldehyde → ABA. ⚠ Do **not** say ABA is made from farnesyl diphosphate in plants (that route is fungal/MVA). \"Apocarotenoid\" is the more accurate label.\n- **\"Stress hormone\"** ✅ (drought, salinity, cold, heat, heavy metals). **Stomatal closure** ✅ (PYR/PYL receptors → inhibit PP2C → SnRK2/OST1 → anion efflux, guard-cell turgor loss). **Seed maturation + dormancy** ✅.\n- **Does ABA cause leaf abscission?** ❌ **NO — the name is a misnomer.** ABA drives abscission in only a small number of species (its discovery context was cotton bolls). **Ethylene is the natural regulator of leaf abscission** (Doubt 1917; Jackson & Osborne, *Nature* 1970, titled exactly \"Ethylene, the natural regulator of leaf abscission\"). Auxin *delays* abscission.\n\n## 5. ETHYLENE\n- **Only gaseous hormone** — ✅ with a caveat: only gaseous **classical** hormone (methyl jasmonate/methyl salicylate are volatile; NO is a gaseous signal).\n- **Neljubow 1901** ✅ — Dimitry Neljubow identified ethylene in **illuminating (coal) gas** as the agent altering **pea seedling** growth. **Triple response** = inhibition of stem elongation + **radial swelling/thickening** of hypocotyl + **diageotropic (horizontal) growth**, with an exaggerated apical hook. (Attribute the triple response to Neljubow's system with care.)\n- **Gane 1934** ✅ — R. Gane, *Nature*: proved **apples (Worcester Pearmain) produce ethylene**; ~1 cm³ over the fruit's whole life; production ceases without O₂. Crocker, Hitchcock & Zimmerman (1935) argued it is a hormone.\n- **Biosynthesis (Yang cycle, S.F. Yang)** ✅ — **methionine → SAM** (SAM/Met adenosyltransferase) → **ACC (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid)** + MTA, by **ACC synthase (ACS, rate-limiting)** → **ethylene**, by **ACC oxidase (ACO, O₂-requiring)**; MTA recycled to Met.\n- **Climacteric** ✅ — sharp autocatalytic ethylene rise + respiration/CO₂ peak marking end of maturation. Immature fruit: negative feedback (System 1); mature: **autocatalytic** (System 2).\n- **Climacteric:** banana, mango, tomato, apple, papaya ✅ (+ avocado, guava, peach, pear, plum, kiwi, passion fruit, sapota). **Non-climacteric:** citrus, grape, strawberry ✅ (+ pineapple, litchi, pomegranate, cherry, watermelon, cucumber, capsicum). Caveat: not airtight — non-climacteric melon/apricot cultivars exist; grape expresses ethylene receptors during ripening.\n- **Epinasty** ✅ — in flooding/hypoxia, roots make ACC → transported up → oxidised to ethylene in leaves → petiole grows faster on the **upper (adaxial) side** → leaf bends downward. **A growth movement.**\n- **\"One bad apple spoils the barrel\"** ✅ literally true — autocatalytic ethylene from one ripe/wounded fruit ripens neighbours.\n- **Ethephon/Ethrel** ✅ = 2-chloroethylphosphonic acid; hydrolyses in planta to release ethylene. Uses: uniform ripening (tomato, coffee, mango), latex flow in rubber, flower induction in pineapple, boll opening in cotton.\n- **Calcium carbide — ACETYLENE, not ethylene.** ❗**CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ (acetylene) + Ca(OH)₂.** Acetylene is only a **weak ethylene analogue (~100× less active)**; it triggers peel de-greening but not proper internal ripening → poor flavour/sugar. **Danger is the impurities:** technical-grade carbide (80–85% CaC₂) contains calcium phosphide/arsenide → **phosphine (PH₃) and arsine (AsH₃)**, plus residual Ca(OH)₂ burns. **India: banned** — FSS (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations 2011, **Reg. 2.3.5**: no person shall sell fruit artificially ripened by **acetylene gas, commonly known as carbide gas**; FSSAI later **permitted ethylene gas up to 100 ppm** in ripening chambers. ⚠**Nepal: carbide ripening is likewise prohibited and routinely seized by DFTQC under the Food Act — confirm the exact Nepali regulation locally before printing.**\n\n## 6. GROWTH\n- **Definition:** permanent, irreversible increase in size/dry mass/cell number accompanied by metabolism. (Contrast with reversible turgor swelling.)\n- **Grand period of growth (Sachs):** **sigmoid/S-shaped** curve; **four phases — (i) lag, (ii) log/exponential, (iii) decelerating/diminishing, (iv) stationary/maturation (plateau).** ⚠ Some texts give three phases (lag, log, stationary); NEB's four-phase version is fine but state that the deceleration phase is the extra one.\n- **Arithmetic growth:** only one daughter cell divides, other differentiates → **linear**; **Lₜ = L₀ + rt**. **Geometric growth:** both daughters divide → **exponential; W₁ = W₀e^{rt}** (r = relative growth rate / efficiency index). Geometric growth characterises the **early** phase only.\n- **Absolute growth rate (AGR)** = total increase per unit time (measured/compared directly). **Relative growth rate (RGR)** = increase per unit initial size per unit time — the correct basis for comparing a small vs large organ.\n- **Instrument: auxanometer** ✅ — **arc auxanometer** (lever/pointer over a calibrated arc; magnification = long-arm/short-arm ratio) and **Pfeffer's auxanometer** (pulley + weight + recording drum). ⚠ **Do not confuse with J.C. Bose's crescograph**, which magnifies (~10,000×) and records growth, and is not an auxanometer.\n- **Three zones of the root/shoot growth region** (behind the root cap, tip→base): **(1) meristematic zone (cell division), (2) zone of elongation, (3) zone of maturation/differentiation.** Most measurable elongation is in zone 2.\n\n## 7. MOVEMENT\n**Tropic (tropism):** growth movement in which the **direction of curvature is determined by the direction of the stimulus**; always a **growth (irreversible) movement**; mediated by differential elongation. **Nastic:** movement whose direction is **fixed by organ anatomy, independent of stimulus direction**; may be growth-based **or** turgor-based.\n\n| Movement | Type | Correct example / mechanism |\n|---|---|---|\n| Phototropism | Tropic, **growth** | Shoot +ve, root −ve. Blue light → **phototropin (phot1/phot2)** → lateral auxin redistribution to shaded side |\n| **Gravitropism** (preferred over \"geotropism\") | Tropic, **growth** | **Root +ve, shoot −ve.** Sensing by **statoliths = dense starch-filled amyloplasts** sedimenting in **statocytes** — **columella cells of the root cap** (and starch-sheath/endodermis in shoots), enmeshed in actin, activating mechanosensitive channels. *pgm1* starchless mutants are gravity-insensitive |\n| **Cholodny–Went hypothesis** | — | Proposed independently **Cholodny (1927) & Went (1928)**: lateral auxin redistribution → differential growth. **Status: still the working framework but modified, criticised and refined** — auxin accumulates on the **lower side in both root and shoot**; opposite bending arises from **opposite tissue sensitivity** (inhibits root elongation, promotes shoot elongation). Refinements: reorientation of **auxin efflux carriers** (PIN3/PIN2), LAZY1, a ~40° \"tipping point\" resymmetrisation, and evidence that **inclination angle rather than statolith weight** is sensed in shoots. Do not present it as unqualified fact |\n| Hydrotropism | Tropic, growth | Roots curve toward higher water potential (MIZ1/MIZ2); overrides gravitropism in dry soil |\n| Chemotropism | Tropic, growth | **Pollen tube growth down the style to the ovule/micropyle** (LURE peptides, Ca²⁺) |\n| Thigmotropism | Tropic, growth | **Tendril coiling** (*Pisum*, *Cucurbita*, *Passiflora*); also root obstacle avoidance |\n| **Nyctinasty / photonasty** | **Nastic — TURGOR** (pulvinar) | \"Sleep movements\" of legume leaves: ***Albizia julibrissin*/*Samanea*, *Medicago*, tamarind, *Lespedeza*, *Oxalis*, *Mimosa***. Mechanism: **pulvinus** motor cells, **K⁺ flux → water flux** between dorsal/ventral motor cells, phytochrome (Pfr/Pr) + circadian control. ⚠ Non-pulvinar nyctinasty via **unequal petiole growth** also exists, so don't claim all nyctinasty is turgor-based. Flower photonasty (*Oxalis*, dandelion, *Mirabilis* opening at dusk) is **growth**-based |\n| **Thermonasty** | **Nastic — GROWTH** | ***Crocus*** and **tulip** perianth opening on warming / closing on cooling, by differential inner-vs-outer petal growth |\n| **Seismonasty / thigmonasty** | **Nastic — TURGOR (variation) movement, NOT growth** | ***Mimosa pudica***: touch → **mechanosensitive Ca²⁺ channels → all-or-none action potential** propagating leaflet → rachis → petiole → main pulvinus; **K⁺ and anion efflux from ventral motor cells → water loss → turgor collapse** → leaflets fold, petiole droops. **Speed: folding begins within ~0.1 s and completes in 1–3 s; AP propagates ~1–3 cm s⁻¹; recovery takes ~10–30 min** (\"a few minutes\" per the *M. pudica* article — give the seconds figure as approximate ⚠). Reversible, no permanent size change → **not growth**. Closure costs ~40% of photosynthesis. Also: *Dionaea* trap shuts in ~0.1 s (turgor + elastic buckling) |\n| Chemonasty | Nastic, turgor | Digestive-gland response of *Drosera*/*Nepenthes* to prey chemicals |\n| **Epinasty / hyponasty** | **Nastic — GROWTH** | Epinasty = faster **upper**-side growth → organ curves **down** (ethylene, waterlogged tomato); hyponasty = faster **lower**-side growth → curves **up** (shade avoidance) |\n\n**Summary rule to print:** *All tropisms are growth movements. Nastic movements split into growth-based (epinasty, hyponasty, thermonasty, floral photonasty) and turgor/variation-based (seismonasty in Mimosa, pulvinar nyctinasty, stomatal movement, Dionaea trap, chemonasty). Turgor movements are reversible and need no new cell growth.*\n\n---\n\n## ERRORS COMMON IN SOUTH ASIAN TEXTBOOKS TO AVOID\n1. **\"Darwin used *Avena* (oat) coleoptiles.\"** → The Darwins (1880) used ***Phalaris canariensis*** canary-grass coleoptiles. *Avena* belongs to **Went's 1928 curvature bioassay**.\n2. **\"Darwin discovered auxin.\"** → They inferred only a transmissible \"influence.\" **Went (1928) named auxin**; Kögl/Thimann (1934–35) identified it as IAA. Also: **no Nobel Prize was given for auxin** — delete that claim.\n3. **\"Calcium carbide releases ethylene.\"** → It releases **acetylene (C₂H₂)**, a weak ethylene mimic; the real hazard is **phosphine/arsine** impurities. It is **illegal in India (FSS Reg. 2.3.5, 2011)** and prohibited in Nepal; **ethylene gas (≤100 ppm) is the legal alternative**.\n4. **\"ABA causes leaf/fruit abscission\" (treating the name as descriptive).** → **Misnomer.** Abscission is regulated mainly by **ethylene** (auxin delays it). ABA = stress/stomatal-closure/dormancy hormone.\n5. **\"ABA is a sesquiterpene made from farnesyl diphosphate.\"** → In plants ABA is an **apocarotenoid**: C40 carotenoid (zeaxanthin→violaxanthin→9′-*cis*-neoxanthin) cleaved by **NCED** → xanthoxin → ABA.\n6. **Auxin:cytokinin ratio reversed.** → **High auxin:cytokinin = ROOTS; high cytokinin:auxin = SHOOTS; equal = callus.** Many Indian/Nepali guides invert this.\n7. **\"Kinetin is a natural plant hormone found in plants.\"** → Kinetin (N⁶-furfuryladenine) is an **artifact/synthetic** from autoclaved herring-sperm DNA (Miller & Skoog, 1955). The **first natural cytokinin is zeatin** (Letham, 1963, from maize milky endosperm — endosperm, not \"kernels\").\n8. **\"Mimosa pudica leaf folding is a tropic/growth movement\"** (or calling it \"thigmotropism\"). → It is **seismonasty/thigmonasty**, a **reversible turgor (variation) movement** of pulvinar motor cells via action potentials and **K⁺/anion efflux** — **~1–3 s**, no growth involved.\n9. **\"2,4-D kills monocot weeds.\"** → Selective against **dicots (broadleaf)**; that is why it is safe in cereals and lawns.\n10. **\"Auxin is synthesised at the root tip; cytokinin at the shoot tip.\"** → **Reversed.** Auxin: **shoot apex/young leaves** (moves down, polar); cytokinin: **root apex** (moves up in xylem).\n11. **\"Cholodny–Went explains gravitropism because more auxin reaches the lower side of the shoot but the upper side of the root.\"** → Auxin accumulates on the **lower side in both**; the opposite bending is due to **opposite tissue sensitivity**. And the hypothesis is **refined, not settled** — PIN carrier relocalisation, LAZY genes, inclination-sensing.\n12. **\"Statoliths are free starch grains.\"** → They are **amyloplasts** (starch-filled plastids) inside **columella cells** of the root cap.\n13. **\"*Fusarium moniliforme* causes bakanae.\"** → Correct current names: **teleomorph *Gibberella fujikuroi*, anamorph *Fusarium fujikuroi***; *F. moniliforme* is obsolete.\n14. **\"Gibberellin was discovered by Kurosawa, who isolated it.\"** → Kurosawa (1926) showed the **cell-free filtrate** caused the symptoms; **Yabuta & Sumiki (1938) crystallised** it; Yabuta coined \"gibberellin\" (1935). Say **136 GAs known (2020)**, not \"about 100.\"\n15. **\"Strawberry/citrus/grape ripen after harvest with ethylene.\"** → **Non-climacteric** — they will not ripen properly off the plant.\n16. **\"Crescograph measures growth rate\"** used interchangeably with auxanometer. → **Auxanometer (arc/Pfeffer's)** is the growth-rate instrument; **Bose's crescograph** is a high-magnification recorder. Keep them distinct.\n17. **\"Auxin promotes growth at all concentrations\" / omitting the root paradox.** → **Bell-shaped** dose–response; **roots are inhibited (10⁻⁶–10⁻⁵ M) at concentrations that promote shoot elongation**; root growth is promoted only near 10⁻¹⁰–10⁻⁸ M. High auxin acts via induced **ethylene**.\n18. **\"Ethylene is the only volatile signal in plants.\"** → It is the only **classical gaseous hormone**; methyl jasmonate, methyl salicylate and NO are also volatile/gaseous signals. Say \"only gaseous classical hormone.\"\n\n**Two source cautions for the chapter:** (i) the 1967 unification date for the ABA name and the exact Nepali statutory ban on carbide ripening are the two items I could not confirm from an authoritative page (WebSearch quota was exhausted; these came from fetched encyclopedic and regulatory context) — verify both before print; (ii) the *Mimosa* folding time in seconds is widely cited but the fetched source states only \"quickly… re-open a few minutes later,\" so present it as approximate. agentId: a697e4d0e69bc895a (use SendMessage with to: 'a697e4d0e69bc895a', summary: '<5-10 word recap>' to continue this agent)\n<usage>subagent_tokens: 49551\ntool_uses: 16\nduration_ms: 410002</usage>"}

## Verify applied zoology Nepal facts

{"output": "Brief complete. Primary source secured: the MoALD statistics yearbook PDF (2081/82 = 2024/25).\n\n---\n\n# FACT-CHECK BRIEF — APPLIED ZOOLOGY (NEB Gr. 12)\n\n## NEPAL OFFICIAL FIGURES — all from one primary source\nMoALD, *Statistical Information on Nepalese Agriculture 2081/82 (2024/25)*, Tables 2.12, 4.1, 4.2, 5.1. **Use this citation; it supersedes the FAOSTAT/older numbers in most textbooks.**\n\n| Item | FY 2081/82 (2024/25) |\n|---|---|\n| Honey | **4,278 MT**; **276,000 hives** (2023/24: 4,945 MT / 276,530 hives) |\n| Total milk | **2,718,177 MT** — cow 1,302,094 (47.9%), **buffalo 1,416,083 (52.1%)** |\n| Total fish | **131,112 MT** — aquaculture 110,112 (**84%**), capture 21,000 (**16%**) |\n| Pond carp culture | 88,254 MT on 15,707 ha; yield **5.62 mt/ha**; 54,685 ponds; Terai = 96% of output |\n| Rainbow trout | **1,332 MT** (9 ha raceway) |\n| Eggs | **1,632,289 thousand** (≈1.63 billion); hen eggs 1,601,997 thousand |\n| Chicken meat | **182,516 MT** |\n| Livestock | cattle 5,141,391; buffalo 3,294,723; **goat 15,954,080**; sheep 652,742; fowl 56,391,680; laying hens 12,405,021 |\n| Per-capita fish | 4.47 kg production / 4.64 kg availability (2080/81) |\n\n⚠️ **Series break:** cattle fell 7,413,196 → 4,750,329 and buffalo 5,132,931 → 3,081,061 between 2021/22 and 2022/23 (census re-basing, not a real crash). Never plot across it.\n\n## 1. APICULTURE\n- **Five economically important spp. in Nepal**: *Apis cerana*, *A. dorsata*, *A. laboriosa*, *A. florea*, *A. mellifera* — only *A. mellifera* is non-native [Thapa et al. 2018].\n- *A. cerana* (Fabricius 1793): multiple combs in cavities → hiveable; 10–11 mm; colony **~6,000–7,000 workers** vs *A. mellifera* \"up to 50,000+\". Kept to **3,500 m**; ~78% of Nepal's hives [MoALD 2019]. \"*A. indica*/*A. cerana indica*\" is **obsolete**.\n- *A. mellifera* **introduced to Nepal 1992** [Kortsch et al. 2024, *Insects* 15:281, citing Devkota 2020]. (1989 = introduction of *A. cerana* movable-comb hives — different event.)\n- *A. laboriosa* Smith 1871: **world's largest honey bee, adults to 3.0 cm**. Taxonomy: pre-1980 a subspecies of *A. dorsata* → species 1980 → back to subspecies by **Engel 1999** → **confirmed full species 2020** on sympatry with no interbreeding [Kitnya et al. 2020, *ZooKeys* 951:67–81]. Nests under **vertical cliff overhangs, 2,500–3,000 m**, forages to 4,100 m; one nest up to 60 kg honey.\n- *A. dorsata*: single open comb \"sometimes nearly three metres in diameter\" [Britannica]. *A. florea*: small single comb on shrubs.\n- **Mad honey**: *A. laboriosa* on ***Rhododendron*** nectar → **grayanotoxins** acting on **voltage-gated Na⁺ channels** → vagal activation, **bradycardia + hypotension in nearly every case**. Nepali source is *R. arboreum* (**laliguras**, national flower) [*Int J Emerg Med* 2026]. ~68 Nepali cases / 5 decades, **no recorded fatalities**, clustered in **Gandaki Province** in spring; ~72% middle-aged men self-medicating [*Toxicon* 2026 review]. Harvested by **Gurung** honey hunters; sells ~5× normal honey [Ahmad, Joshi & Gurung 2003, ICIMOD].\n- **Castes**: egg hatches **3 d** in all castes; emergence **queen 16 d, worker 21 d, drone 24 d** (*A. mellifera*) [Britannica]. **Unfertilised eggs → haploid drones** (arrhenotoky); queen controls fertilisation from the **spermatheca**. **Royal jelly** from **hypopharyngeal glands of nurse workers** — *all* larvae receive it; worker/drone larvae are **weaned off after ~3 days**.\n- **Langstroth**: Rev. **L. L. Langstroth** (1810–95) found in **1851** that bees neither build in nor propolise a gap of **6.4–9.5 mm (¼–⅜ in)** = **bee space**; **US Patent 9300, 5 Oct 1852**. Precursors: Prokopovych 1814, Dzierżon 1835.\n- **Pests**: ***Varroa destructor* Anderson & Trueman 2000** split from *V. jacobsoni* (*Exp Appl Acarol*) — *V. destructor* is the *A. mellifera* pest. **Thai sacbrood + European foulbrood have afflicted *A. cerana* in W. Nepal \"since the 1990s\"** [Saville 2000, via Kortsch et al. 2024]; sacbrood drove Asia-wide *A. cerana* declines with recent recovery [Ilyasov et al. 2022]. *Tropilaelaps mercedesae* is an under-rated Asian threat. *A. cerana* smears faeces at nest entrances against the hornet *Vespa soror* [Mattila et al. 2020].\n- **Pollination**: **87 of the leading global food crops** depend on animal pollination; 35% of production volume [Klein et al. 2007, *Proc R Soc B* 274:303]. Nepal: *A. c. cerana* gives **>50% of flower visits** to apple/cucumber/pumpkin in Jumla; honey = 16% of household income; yield/hive **−50%** and occupied hives **−44%** (2012–22) [Kortsch et al. 2024]. National yield **16.45 kg/hive** [MoALD 2019].\n\n## 2. SERICULTURE\n- *Bombyx mori* (Bombycidae), from wild *B. mandarina* ~4,600 yr BP; **flightless, not found wild**; monophagous on *Morus alba*.\n- **5 larval instars, 4 larval moults** — verified; spinning begins after the 4th moult; the 5th moult (larva→pupa) occurs inside the cocoon. Egg hatch ~14 d (9–12 d polyvoltine); **larval period 29–30 d** (698–718 h) [Tzenov et al., *Insects* 2025, PMC12734233]; spinning 2–3 d; adult **does not feed**; **300–500 eggs/female**.\n- **Filament — resolve the discrepancy**: total spun ~1,000–1,600 m (measured **925–1,225 m**); **usable/reelable as one continuous filament = 600–900 m** [Britannica]. Fibre ~10 µm, triangular cross-section.\n- **Cocoons per kg raw silk = 4,000–7,000** (the familiar \"2,000–3,000\" is **per POUND**). Cocoon 1.8–2.0 g; shell ratio 18–21%; raw silk % 36–40%. **Renditta = kg cocoons per kg raw silk ≈ 3.2–3.6** (dry basis) — *not* a count of cocoons.\n- **Raw silk = fibroin 75–80% + sericin 20–25%**; degumming removes up to 30% of weight. Fibroin = antiparallel **β-sheets**, repeat **(Gly-Ser-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala)ₙ**, Fib-H + Fib-L (disulfide) + P25. Two brins glued by sericin = **bave**. Sericin is a hot-water-soluble glycoprotein.\n- Chain: stifling (steam/hot air) → deflossing → cooking → **reeling** → throwing → degumming; **filature** = reeling factory; broken cocoons → **spun silk**.\n- **Vanya (Saturniidae)**: tasar ***Antheraea paphia*** (*A. mylitta* is a **junior synonym**), hosts *Terminalia arjuna/tomentosa*, *Shorea robusta*; oak tasar ***Antheraea* × *proylei*** — a **man-made hybridogenic taxon** (♂ *A. pernyi* × ♀ *A. roylei*, backcrossed to *A. pernyi*), on *Quercus*; eri ***Samia ricini*** (= *Philosamia ricini*) on castor *Ricinus communis*, cocoon **open-mouthed → spun, not reeled** = ahimsa silk; muga ***Antheraea assamensis*** on **som *Persea bombycina*** and **soalu *Litsea* spp.**, 99% from Assam.\n- **Nepal**: ISC classes Nepal among producers of **\"negligible quantities\"**. First attempt **1911** (PM Chandra Shamsher); state **Silk Farming Centre 1975**; **Sericulture Development Centre, Khopasi, Kavrepalanchok** is the hub, with **nine government farms**. **1,538 ha mulberry, 39 MT production** (MoALD 2020/21 — almost certainly cocoon, not raw silk). Only **bivoltine *B. mori***; no commercial vanya sector. 38 mid-hill districts (750–1,500 m) declared feasible. India = only country producing all four silks; China = largest producer.\n\n## 3. PISCICULTURE\n- **Taxonomy resolved**: *Labeo rohita* (accepted). **Catla → use *Labeo catla*** (FishBase accepted; syn. *Catla catla*, *Gibelion catla* — GBIF backbone still shows *Gibelion*). *Cirrhinus mrigala* — **and *C. cirrhosus* is a separate accepted species, not a synonym**. *Hypophthalmichthys molitrix*; *Ctenopharyngodon idella*; *H. nobilis* (**not** *Aristichthys nobilis*); *Cyprinus carpio*. All Cyprinidae.\n- **Why polyculture works — niches [FAO Cultured Species sheets]**: catla = **surface/mid-water zooplankton** (upturned mouth, long gill rakers), 20–30%; silver carp = **surface phytoplankton**; **bighead = zooplankton** (don't co-stock with silver carp as fingerlings); grass carp = **macrophytes** (5–20% of stock); mrigal = **illiophage, bottom detritus/decayed vegetation** (15–20%); common carp = **bottom omnivore** (~25%); rohu = **column omnivore** (convention, not explicitly FAO-stated). Yields 3–5 t/ha/yr; Nepal average **5.41–5.62 mt/ha**. FAO notes **bighead substitutes for a species in Nepal's six-species system**.\n- **Indigenous**: *Tor putitora* (sahar) — **Endangered, EN A2abcd, assessed 5 Aug 2018**; **NOT an official national fish** (Nepal's gazetted symbols are cow, Himalayan monal, *Rhododendron arboreum*). *Schizothorax richardsonii* (asala) — **Vulnerable, 2010**. *Neolissochilus hexagonolepis* (katle) — **Near Threatened, 2009**.\n- **Rainbow trout *Oncorhynchus mykiss***: introduced **1969 from India**, again **from England and Japan in 1988**; production began **government farms 1995, private 1998**; commercialised in **Rasuwa/Nuwakot** via NARC+JICA. Optimum culture **below 21 °C**. Now **1,332 MT** [MoALD 2081/82].\n- **Induced breeding**: carps **mature in ponds but fail to spawn** (no riverine/monsoon cues). **Hiralal Chaudhuri, Cuttack (CIFRI), 10 July 1956** — India's National Fish Farmers Day; FAO dates catla success to 1957. **Ovaprim = 20 µg/mL sGnRHa + 10 mg/mL domperidone** (Syndel) [*Conserv Physiol* 2024].\n\n## 4. POULTRY\n- *Gallus gallus domesticus*, **Galliformes: Phasianidae**; ancestor **red junglefowl *G. gallus*** with introgression from *G. sonneratii*, *G. lafayettii*, *G. varius*; domestication ~8,000 yr BP, **multiple maternal origins**. Nepal's native subspecies *G. g. murghi*.\n- **Broiler**: \"most commercial broilers reach slaughter weight between **four and six weeks**.\" **Layer**: Hy-Line Brown approaches **500 eggs to 100 weeks** — quote per-100-weeks, not \"per year.\"\n- **Nepal has exactly three recognised indigenous breeds: Sakini, Ghanti Khuile (naked neck, Na gene), Pwankh Ulte (frizzle)** — dual-purpose, hardy [*Sustainability in Food & Agriculture*, 10.26480/sfna.01.2021.21.24]. NARC ran G0→G3 selection on **Sakini** [*JNARC* 6]. White Leghorn: Tuscany/**Livorno**, Italy.\n- **Agents**: Newcastle/**Ranikhet** = **avian paramyxovirus type 1**, pathotypes lentogenic/mesogenic/velogenic, mortality to 100% [WOAH]. Marek's = ***Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2***, genus *Mardivirus*; enlarged peripheral nerves, **bursa atrophic**; vaccines HVT / CVI988-Rispens, at hatch or **in ovo d18** [MSD Vet Manual]. Fowl pox = *Avipoxvirus*. Coccidiosis = **Apicomplexa**, *Eimeria*: ***E. tenella* = CECA only**, *E. necatrix* = mid small intestine, *E. acervulina* = upper SI, most common.\n- **H5N1 in Nepal: first two outbreaks Jhapa, 2009**; third **Pokhara 2010** (>11,000 birds culled) [Karki 2017, *Nepalese Vet J* 34:26]. Periodic **H5 and H9 since 2009**; **first human case April 2019**; **2023** Bagmati outbreaks, clade **2.3.4.4b** + a reassortant [*Viruses* 2025].\n\n## 5. ANIMAL HUSBANDRY / DAIRY\n- **Lulu** (Manang/Mustang, 2,500–4,500 m): **humpless, predominantly taurine**, with some zebuine and **yak** genes; cows 74–90 cm, 68–153 kg; milk 1–2 kg/d. **Achhami**: zebu, **<1 m at withers**, \"**Naumuthe**\" (nine fists); cows 88 cm/110 kg, bulls 97 cm/150 kg [NARC Animal Breeding Division 2005]; Achham, Bajhang, Bajura, Doti. **Siri**: from Sikkim/Darjeeling/Bhutan, draught.\n- **Buffalo *Bubalus bubalis***: Nepal has the world's **4th-largest** population; supplies **~52% of milk** (MoALD 2081/82; a 2023 paper says 57%). **\"Almost all buffaloes in the country are of the riverine type\"** — swamp type only as wild population at Koshi Tappu. **~65% indigenous = Lime, Parkote, Gaddi**; **Terai buffalo** recently recognised as the 4th indigenous breed; **Murrah + crosses = 35%** [*Animals* 2023, 10.3390/ani13010070]. Lime/Parkote carry cardiac–pulmonary selection signatures (KCNE1, CSF1R, PDGFRB) [*BMC Genomics* 2024].\n- **Goat**: \"four indigenous breeds by altitude — **Chyangra, Sinhal, Khari, Terai**\"; FGF5/EPAS1 high-altitude variants [*Anim Sci J* 2021]. **Sheep**: \"four major breeds — **Bhyanglung, Baruwal, Kage, Lampuchhre** — contributing **>90%** of the population\" [*Sci Rep* 2016, 10.1038/srep29963].\n- **Yak/chauri — the exam point, verified from FAO**: \"Names for the first generation hybrids of yak and cattle include **dzo** in Tibetan areas… and **chauri**, the name used in **Nepal**.\" **\"The female hybrids — F1 and backcross generations — have normal fertility. The males, by contrast, are sterile.\"** \"**F1 males are sterile**… their semen does not contain sperm\" — used as a **teaser bull**; B1/B2 males also sterile; spermatocytes appear only by the 3rd backcross, fertility not assured until the 4th–5th [FAO, *The Yak*, 2nd ed., RAP 2003/06, Ch. 3 & 7]. Hybrid milk **yield exceeds** pure yak but **fat % is usually LOWER** than yak. Nepal yak milk: 17.4% total solids, **6.5% fat**. **Chhurpi** from buttermilk/whey, among the hardest cheeses in the world; Ilam a hub.\n\n## 6. VERMICOMPOSTING\n- ***Eisenia fetida*** is the **accepted** spelling; \"*E. foetida*\" returns SYNONYM [GBIF]. *Eudrilus eugeniae* (Eudrilidae), *Perionyx excavatus* (Megascolecidae), *Lampito mauritii* (South Asia). *E. andrei* is a distinct, hybridising species.\n- **Epigeic** = litter/surface dwellers, no permanent burrows, high intake + reproduction, tolerate shallow bins → **the vermicomposting group**. **Anecic** = deep vertical burrows (*Lumbricus terrestris*) — **confirmed unsuitable**, \"adapt poorly to shallow compost bins and should be avoided.\" **Endogeic** = horizontal burrows in mineral soil, geophagous.\n- Moisture **60%**; castings ~neutral pH, odourless; *E. fetida* tolerates **4.5–32 °C**; stocking **1 kg (~1,000 worms) per 1×1×0.5 m bed**, fed ~half body weight/day; waste **pre-digested 20 days** with dung slurry then mixed with **30% cattle dung** (fresh manure overheats and releases ammonia) [TNAU].\n- **Duration: ~60–140 days (2–4 months)** in published trials — not 4–6 weeks. Finished **C:N ≈ 21**.\n- **NPK [TNAU]: vermicompost N 0.5–1.50%, P 0.1–0.30%, K 0.15–0.56%**, OC 9.5–18%. **FYM (well decomposed): N 0.5%, P₂O₅ 0.2%, K₂O 0.5%.** Castings vs topsoil: 5× available N, 7× available potash. Contains auxins, cytokinins, enzymes, *Azotobacter*/*Rhizobium* + P-solubilisers.\n- Hermaphroditic, normally cross-copulating **but uniparental reproduction is possible**; ~3 cocoons/worm/week, 1–9 eggs each, hatch ~3 weeks at 25 °C.\n- **Vermiwash** = liquid extract from a worm-rich vermibed; **at 5–10% dilution inhibits pathogenic fungal mycelium**; foliar spray initiates flowering [*Heliyon* 2021 review]. **Nepal**: four commercial brands (Divya, Praramva, Bio-Comp, Sathi); okra yield **+126%**, B:C 1.00–1.59; authors note \"limited studies… in Nepal\" [*Heliyon* 2024].\n\n## 7. PEARL CULTURE\n- *Pinctada* is now placed in **Margaritidae** (WoRMS 2026), order Ostreida — **not Ostreidae, and no longer Pteriidae**. ***P. fucata*** is accepted as distinct; \"*P. fucata* = *P. imbricata radiata*\" is **outdated**. *P. margaritifera* (black-lip), *P. maxima* (South Sea). Freshwater: *Lamellidens marginalis* (Unionidae); ***Hyriopsis cumingii* is now *Sinohyriopsis cumingii***.\n- **Shell**: periostracum → prismatic layer of **calcite** → nacreous layer of **aragonite** = hexagonal tablets ~10–20 µm wide × 0.5 µm thick in laminae separated by organic matrix; **conchiolin** is the albuminoid protein; iridescence because platelet thickness ≈ visible wavelength.\n- **Sand myth busted**: \"The commonly held belief that a grain of sand acts as the irritant is **rarely** the case. Typical stimuli include organic material, **parasites**, or damage that **displaces mantle tissue**.\" Historically: sand-grain theory R. Redding 1674; parasite theory von Baer 1830; **pearl-sac theory Saville-Kent 1893**.\n- **Cultured**: bead nucleus (cut from freshwater mussel shell) **plus a mantle graft, the *saibo*** (2×2–4×4 mm) → forms the **pearl sac** that secretes nacre. Marine: into the **gonad**, usually one pearl at a time. Freshwater: **tissue-only/non-nucleated**, into the mantle, up to **25 grafts per valve**. Pearl sac complete by day 5, regular nacre from day 25–30. **>95% of pearls sold are cultured.** Blister/mabe = fused to shell.\n- **Mikimoto Kōkichi** (1858–1954): first **semiglobular/blister** pearls **1892** (Britannica) or **11 July 1893** (Wikipedia) — sources disagree; patent **1896**. **Tatsuhei Mise** (1907 grafting-needle patent) and **Tokichi Nishikawa** independently devised nucleus+graft → the **Mise–Nishikawa method**; both drew on **William Saville-Kent**. Mikimoto gained access via a **1916** patent.\n- **Nepal: pearl culture is NOT practised.** Landlocked → no marine culture; Europe PMC and Crossref return **zero** records for freshwater pearl culture in Nepal. **State this plainly.** China produces **>95% of world freshwater pearls** on *H. cumingii*.\n\n## LAC CULTURE\n- ***Kerria lacca*** (syn. *Laccifer lacca*, *Tachardia lacca*), family **Kerriidae** (not Tachardiidae), **Hemiptera**. Described as *Coccus lacca* by **James Kerr**, Patna, 1781/82. **Resin secreted by the FEMALE**; first instars are \"crawlers\"; the resin tubes are **not** cocoons; >400 host plants.\n- Hosts: ***Butea monosperma*** (palas; \"*B. frondosa*\" is an older synonym), ***Schleichera oleosa*** (kusum — **best quality and yield, palest lac**), ***Ziziphus mauritiana*** (ber). *Flemingia semialata* is an emerging superior host.\n- **Yield/tree: kusum 6–10 kg, ber 1.5–6 kg, dhak 1–4 kg**; **two sticklac crops/year**; **50,000–300,000 insects per kg shellac**. Strains **rangeeni** (Baisakhi crop on *B. monosperma*) and **kusmi**.\n- Chain: sticklac → **seedlac** (3–5% impurity) → shellac flakes / **buttonlac**; wax 3–5%. Aleuritic, jalaric and shellolic acids; **the only commercial resin of animal origin**. **Lac dye = laccaic acids A–E** (anthraquinones) from the **haemolymph**. Uses: varnish, 78 rpm records, sealing wax, confectioner's glaze, citrus coating.\n- **India ≈ at least half of world production, ~20,000 t raw lac/yr**; **Jharkhand** leads, then Chhattisgarh, W. Bengal, Maharashtra; only ~5% of host trees utilised. Institute: ILRI → **ICAR-IINRG, Namkum, Ranchi** → **now renamed National Institute of Secondary Agriculture (NISA)**.\n- **Nepal: effectively absent.** Zero literature; producer lists (India, Thailand, China, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Vietnam, Laos, Sri Lanka, Mexico) **do not include Nepal**.\n\n---\n\n## CLAIMS I COULD NOT VERIFY — DO NOT PRINT\n1. **Exact year of the Thai sacbrood virus epidemic in Nepal** and colony-loss percentages. Only \"since the 1990s\" (Saville 2000) is sourced. Do not print a year.\n2. **Newton hive** — designer (\"Rev. Fr. Newton\"), date, frame count, dimensions. No accessible source. Print only \"Newton hive, a movable-frame hive sized for *A. cerana*.\"\n3. **Gallai et al. 2009 \"€153 billion / 9.5% of crop value.\"** Citation confirmed (*Ecological Economics* 68:810–821) but the figure was not text-verified. Use Klein et al. 2007 (87 crops) instead.\n4. **Achhami = \"the world's smallest cattle.\"** The source says only \"**less than 1 metre at the withers**\" and never claims a world record. Do not print the superlative.\n5. Queen/worker/drone **lifespans**, drones per colony, *A. cerana*-specific development days; propolis and bee-pollen composition; any Nepal-specific monetary pollination value.\n6. **Pupal duration, adult moth lifespan, and total *B. mori* cycle length** (\"45–55 days\"). Only egg (~14 d) and larval (29–30 d) are sourced.\n7. Single-filament **denier** (\"2.5–3 d\") and the \"20/22 denier\" grade; **Karnataka** as India's top silk state (csb.gov.in unreachable); Nepal's raw-silk tonnage/farmer count/import status.\n8. Introduction **years for common carp, Chinese carps and Indian major carps into Nepal**; Houssay (1930, Argentina); K. H. Alikunhi's co-credit; Wova-FH composition; Ovaprim **dosage and latency period**.\n9. Broiler **\"2–2.5 kg at 35–42 days\" and FCR 1.5–1.8**; layer \"280–320 eggs/year\"; point of lay 18–20 wk; egg yield/body weight of indigenous Nepali hens; origin of the name \"Ranikhet\"; ICTV name *Avian orthoavulavirus 1* (WOAH still says APMV-1).\n10. **Khaila** cattle as a recognised breed; Lime vs Parkote horn/chevron/colour distinctions; Chyangra–Changthangi relationship and \"Chyangra Pashmina\" GI/trademark status; *Bos grunniens* vs *B. mutus* split; \"**nak**\" for the female yak; the names dzopkyo/urang/dimjo; chauri altitude range.\n11. Pearl as \"~90% CaCO₃ / 6% conchiolin / 4% water\"; year of Mikimoto's first **spherical** pearl (1905 vs 1907); **ICAR-CIFA Bhubaneswar** as the Indian freshwater-pearl institute (DNS blocked).\n12. **E904** as shellac's E-number; lac crop names **katki, aghani, jethwi** (only *Baisakhi* verified); post-2000 global lac tonnage; Bouché (1977) primary citation; NARC vermicompost programme (narc.gov.np returns 403); FAO **DAD-IS** breed sheets (Firebase app, anonymous REST denied).\n\n## SPECIFIC WRONG FACTS COMMON IN INDIAN/NEPALI BOARD TEXTBOOKS\n1. **\"2,000–3,000 cocoons per kg of raw silk\"** — that is the **per-pound** figure; per kg it is **4,000–7,000**. The single most-copied sericulture error.\n2. **\"4 instars\" or \"5 moults\"** for *B. mori*. Correct: **5 instars, 4 larval moults**.\n3. **Silver and bighead carp diets swapped.** Silver = **phytoplankton**; bighead = **zooplankton**. The commonest pisciculture error. Also: rohu called a bottom feeder, catla called a phytoplankton feeder.\n4. **\"Carps cannot mature in ponds.\"** They mature; they fail to **spawn** without riverine/monsoon cues.\n5. ***Catla catla* / *Aristichthys nobilis*** printed as current names (both synonyms); *Cirrhinus cirrhosus* treated as a synonym of *C. mrigala* (they are separate species).\n6. ***Tor putitora*** called Nepal's **official national fish** (it is not gazetted) or listed as **Critically Endangered** (it is **Endangered**, 2018).\n7. **\"*Apis indica*\"** or \"*A. cerana indica*\" for Nepal's hive bee — obsolete; use *A. cerana*. And *A. laboriosa* listed as a **subspecies of *A. dorsata*** (corrected 2020), or called \"the largest bee\" (it is the largest **honey bee**; *Megachile pluto* is larger).\n8. **Mad honey attributed to *R. ponticum* / *R. luteum*** — those are the **Turkish** Black Sea sources; Nepal's is Himalayan *R. arboreum*.\n9. **\"Only queen larvae are fed royal jelly.\"** All larvae receive it for ~3 days.\n10. ***Varroa jacobsoni*** named as the *A. mellifera* pest — it is ***V. destructor*** since 2000. Bee space given as a single \"9.5 mm\" (range is 6.4–9.5 mm) and the Langstroth patent dated 1851 (discovery 1851, **patent 5 Oct 1852**).\n11. **\"*A. mellifera* introduced to Nepal in the 1980s\"** — best source says **1992**.\n12. ***Antheraea proylei*** presented as a natural species — it is **man-made**, properly ***A.* × *proylei***; and *proylei*/*roylei* are constantly swapped. ***A. mylitta*** is a junior synonym of ***A. paphia***.\n13. **Eri silk described as reeled.** The cocoon is **open-mouthed** → staple fibre, **spun** — which is *why* it is ahimsa silk.\n14. **Nepali hill buffaloes called swamp type** — they are **riverine**.
