Nepal: re-emerged post-2015 earthquake, now all 7 provinces, leading cause of acute undifferentiated fever ⚠ |\n| Japanese encephalitis | JEV, *Flaviviridae* | RNA virus | ***Culex tritaeniorhynchus***; pigs + ardeid birds amplify; humans dead-end | 5–15 d | Fever, altered consciousness, seizures, sequelae; CFR 20–30% | **Live attenuated SA 14-14-2** in Nepal's schedule (Terai campaigns from 2006) |\n| Influenza | Influenza A/B/C/D, *Orthomyxoviridae*, segmented −ssRNA | Virus | Droplets | 1–4 d | Abrupt fever, myalgia, dry cough | Annual reformulated vaccine; drift→epidemics, **shift (reassortment)→pandemics**; oseltamivir |\n\n## PART B — APPLIED MICROBIOLOGY\n\n**Antibiotics.** Fleming, 1928, St Mary's: *Staphylococcus* plate contaminated by a mould he named *Penicillium notatum*. **Confirmed: in 2011 Houbraken, Frisvad & Samson re-identified Fleming's strain (CBS 205.57/NRRL 824) as *Penicillium rubens*** — \"*P. notatum*\" is a synonym of *P. chrysogenum* [*IMA Fungus* 2011]. Florey, Chain (+Heatley) purified it at Oxford 1940–41; **Nobel 1945 = Fleming, Chain, Florey** (Heatley excluded). Waksman coined \"antibiotic\" (1941–42); **streptomycin isolated 1943 by Albert Schatz** in his lab from ***Streptomyces griseus*** — a filamentous **bacterium (actinomycete), not a fungus**; first anti-TB drug; **Nobel 1952 to Waksman alone**. Broad-spectrum: tetracycline, chloramphenicol, ampicillin. Narrow: penicillin G, vancomycin, isoniazid. Bactericidal: β-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, rifampicin. Bacteriostatic: tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol. **Antibiotics fail against viruses** because their targets are prokaryote-only — peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosome, DNA gyrase, folate synthesis; viruses are acellular, wall-less, ribosome-less, and replicate using host machinery (need antivirals: acyclovir, oseltamivir, ART). **AMR** mechanisms: β-lactamases/ESBL/NDM-1, efflux pumps, target change (MRSA *mecA*→PBP2a), reduced permeability; spread by plasmids/conjugation, transposons, integrons; drivers = OTC sale, incomplete courses, veterinary use. ~1.14 million deaths directly attributable globally, 2021 [GRAM, *Lancet* 2024].\n\n**Vaccines.** **Jenner 1796** inoculated James Phipps with **cowpox** matter against smallpox (*Variola virus*) — modern smallpox vaccine actually uses *Vaccinia virus*, a distinct species. **Pasteur** coined \"vaccine/vaccination\" (1881, honouring Jenner) and developed attenuation: fowl cholera 1879, anthrax 1881, **rabies 1885 (Joseph Meister)**. Types: **live attenuated** — BCG, MMR, OPV, JE SA 14-14-2; **killed/inactivated** — IPV (Salk), Hep A, cell-culture rabies, Covaxin; **subunit/recombinant/conjugate** — Hep B (HBsAg), HPV VLP, Hib, PCV, TCV; **toxoid** — tetanus, diphtheria; **mRNA** — Comirnaty BNT162b2; **viral vector** — ChAdOx1 (Covishield), rVSV-ZEBOV (Ebola). **Nepal NIP covers**: TB (BCG), polio (OPV+fIPV), diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, Hep B, Hib (pentavalent), pneumococcal (PCV10), rotavirus, measles–rubella, JE, typhoid (TCV, 2022), plus Td in pregnancy and HPV for girls. **Smallpox: last natural case Oct 1977 (Somalia); eradication declared by the World Health Assembly 8 May 1980.** **Polio: Nepal's last indigenous WPV case Aug 2010; WHO South-East Asia Region certified polio-free 27 March 2014**; globally only WPV2 (2015) and WPV3 (2019) are eradicated, WPV1 endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan; cVDPV remains a risk.\n\n**Immunity.** *Innate* — non-specific, from birth, no memory: skin, mucus, lysozyme, gastric HCl, normal flora, phagocytes, NK cells, complement, interferons, inflammation, fever. *Acquired* — specific, with memory: humoral (B) + cell-mediated (T). *Active* (own response, slow, lasting, memory) vs *passive* (ready-made antibodies, immediate, short, no memory). Natural active = recovery from infection; artificial active = **vaccination**; natural passive = maternal **IgG across placenta** + **IgA in colostrum**; artificial passive = ATS, anti-rabies Ig, antivenom. *Primary response*: lag 5–10 d, low titre, **IgM** first. *Secondary*: lag 1–3 d, 100–1000× titre, **IgG**, higher affinity — the basis of boosters. Antigen = immunogenic molecule (epitope = binding site); antibody = Y-shaped Ig, 2 heavy + 2 light chains, Fab/Fc, 2 antigen-binding sites. **Ig classes:** IgG — most abundant (~75%), secondary response, only one crossing the placenta, opsonisation; IgA — dimeric secretory, mucosal/saliva/tears/colostrum; IgM — pentamer, largest, first in primary response, best complement activator; IgE — least abundant, mast-cell bound, allergy + anti-helminth; IgD — B-cell surface receptor. **B cells** mature in **bone marrow** (bursa of Fabricius only in birds) → plasma + memory cells. **T cells** originate in bone marrow, **mature in the thymus**: Th (CD4+) coordinate via cytokines, Tc (CD8+) kill infected cells with perforin/granzyme, plus memory and regulatory T cells. Thymus = T maturation and self-tolerance, involutes after puberty; bone marrow = haematopoiesis + B maturation (both **primary** lymphoid organs; spleen, nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches are secondary).\n\n**Useful microbes.** *Lactobacillus* (+ *Streptococcus thermophilus*) — ferments **lactose→lactic acid**, coagulating casein: dahi/curd, yoghurt, B₁₂ enrichment. *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* — bread (CO₂), beer/wine, bioethanol. *Aspergillus niger* — citric acid. *Rhizobium* — symbiotic N₂ fixation in legume root nodules (leghaemoglobin shields nitrogenase). *Azotobacter* — free-living aerobic N fixer (*Clostridium pasteurianum* anaerobic). ***Anabaena azollae*/*Nostoc*** — cyanobacteria; *Anabaena* lives in the **dorsal leaf cavities** of *Azolla*, a rice green manure; heterocysts fix N. *Bacillus thuringiensis* — Cry δ-endotoxin protoxin crystals activated in alkaline insect midgut (Bt cotton). *Trichoderma harzianum/viride* — fungal biocontrol + cellulase. **Biogas** — methanogenic **archaea** *Methanobacterium*, *Methanobrevibacter*; hydrolysis→acidogenesis/acetogenesis→methanogenesis; 50–70% CH₄. *Streptococcus* (Gp C, *S. equisimilis*) — **streptokinase**, clot-buster for MI. *Monascus purpureus* — red yeast rice → monacolin K = **lovastatin**. *Penicillium roqueforti* (blue cheese), *P. camemberti* (Camembert); *Propionibacterium freudenreichii* makes Swiss-cheese holes. *Clostridium butylicum/acetobutylicum* — ABE fermentation (butanol, acetone). **SCP**: Spirulina (correctly ***Arthrospira platensis*, a cyanobacterium**), *Methylophilus methylotrophus*, *Fusarium venenatum* (Quorn). **Sewage**: primary = physical settling; secondary = aeration tank where **flocs** (aerobic bacteria + fungal mycelia) cut BOD ~90%; settling tank yields **activated sludge**, part recycled as inoculum, the rest to an anaerobic digester producing biogas.\n\n## SPECIFIC WRONG FACTS IN INDIAN/NEPALI BOARD TEXTBOOKS\n\n1. \"*Salmonella typhi*\" — obsolete. Correct: *Salmonella enterica* subsp. *enterica* serovar Typhi, written ***Salmonella* Typhi**. Also typhoid ≠ typhus.\n2. \"Widal test confirms typhoid\" — it is a low-specificity agglutination test, positive after past infection or vaccination; **blood culture is the gold standard** (bone marrow most sensitive).\n3. \"El Tor is a serotype of cholera\" — El Tor is a **biotype** of serogroup **O1**; Ogawa/Inaba are serotypes; **O139** is a separate serogroup.\n4. \"ORS is just salt and sugar water\" — WHO **reduced-osmolarity** formula (245 mOsm/L: glucose, NaCl, KCl, trisodium citrate); works by glucose–Na⁺ co-transport; it rehydrates, it does not stop the diarrhoea.\n5. \"Ringworm is caused by a worm\" (or by *Rhizopus*) — it is dermatophyte **fungi**: *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, *Epidermophyton*.\n6. \"Rabies treatment = 14 injections around the navel\" — obsolete nerve-tissue Semple vaccine. Current PEP = wound washing + **cell-culture vaccine (4–5 IM or ID)** ± rabies immunoglobulin for Category III. Species name is ***Lyssavirus rabies***, not \"Rabies virus\" as a binomial.\n7. \"Malaria is spread by *Culex*\" / \"male *Anopheles* bites\" — only **female *Anopheles*** (*An. fluviatilis* primary in Nepal). *Culex tritaeniorhynchus* = JE; *Culex quinquefasciatus* = filariasis.\n8. \"*P. vivax* causes cerebral/malignant malaria\" — **falciparum** does (malignant tertian). *P. vivax* = benign tertian, relapses from **hypnozoites**; *P. malariae* = quartan. Textbooks listing only 4 species omit ***P. knowlesi***.\n9. \"The mosquito is the intermediate host of *Plasmodium*\" — reversed. The mosquito is the **definitive host** (sexual/sporogonic cycle); humans are the intermediate host.\n10. \"Kala-azar is spread by houseflies / tsetse fly / *Phlebotomus papatasi*\" — **female *Phlebotomus argentipes*** sandfly in the Indian subcontinent. Also: claiming Nepal is \"WHO-certified kala-azar free\" is wrong — **only Bangladesh has been validated (2023)**.\n11. \"Dengue is spread by night-biting *Culex*\" — ***Aedes aegypti*/*Ae. albopictus*, day-biting**, breeding in clean stored water. \"No dengue vaccine exists\" is also outdated (Qdenga, Dengvaxia) — just not in Nepal's programme.\n12. \"HIV destroys RBCs / all WBCs\" and \"spreads by mosquitoes, handshakes, sharing food\" — HIV infects **CD4+ T-helper cells**, macrophages and dendritic cells only, and is not vector- or casual-contact-borne. **HIV ≠ AIDS**: AIDS is the late stage (CD4 <200/µL).\n13. \"COVID-19 is the virus\" — COVID-19 is the **disease**, SARS-CoV-2 the virus. Also, **Covaxin is inactivated whole-virion**, and **Covishield is a chimpanzee-adenovirus vector** — neither is mRNA or DNA.\n14. \"BCG gives lifelong full protection against TB\" — BCG (attenuated ***M. bovis***, **not** *M. tuberculosis*) mainly prevents miliary TB and TB meningitis in children; protection against adult pulmonary TB is variable (0–80%) and wanes.\n15. \"DOTS is a drug\" / \"MDR-TB = resistant to all drugs\" — DOTS is a five-component **strategy**; **MDR-TB = resistance to at least isoniazid AND rifampicin**; WHO revised the XDR-TB definition in 2021. Nepal's sixth national DR-TB survey (Dec 2022–Jan 2024) found rifampicin resistance in **2.2% of new and 10.1% of previously treated** patients [Europe PMC].\n16. \"Hepatitis B spreads through contaminated food and water\" — that is **A and E**. And \"vaccines exist for all hepatitis types\" is false: **no licensed HCV vaccine**; HDV is prevented via the HBV vaccine; the HEV vaccine (Hecolin) is licensed **only in China**.\n17. \"Penicillin came from *Penicillium notatum*\" — Fleming's strain was re-identified in 2011 as ***Penicillium rubens***; \"*P. notatum*\" is a synonym of *P. chrysogenum*. The **1945 Nobel** went to Fleming, **Chain and Florey** — not Fleming alone.\n18. \"*Streptomyces griseus* is a fungus\" — it is a Gram-positive filamentous **bacterium**. Streptomycin was isolated by **Schatz (1943)**; Waksman coined \"antibiotic\" and took the 1952 Nobel alone.\n19. \"Antibiotics cure colds and flu\" — false; no bacterial cell wall, 70S ribosome, gyrase or folate pathway exists in a virus to target.\n20. \"Jenner coined the word vaccine / used smallpox pus\" — he used **cowpox**; **Pasteur** coined \"vaccine\" in 1881.\n21. \"Smallpox eradicated in 1977/1979\" — last natural case 1977, **declaration 8 May 1980**. \"Polio is eradicated\" — only **WPV2 (2015) and WPV3 (2019)**; Nepal was certified polio-free with WHO SEAR on **27 March 2014**.\n22. \"IgM crosses the placenta\" / \"IgE is most abundant\" — only **IgG** crosses the placenta; **IgG** is most abundant, **IgE** the least.\n23. \"B cells mature in the bursa of Fabricius\" (avian only — in humans, **bone marrow**) and \"T cells are produced in the thymus\" (produced in bone marrow, they **mature** in the thymus).\n24. \"Vaccination gives passive immunity\" — it is **artificial active** immunity; antiserum/immunoglobulin is artificial passive.\n25. \"Spirulina is an alga\" — it is a **cyanobacterium**, correctly ***Arthrospira platensis***. Likewise **methanogens are Archaea, not bacteria**, and *Anabaena azollae* sits in *Azolla*'s **leaf cavities, not roots**.\n26. \"Scrub typhus is louse- or tick-borne\" — it is transmitted by **larval trombiculid mites (chiggers)**; *Orientia tsutsugamushi* left the genus *Rickettsia* in 1995. Louse-borne typhus is *Rickettsia prowazekii*.\n27. \"Tetanus is contagious\" — no; *C. tetani* **spores from soil** enter wounds. Toxoid = active immunity, ATS/TIG = passive.\n28. \"*Lactobacillus* converts milk protein into lactic acid\" — it ferments **lactose (sugar)**; the acid then coagulates casein.\n\n⚠ Re-verify before print against primary sources: Nepal's current TB incidence/case number (WHO Global TB Report country profile — WHO SEAR 2024 only places Nepal in the 146–269/100,000 band and notes Nepal has **entered** the regional MDR/RR-TB high-burden list); Nepal's malaria elimination target year (national NMSP says 2026, regional literature says \"2025–2030\"); exact 2023/2024 dengue and scrub typhus totals (EDCD EWARS bulletins, analysis.edcd.gov.np). agentId: aaa1f5eed6e34e504 (use SendMessage with to: 'aaa1f5eed6e34e504', summary: '<5-10 word recap>' to continue this agent)\n<usage>subagent_tokens: 60496\ntool_uses: 26\nduration_ms: 597537</usage>"}

Scientific Research is a Token of Humankind's Survival (Vladimir Keilis-Borok)** p. 280\n\n\"Unit 15/17/18/20\" are continuous numberings invented by study sites. Section I (Language Development) separately has 20 numbered thematic units — Unit 17 there is \"Globalisation and Diaspora\", Unit 20 is \"Science and Technology\", which is likely where the confusion originates.\n\nAlso: there is **no \"Working with words\"** exercise — that string occurs zero times in the book. Section I units use \"Ways with words\"; Section II literature texts get \"Before Reading\" → \"Reading\" → \"NOTES\" → \"Glossary\" → the three exercise headings.\n\n---\n\n# TEXT A — \"What I Require from Life\", J.B.S. Haldane\n\n## A1. Author — verification results\n\n**CONFIRMED:** John Burdon Sanderson Haldane, b. **5 November 1892, Oxford**; d. **1 December 1964, Bhubaneswar, Orissa, India**, aged 72. Nicknamed \"Jack\"/\"JBS\". Father **John Scott Haldane**, physiologist; mother Louisa Kathleen Trotter; sister the novelist Naomi Mitchison.\n\n**Education — CONFIRMED:** Oxford Preparatory School (Dragon School) from 1897 → **Eton** from 1905 → **New College, Oxford**; first-class honours in mathematical Moderations (1912) and in Greats/classics (1914). His degree was in classics, not science. (Textbook headnote: \"He obtained his M.A. in 1914.\")\n\n**WWI — CONFIRMED:** Commissioned temporary 2nd Lt, **3rd Battalion, Black Watch**, 15 Aug 1914; temp. lieutenant 18 Feb 1915; temp. captain 18 Oct 1915. Trench mortar officer; wounded in France, wounded again in Mesopotamia 1916, then posted to India. Relinquished commission 1 April 1920 retaining rank of captain. Commander's description: \"bravest and dirtiest officer in my Army.\"\n\n**Academic posts — CONFIRMED:** Fellow of New College, Oxford 1919–22; **Reader in Biochemistry, Cambridge 1923–1932** (Britannica gives 1922–32; his own c.1940 autobiographical note says \"at Cambridge from 1922-1932\"); John Innes Horticultural Institution 1927–37; Fullerian Professor of Physiology, Royal Institution 1930–32; FRS 1932; **Professor of Genetics, UCL from 1933**, first Weldon Professor of Biometry 1936; editor of *Journal of Genetics* 1933 until death; team at Rothamsted 1941–44.\n\n**Marxism / Daily Worker — PARTIALLY VERIFIED.** Open supporter of the CPGB from 1937; **joined the Party 1942, left 1950**. 1938: \"I think that Marxism is true.\" Wikipedia says only that \"he wrote many articles for the *Daily Worker*.\" Britannica says he \"assumed editorship of the party's London paper, the *Daily Worker*\" but gives **no years**. Multiple study sources state he wrote a science column for the *Daily Worker* **1937–1950**, and similar pieces for *The Hindu* (Madras) 1957–1964 after moving to India. ⚠️ **I could NOT verify the frequently-repeated claim that he was chairman of the Daily Worker editorial board (1940–1949)** from any authoritative source in this session — treat that as unconfirmed.\n\n**Move to India — YOUR DATE OF 1957 IS DISPUTED.** Wikipedia: he **left UCL and joined the Indian Statistical Institute, Calcutta, in 1956**, citing the Suez Crisis (\"recent acts of the British Government have been violations of international law\"). Britannica: \"**In 1957** Haldane moved to India, where he took citizenship.\" The CDC textbook headnote: \"His political dissent led him to renounce his British citizenship in **1956** and live in India.\" Wikipedia separately dates **Indian citizenship to 1961**. Resigned from ISI Feb 1961 after the Mahalanobis dispute, moved to the new biometry unit in Bhubaneswar. \"Sixty years in socks is enough.\" Safest formulation: *left Britain 1956/57; naturalised Indian citizen 1961.*\n\n**Death — CONFIRMED:** Abdominal pain autumn 1963; **colorectal cancer**; surgery London Feb 1964; recurrence June 1964; terminal by August; died 1 Dec 1964. Willed his body to Rangaraya Medical College, Kakinada. **\"Cancer's a Funny Thing\" first printed in the *New Statesman*, 21 February 1964** — opens \"I wish I had the voice of Homer / To sing of rectal carcinoma.\"\n\n**Works — dates verified against the authoritative bibliography at `jbshaldane.org/bib/JBS-Haldane-Bibliography.html`:**\n\n| Work | Verified |\n|---|---|\n| *Daedalus, or Science and the Future* | **1923** Kegan Paul, London; EP Dutton, New York **1924**. ⚠️ Britannica and the CDC textbook both print \"1924\" — your 1923 is correct for first publication |\n| *Callinicus: A Defence of Chemical Warfare* | 1925 |\n| *Possible Worlds and Other Essays* | **1927** Chatto and Windus ✓ |\n| *Animal Biology* (with Julian Huxley) | 1927 ✓ (textbook/Britannica) |\n| *Science and Ethics* | 1928 |\n| *Enzymes* | 1930 |\n| *The Inequality of Man and Other Essays* | **1932** Chatto and Windus ✓ (US edition = *Science and Human Life*, Harper, 1933) |\n| *The Causes of Evolution* | **1932** Longmans, Green ✓ |\n| *The Marxist Philosophy and the Sciences* | 1938 ✓ |\n| *Science and Everyday Life* | **1939** ✓ (Lawrence and Wishart, London / Macmillan, New York) |\n| *Keeping Cool and Other Essays* | **1940** Chatto and Windus — **US edition = *Adventures of a Biologist*, Harper, New York, 1940** (explicitly noted as the same book) |\n| *Science Advances* | 1947 ✓ |\n| *The Biochemistry of Genetics* | 1954 ✓ |\n| *\"On Being the Right Size\"* | ⚠️ **first published March 1926 in *Harper's Magazine*, pp. 424–427**, not 1928 as marxists.org labels it; reprinted in *Possible Worlds* |\n\n**Scientific contributions — all CONFIRMED:**\n- Population genetics / modern synthesis: one of the three founders of mathematical population genetics with **R.A. Fisher and Sewall Wright**. *A Mathematical Theory of Natural and Artificial Selection*, ten papers, **1924–1934**.\n- Genetic linkage: first demonstration in mammals (with Naomi Mitchison and A.D. Sprunt, paper Dec 1915, *Journal of Genetics*) — James Crow called it \"the most important science article ever written in a front-line trench.\" First in chickens 1921; first in humans (with Julia Bell) 1937.\n- Enzyme kinetics: **Briggs–Haldane (1925)** rederivation of Michaelis–Menten via the quasi-steady-state approximation.\n- Primordial soup: **1929**, \"The Origin of Life\", *The Rationalist Annual* — the primitive ocean as a \"vast chemical laboratory\" holding a \"hot dilute soup\". Now the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis; Haldane conceded Oparin's priority.\n- **Haldane's rule**: sterility in the heterogametic sex of species hybrids.\n- **Haldane's dilemma / \"cost of natural selection\"**: **1957**, \"The cost of natural selection\", *Journal of Genetics* 55(3):511–524.\n- **Kin selection quip — CONFIRMED but flagged**: \"I would lay down my life for two brothers or eight cousins.\" Wikipedia's *Kin selection* article dates the allusion to **1955** (with a briefer 1932 reference) and describes it as a joke — it is an anecdote, not a formal statement in a paper.\n- Others: Haldane's sieve (1927); malaria hypothesis (1949, confirmed by Allison 1954); first human mutation-rate estimate (1932, in *The Causes of Evolution*); coined \"clone\", \"cloning\", \"ectogenesis\"; first proposed the core idea of IVF; \"an inordinate fondness for beetles.\"\n\n## A2. The essay — publication and actual argument\n\n**Publication — PARTIALLY VERIFIED.** The CDC textbook headnote states: *\"The essay 'What I Require from Life' (**1940**), **first published in The Daily Worker**, reflects socialistic convictions demanding democratic activities in work places.\"* Internal evidence supports ~1939–40: it refers to the Madrid siege as \"recent\" (Haldane was there 1936–38), says \"War is spreading at present,\" and hopes it \"will not spread over the world, as it spread from 1914 to 1917.\"\n\n⚠️ **I could NOT independently verify the *Daily Worker* 1940 attribution** from a bibliographic authority. jbshaldane.org's bibliography does not index his journalism; marxists.org's Haldane archive does not hold it; HathiTrust, Google Books and archive.org search-inside are all blocked/quota'd from this environment.\n\n⚠️ **I could NOT verify that it appears in *Keeping Cool and Other Essays* / *Adventures of a Biologist* (1940).** Those are the same book (UK/US editions), both 1940, but I could not obtain a table of contents.\n\n**CONFIRMED:** it is the title essay of **Krishna Dronamraju (ed.), *What I Require from Life: Writings on Science and Life from J.B.S. Haldane*, Oxford University Press, 2009**, xxxvi + 231 pp. A ScienceBlogs review (24 Feb 2009) describes that book as \"a motley collection of Haldane's short essays written for the communist newspaper *The Daily Worker* (1937–1950) and pieces he wrote after he moved to India (1957–1964)\", with introductory material by James Crow, Dronamraju, and the late Arthur C. Clarke.\n\n**THE ACTUAL TEXT.** I have the complete essay as printed in the textbook, pp. 268–271. His argument in order:\n\n1. **Premise — accept the world as given.** Opening line: *\"I have got to accept the universe as it is. I must not require the impossible, and I shall do harm rather than good if I try to imagine perfect beings in a perfect world.\"*\n2. **Peaceful age vs. heroic age.** *\"I was born in a peaceful age, and in my youth I looked forward to a life of peace. Since 1914 I have been living in a heroic age, and I see no prospect of surviving into another epoch of peace and quiet.\"* He assumes food, water, clothes and shelter as given.\n3. **Work** — and a decent wage. *\"Aristotle defined happiness, not as a sum of pleasures, but as unimpeded activity. I want work which is hard but interesting, work of which I can see the fruits.\"* He notes he is exceptionally lucky in being able to choose his own work.\n4. **Freedom**, especially freedom of speech. He would like to write about \"Lord Blank's newspapers, Mr Dash's pills, and Sir John Asterisk's beer, all of which are poisonous\" — *\"The law of libel prevents me from doing so.\"*\n5. **Health.** Doesn't mind occasional illness, *\"But I want to be fit for work and enjoyment in the intervals, and to die when I can work no longer.\"*\n6. **Friendship.** *\"I want the society of equals who will criticize me, and whom I can criticize. I cannot be friends with a person whose orders I have to obey without criticism before or after, or with one who has to obey my orders in a similar way.\"*\n7. **\"These four things are general human needs.\"** (= work, freedom, health, friendship.) For *himself* he additionally **demands adventure** — but rejects gratuitous risk: not mountaineering or motor racing, but self-experimentation and \"wars and revolutions of which I approve.\" Madrid: *\"The only thrill that I got there was from reading Rimbaud's poetry. The satisfaction of adventure is something much more solid than a thrill.\"*\n8. **Desires vs. demands.** *\"There are other things which I desire, but do not demand\"* — a room of his own with books, a motor-car, a daily bath, a garden, bathing-pool, beach or river. *\"But I have not, and I bear up quite happily.\"*\n9. **The pivot to politics.** *\"And I cannot be completely happy while they are unhappy.\"*\n10. **Unemployment.** *\"I am a socialist because unemployment, at least during times of depression, is an essential feature of capitalism.\"* And: *\"I want the workers to see the fruit of their own work not in profits for others, but in their own and their friends' well-being.\"* His personal complaint: his discoveries go unapplied because \"although the community would benefit, no individuals would make profits from their application.\"\n11. **Workers' control.** Hunting and gardening — the work of \"our paleolithic and neolithic ancestors\" — are our favourite leisure occupations, proving work need not be dull. *\"I am a socialist because I want industry to be controlled by the workers. Freedom should begin in the workshop.\"*\n12. **Universal health** — food, housing and medical attendance of the quantity and quality \"which human biology demands and modern technique can supply.\"\n13. **Class and sex subjection.** *\"I want to see the end of class subjection and sex subjection. Only so will the equality which is the condition for fraternity be achieved.\"* Since the barriers are economic, he looks to \"a revolution in the economic field.\"\n14. **Summary of socialism.** *\"…if I live to see capitalism overthrown and the workers in power through most of Europe I shall die happy.\"*\n15. **Peace and security — deliberately omitted.** *\"It is futile to require things which one is most unlikely to obtain. Fascism is a living reality, and fascism, as Hitler and Mussolini explicitly state, and prove by their actions, implies war.\"* Then the key concession: *\"I am a child of my age, and all the worse for being one. **I therefore demand security rather than adventure for others.**\"*\n16. **Also desired:** spread of education and \"an increasing application of scientific methods in all branches of life.\"\n17. **The summing-up.** *\"To sum up, for myself I require food, warmth, work, liberty, health, and friendship. For the society in which I live I require socialism.\"*\n18. **Requirements of death.** Socrates' death is \"the most enviable\" on three counts: he died for his convictions when he could have survived by betraying them; he died at about seventy still in full possession of his faculties, having completed all the work he could reasonably hope to do; *\"And he died laughing. His last words were a joke.\"* Closing: *\"But if I can achieve even two of them I shall have done well, and though my friends may lament me, I trust that they will not pity me.\"*\n\n**Textbook NOTES gloss:** Aristotle (384–322 B.C.); \"Lord Blank, Mr Dash, Sir John Asterisk: names invented for humorous effect\"; Madrid; Rimbaud (1854–1891); Fascism; Hitler (1889–1945); Mussolini (1883–1945); Socrates (470–399 B.C.).\n\n## A3. Counts are 5 / 4 / 3.)*\n\n---\n\n# TEXT B — \"Scientific Research is a Token of Humankind's Survival\", Vladimir Keilis-Borok\n\n## B1. Author — verification results\n\n**CONFIRMED:** **Vladimir Isaakovich Keilis-Borok** (Влади́мир Исаа́кович Ке́йлис-Бо́рок), known as \"Volodya\". Born **31 July 1921, Moscow**; died **19 October 2013, Culver City, California**, aged 92, after an extended illness. Father a jeweller; mother from Lithuania; both Jewish. **Ph.D. in mathematical geophysics, Academy of Sciences, Moscow, 1948.**\n\n**Affiliations — CONFIRMED:**\n- **International Institute of Earthquake Prediction Theory and Mathematical Geophysics, Moscow** — founder, first director, later Director Emeritus and research group leader (Russian Academy of Sciences). ⚠️ Note the textbook headnote writes \"International Institute **for** Earthquake Prediction Theory\" — the institute's own name uses \"**of**\".\n- **UCLA** — arrived **1998 as Regents' Professor**; held a professorship in the **Institute of Geophysics and Planetary Physics** and the **Department of Earth and Space Sciences**; left the faculty 2010; Professor Emeritus until his death. The ICTP book's contributor list (2004) gives exactly: \"Institute of Geophysics and Planetary Physics & Department of Earth and Space Science, University of California, Los Angeles, USA; vkb@ess.ucla.edu\".\n- **ICTP Trieste** — Co-Director and Founder of the Research Programme on non-linear dynamics and earthquake prediction.\n- President, **IUGG 1987–1991**; Vice-President IASPEI 1983–87; founding chairman, International Committee for Geophysical Theory and Computers 1964–79.\n\n**Nuclear test ban — CONFIRMED:** Wikipedia lists him as \"Expert, Technical meetings on the **Nuclear Test Ban Treaty (1960–1990)**\". This matches the essay's own account exactly. ⚠️ The UCLA obituary does **not** mention the test-ban work at all.\n\n**Earthquake prediction — CONFIRMED with caveats:** He called prediction \"the Holy Grail of earthquake science\" (2004, UCLA). His group forecast the Hokkaido (Sept 2003, M8.1) and San Simeon (Dec 2003) earthquakes; a 2004 California forecast for 2005 **failed** (no quake in the predicted window). USGS: \"a legitimate approach to earthquake prediction research. However, the method is unproven.\" He also co-created **\"The Keys to the White House\"** with Allan Lichtman.\n\n**Honours:** First recipient of the **Lewis Fry Richardson Medal (1998)**. Member of seven academies: American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1969), US NAS (1971), Russian Academy of Sciences (1988), Royal Astronomical Society (1989), Austrian Academy of Sciences (1992), Pontifical Academy of Sciences (1994), Academia Europaea (1999). The IUGG created the **Vladimir Keilis-Borok Medal** in 2021.\n\n## B2. The essay — origin and actual argument\n\n**ORIGIN — FULLY VERIFIED.** This is **not** a stand-alone publication. It is:\n\n> Keilis-Borok, V.I. (2004). \"Scientific Research is a Token of Humankind's Survival.\" In **K.R. Sreenivasan (ed.), *One Hundred Reasons to be a Scientist*. Trieste: The Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics, pp. 124–126.** ISBN 92-95003-29-2. Copyright © 2004 ICTP; first edition; printed in Trieste.\n\nThe book was produced for **ICTP's 40th anniversary** and distributed free to high schools worldwide. Sreenivasan (then ICTP Director) wrote the preface, whose theme is \"while our societies have come to depend on technological advances as never before, the interest in basic sciences is diminishing at all levels.\" Each of the ~100 contributions is a short personal piece by a working scientist on why they became one. The essay sits between Kasturirangan's and Joseph B. Keller's contributions.\n\n**THE ACTUAL ARGUMENT.** I have the full original. Its structure is four sections, each opened by an epigraph:\n\n1. **Epigraph:** *\"If you are so clever, why are you so poor?\"* /Popular expression/. Opening question: *\"Why is it that some of us still decide to become scientists, despite the fact that businessmen, lawyers, and doctors enjoy a much higher income?\"*\n   **The Tolstoy answer:** *\"A famous Russian writer L. Tolstoy once wrote that a writer is not merely a person who writes; a writer is a person who cannot live without writing. The same, I believe, is true for a scientist. **Science is an exciting adventure where major reward comes from the discovery itself. What you get instead of big money is freedom, camaraderie, independence.** The honours and promotions will depend on yourself more than in the other occupations. And you will have the overwhelming feeling of uncovering yet another one of nature's mysteries.\"*\n\n2. **Epigraph:** *\"An instant understanding, the efficiency of thought and action, and a good feeling that comes when the like-minded people work together…\"* /F. Press/.\n   **The Geneva narrative (the core of the essay).** 1960, height of the Cold War; he was in Moscow on the theory of seismic waves, absorbed in the mathematics, not thinking about real life. Summons from the President of the (then Soviet) Academy of Sciences: a letter from the Palace of Nations in Geneva, where technical experts from the USSR, US and UK met behind closed doors; the American scientist **Frank Press** had quoted his work while arguing with Moscow experts. *\"And, to my great surprise, I found myself in Geneva.\"*\n   Context: *\"every man, woman, and child on the Earth lived under the threat of annihilation by nuclear weapon\"*; the 20-minute rocket flight time; *\"Mutually Assured Destruction\", with ominous acronym \"MAD\", was for some years the only thin thread protecting all of us from the common fatal fate.*\n   The formal problem: if the powers sign a test ban and one secretly conducts an underground nuclear explosion, **how can the others detect the violation?** This connects directly to seismic-wave theory, since underground explosions produce tremors resembling earthquakes. *\"Suddenly, my theoretical knowledge had a direct application in the area of survival of the humankind.\"*\n   **The unifying claim:** *\"In the atmosphere of the ongoing Cold War… scientists and engineers from the opposite sides of the Iron Curtain had to find a solution, which outwardly seemed impossible, given all our differences in cultural background. **What saved us was a clear and obvious distinction. We were all scientists. We were able to work out a common language, based on respect to hard evidence, undisputable ranking by expertise only, and persistent self-criticism.**\"* This allowed politicians to reach \"one of the most important decisions of their times: nuclear test ban.\"\n   **The lesson:** *\"This episode taught me that as a scientist I have people all over the world who think and interact the way I do. It taught me never to feel lonely abroad. And, above all, it taught me that **while there is science, there is hope of survival and well-being for all of us**.\"*\n\n3. **Epigraph:** *\"Were Napoleon as wise as Spinoza, he would spend his life at the attic writing four volumes of essays\"* /A. France/.\n   **Scientists are the most practical people in the world.** He concedes the absent-minded-professor lore (a great mathematician leaving home \"wearing shoes from two different pairs\") then rebuts it: *\"All new technologies, all new brands of industry from defence to entertainment stem from fundamental research.\"* Past examples: antibiotics, electronics, biotechnology, synthetic fibres, the green revolution, genetic forensic diagnosis. Future: *\"new sources of energy; new mineral deposits; **efficient defence from terrorism**; cure from cancer; new forms of transportation.\"* Theoretical physicists are headhunted by financial institutions; biologists found pharmaceutical companies. *\"So, knowledge of basic science will give you a head start in whatever career you choose.\"*\n\n4. **Epigraph:** */These dangers/ \"are a threat to civilization's survival, as great as ever posed by Hitler, Stalin, or the atom bomb\"* /J. Wiesner/.\n   **Disaster.** *\"the very survival of our civilisation is threatened by natural and man-made disasters. Among them are earthquakes, self-inflicted destruction of megacities, environmental catastrophes, economic and social crises.\"* Any one can *\"cause up to a million of casualties, render large part of our world inhabitable, trigger global economic depression, or a war in a 'hot' region. Such dangers keep growing, although trillions dollars a year are spent to contain them.\"*\n   *\"**The hope and the responsibility for breaking the stalemate rest not on the money but on intellectual resources**, though the money is more popular, according to the French proverb: 'Nobody is satisfied with his wealth, everybody is satisfied with his wisdom.' Only the basic research can create a springboard for developing new disaster preparedness industry.\"*\n\n5. **Epigraph:** *\"Ours is the time of contest over issues not completely understood\"* /McGeorge Bundy/.\n   **Conclusion:** *\"Scientific research in an exciting venture into the great unknown and the token of humankind's survival. It is the scientists with their tools that are up to the challenge and can ensure that we all safely move with the time.\"* Final caveat: *\"Finally I have to remind you that the science is not the beginning and the end. More important for the humankind and for each individual are the human qualities. **However, if humanly used, science is their indispensable guardian and caretaker.**\"*\n\n**Your hypothesis list, checked:**\n| Your belief | Verdict |\n|---|---|\n| Joy/beauty of scientific research | ✓ — freedom, camaraderie, independence, \"the discovery itself\" |\n| Research done by an international community across borders | ✓ — \"I have people all over the world who think and interact the way I do\" |\n| Scientists communicate across political divides | ✓ — the central Geneva episode |\n| Role of science in preventing catastrophe (earthquakes, nuclear war, terrorism) | ✓ — all three named explicitly |\n| Science as a unifying human activity | ✓ — \"We were all scientists… a common language\" |\n| **Risk of losing young scientists** | ✗ **NOT IN THE ESSAY.** That theme is in **Sreenivasan's preface** to the ICTP volume (\"the interest in basic sciences is diminishing at all levels… particularly distressing is the lukewarm interest shown towards sciences by the brightest students at the high school level\"), not in Keilis-Borok's contribution. |\n\n**Two further cautions about Nepali study notes:** several sites (e.g. subodhbhattarai.com) attach to this essay the Churchill line *\"This is not the beginning of the end, it's the end of the beginning\"* and the claim that \"earthquakes can and should be predicted\" / \"the Holy Grail of earthquake science.\" **Neither appears in the essay.** Those come from Keilis-Borok's separate earthquake-prediction work and a 2004 UCLA press release. The essay does not argue for earthquake prediction at all — earthquakes appear only as (a) the source of the seismic waves he studied and (b) one item in the disaster list. Also, one site misquotes \"major reward**s** come\" — the original is singular, \"major reward comes.\"\n\n**Textbook vs. original — the CDC text is faithful but lightly edited:**\n- The opening epigraph is run inline into the first paragraph: \"If you are so clever, why are you so poor? (Popular expression)\".\n- Attribution format changed from `/F. Press/` to `(F. Press)`.\n- **The A. France (Napoleon/Spinoza) and J. Wiesner epigraphs are cut entirely.**\n- Two errors in the ICTP text are silently fixed: \"a greatest mathematician of **out** time\" → \"our time\"; \"Scientific research **in** an exciting venture\" → \"**is** an exciting venture.\"\n- Quotation marks changed to curly singles for 'Mutually Assured Destruction' and 'MAD'.\n\n**Textbook NOTES gloss:** Iron Curtain; L. Tolstoy; \"Mc George Bundy: He was United States National Security Advisor to presidents John F. Kennedy and Lyndon Johnson.\" *(Sic — the book splits \"McGeorge\" into two words.)*\n\n## B3. Textbook-internal oddities, all genuine and worth knowing before you answer: \"Keilis Borok's\" in Understanding-c is printed unhyphenated with a straight apostrophe; the exercise quotes \"If you are **clever**\" while the essay body reads \"If you are **so** clever\"; Understanding-d asks about a decision taken \"**before** Geneva Summit\" although the essay describes the test ban as the outcome that Geneva enabled; Reference-to-the-context d reads \"scientific research is **the** humankind's survival\"; and c-ii reads \"help survival of the mankind.\")*\n\n---\n\n# SUMMARY OF WHAT I COULD **NOT** VERIFY\n\n1. **Haldane as chairman/editor of the *Daily Worker* editorial board, and the years.** Britannica says \"assumed editorship\" with no dates; Wikipedia says only that he wrote many articles. The Threepenny Review's own sample page carried the HTML title \"Threepenny: Sacks, On Libraries,\" with the issue line \"Fall 2014\" printed above the title and byline, followed by the full text of the essay and a closing contributor note describing Sacks as \"a writer and neurologist\" and author of a dozen books.\n\n- Live URL (now 404 — the magazine migrated to WordPress and the old `/samples/` tree is gone): `https://www.threepennyreview.com/samples/sacks_f14.html`\n- **Working archived copy:** `http://web.archive.org/web/20140905232130/http://www.threepennyreview.com/samples/sacks_f14.html` (Wayback capture 5 Sept 2014)\n- Located via the Wayback CDX API: `http://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=threepennyreview.com*&filter=urlkey:.*sacks.*` — which returns exactly two Sacks sample pages, `sacks_f14.html` (this essay) and `sacks_w05.html` (\"On Memory,\" Winter 2005).\n\nThe magazine's naming convention (`_f14` = Fall 2014, matching `berry_f14`, `boland_f14`, `dyer_f14`, `buckingham_f14`, `haas_f14` in the same CDX listing) independently corroborates the Fall 2014 issue.\n\n**COULD NOT VERIFY:** the *volume and issue number* of that Fall 2014 issue. So \"Fall 2014\" is solid; a Vol./No. citation is not something I could substantiate.\n\n**Book collection:** *Everything in Its Place: First Loves and Last Tales* — Oliver Sacks's **posthumous final collection, 2019**.\n\n- Sacks's official site confirms the book, the subtitle, the year 2019, the description \"Published posthumously in 2019,\" and — importantly — lists **\"Libraries\" explicitly among the book's topics** (alongside Alzheimer's, Botany, Chemistry, Dementia, Gardens, Mental Health, Schizophrenia, Tourette's). Knopf** (US, 23 April 2019, ISBN 978-0-451-49289-0), **Picador / Pan Macmillan** (UK, 2 May 2019, ISBN 9781509821792), **Knopf Canada**, and **Companhia das Letras** (Brazil). Sources: `https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=Everything+in+Its+Place+Oliver+Sacks` and `https://openlibrary.org/works/OL20150464W/editions.json`\n- Wikipedia's Sacks bibliography lists: *Everything in Its Place: First Loves and Last Tales* (2019), ISBN 978-0451492890. Source: `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Sacks`\n\n**PARTIALLY VERIFIED / FLAGGED:** I could **not** obtain the book's actual table of contents, so I cannot confirm whether the chapter inside the book is headed **\"Libraries\"** (without \"On\") or **\"On Libraries.\"** Open Library holds no `table_of_contents` field for any of the nine editions; the Internet Archive's scanned copy (`archive.org/details/everythinginitsp0000oliv`, Picador 2019) exposes no search-inside API to me; Google Books API returned HTTP 429 quota-exceeded; the Penguin Random House product page 404'd; Library of Congress returned 403. Given that oliversacks.com's topic tag reads bare \"Libraries,\" the book chapter is *most likely* titled \"Libraries\" — but treat that as inference, not verification.\n\n**Net answer on provenance:** both of your hypotheses are correct and they are not alternatives. The essay was **first published in The Threepenny Review, Fall 2014** (while Sacks was alive — he died August 2015), and was **subsequently collected in the posthumous *Everything in Its Place: First Loves and Last Tales*, Knopf/Picador, 2019**. The Nepal CDC textbook title \"On Libraries\" matches the *Threepenny Review* form of the title.\n\n---\n\n## 2. FULL CONTENT — ACTUAL STRUCTURE, IN ORDER\n\nThis is my summary of the archived Threepenny Review text. The essay is short — roughly 1,650 words in sixteen paragraphs — and is purely autobiographical until its final movement, when it turns into an argument. I am summarising rather than reproducing, with only the short verbatim fragments you asked for marked as QUOTE.\n\n### Movement I — The home library (paras 1–4)\n\n**Para 1 — the oak-panelled room.** Sacks opens in childhood: his favourite room at home was the library, a large oak-panelled room with bookcases on all four walls and a solid table in the middle for writing and studying. He then inventories that room by owner:\n- His **father's** special library — his father was a **Hebrew scholar**.\n- **All of Ibsen's plays** — with the biographical detail that his parents had originally met in a **medical students' Ibsen society**.\n- On a single shelf, the **young poets of his father's generation, many killed in the Great War**.\n- On the lower shelves, placed so the child could reach them, the **adventure and history books belonging to his three older brothers**.\n- It was here he found ***The Jungle Book***; he QUOTE \"identified deeply with Mowgli\" and used Mowgli's adventures as a launching point for his own fantasies.\n\n**Para 2 — his mother's separate bookcase**, in the lounge, not the library: **Dickens, Trollope, and Thackeray**; **Bernard Shaw's plays in pale green bindings**; an entire set of **Kipling bound in soft morocco**; a beautiful **three-volume set of Shakespeare**; a **gilt-edged Milton**; and other books, mostly poetry, that his mother had won as **school prizes**.\n\n**Para 3 — one sentence, and a joke.** The **medical books** were kept in a special **locked cabinet in his parents' surgery** — but, he notes parenthetically, the key was in the door, so it was easy to unlock.\n\n**Para 4 — absorption.** The oak-panelled library was to his eyes the quietest and most beautiful room in the house, and it **vied with his little lab** as his favourite place to be. He would curl up in a chair and lose all sense of time. This is the source of the textbook's first exercise question: whenever he was late for lunch or dinner, he could be found in the library, completely absorbed by a book. He **learned to read early, at three or four**, and books and the library are among his **first memories**.\n\n> **Note for your purposes:** the exercise answer circulating on Nepali sites that says he was found \"in his little laboratory\" is a misreading — the essay says he was found *in the library*, and separately mentions that the library competed with his lab for his affection.\n\n### Movement II — The public library (paras 5–6)\n\n**Para 5 — the Ur-library.** He calls the **Willesden Public Library**, his own local public library, QUOTE \"the Ur-library\" for him. His house was a **five-minute walk** from it; he spent many of the happiest hours of his growing-up years there; and it was there, he says, that he received his **real education**.\n\n> **Correction to your brief:** the essay names **Willesden** only. **\"Hampstead\" does not appear anywhere in this essay.** You may be thinking of The Hall School, Hampstead, which Sacks attended as a boy (documented on Wikipedia, not in this essay), or of his other memoir writing. Do not attribute a Hampstead library to \"On Libraries.\"\n\n**Para 6 — the anti-school passage.** This is the essay's most-quoted paragraph and the source of two textbook questions. He disliked school, sitting in class, receiving instruction; information QUOTE \"seemed to go in one ear and out by the other.\" He could not be passive — he had to be active, learn for himself, learn what he wanted, in the way that suited him best.\n\nThe famous line: QUOTE **\"I was not a good pupil, but I was a good learner.\"**\n\n> **IMPORTANT TEXTUAL POINT.** The archived Threepenny Review text reads **\"a good learner.\"** The Nepal CDC textbook and every Nepali study site render the exercise question as **\"I was not a good pupil, but I was a good listener.\"** Either the book version differs from the magazine version, or — more likely — the textbook introduced a transcription error that has propagated through every set of Nepali notes. Flag this: the exercise as printed says *listener*; the verifiable published text says *learner*. \"Learner\" also makes far better sense of the surrounding argument, which is explicitly about *not* absorbing things by being talked at.\n\nHe continues: in Willesden Library, and all the libraries that came later, he roamed the shelves and stacks, had the freedom to select whatever he wanted, to follow the paths that fascinated him, QUOTE \"to become myself.\" At the library he felt **free** — free to look at tens of thousands of books, free to roam, and free to enjoy the special atmosphere and the QUOTE \"quiet companionship of other readers,\" all of them, like himself, on quests of their own.\n\n### Movement III — School and the Science Museum (para 7)\n\nAs he got older his reading tilted towards the **sciences, especially astronomy and chemistry**. He went to **St. Paul's School at the age of twelve**. Its general library was called the **Walker Library** — excellent, and QUOTE \"particularly heavy in history and politics\" — but it could not supply the science and especially chemistry books he now hungered for.\n\nSo, with a **special testimonial from one of the school masters**, he obtained a ticket to the **library of the Science Museum**, where he devoured:\n- the many volumes of **Mellor's *Comprehensive Treatise on Inorganic and Theoretical Chemistry***\n- the even longer **Gmelin's *Handbook of Inorganic Chemistry***\n\n> Note the actual reason for the science bias: it is straightforwardly that his interests had narrowed to astronomy and chemistry. The Nepali model answer claiming he was motivated because \"all the children used to dream of being astronauts\" is invented — there is no such statement in the essay, and it is anachronistic for a boy at school in the mid-1940s.\n\n### Movement IV — Oxford: the Bodleian and Theodore Hook (paras 8–9)\n\n**Para 8 — the two great university libraries.** At university he had access to Oxford's two great university libraries, the **Radcliffe Science Library** and the **Bodleian**, which he describes as a wonderful general library that could **trace itself back to 1602**.\n\n**The Theodore Hook anecdote** — get these details right, because the textbook exercise asks about it:\n- It was **in the Bodleian** that he stumbled on the now-obscure and forgotten works of **Theodore Hook**.\n- Hook was **greatly admired in the early nineteenth century** for his **wit** and his **genius for theatrical and musical improvisation**.\n- He was **said to have composed more than five hundred operas on the spot**. (Sacks reports this as a claim — \"he was said to have\" — not as fact.)\n- Sacks became so fascinated that he decided to write a sort of **biography or \"case-history\"** of Hook. The phrase QUOTE \"case-history\" is his, in scare quotes — a nice early glimpse of the form he would later make his own.\n- He adds that **no other library apart from the British Museum Library** could have supplied the materials he needed, and that the **tranquil atmosphere of the Bodleian** was perfect for writing.\n\n> **On the \"prize essay\" in your brief: NOT IN THIS ESSAY.** The Threepenny Review text says nothing about a prize, a prize essay, or winning anything for the Hook piece. The only \"prize\" in the whole essay is the school prizes his *mother* won, which is how she acquired some of her poetry books (para 2). Sacks did write elsewhere (in *Uncle Tungsten* / *On the Move*) about Oxford prize essays, but if your source claims \"On Libraries\" contains a prize-essay anecdote, that is an import from another text. **Unverified — treat as absent.**\n\n**Para 9 — Queen's College, the longest paragraph in the essay (~260 words).** This is the library he says he **most loved at Oxford** — QUOTE \"our own library at the Queen's College.\"\n- The **magnificent library building had been designed by Christopher Wren**.\n- **Beneath it**, in QUOTE \"an underground maze of heating pipes and shelves,\" lay the **vast subterranean holdings**. He later calls these the **\"catacombs\"** and the **\"vaults.\"**\n- Holding **ancient books, incunabula**, in his own hands was a new experience.\n- He particularly adored **Gesner's *Historiae Animalium* (1551)**, richly illustrated, mentioning **Dürer's drawing of a rhinoceros**; and **Agassiz's four-volume work on fossil fishes**.\n- There he saw **all of Darwin's works in their original editions**.\n- In the stacks he found and fell in love with all the works of **Sir Thomas Browne** — naming ***Religio Medici***, ***Hydriotaphia*** (printed \"Hydrotaphia\" on the page), and ***The Garden of Cyrus (The Quincunciall Lozenge)***. He remarks how absurd some of it was, but how magnificent the language.\n- When Browne's QUOTE \"classical magniloquence\" became too much, he could switch to the QUOTE \"lapidary cut-and-thrust\" of **Swift**, all of whose works were also there in original editions.\n- Crucially: **all these books were freely available** — *not* in a special, locked-away rare books enclave, but **just sitting on the shelves**, as (he imagined) they had done since their original publication.\n- Whereas he had grown up on the **nineteenth-century** works his parents favoured, it was the Queen's catacombs that introduced him to **seventeenth- and eighteenth-century literature — Johnson, Hume, Pope, and Dryden**. (The archived page hyphenates it as \"John-son,\" a scanning artefact of the original print line break.)\n- His conclusion: it was in the vaults of the Queen's College that he really gained a sense of **history, and of his own language**.\n\n> **Correction to the Nepali model answer:** the textbook notes say the library held editions QUOTE \"from Gesner to Darwin,\" which is a fair paraphrase; but the notes' claim that Wren designed the building \"in a form of palace\" is not in the text, and Sacks says Wren designed the *library building*, with the holdings *beneath* it.\n\n### Movement V — New York and the Einstein library (paras 10–12)\n\n**Para 10.** He **first came to New York City in 1965**. He had a **horrid, pokey little apartment** with almost no surfaces to read or write on — he was just able, QUOTE \"holding an elbow awkwardly aloft,\" to write **some of *Migraine* on top of the refrigerator**. He **longed for spaciousness**. Fortunately the library at the **Albert Einstein College of Medicine**, where he worked, had spaciousness in abundance. He would sit at a large table to read or write, then wander the shelves and stacks — never knowing what his eyes might alight on, sometimes discovering QUOTE \"unexpected treasures, lucky finds,\" and bringing them back to his seat. This is the essay's case for **serendipity**.\n\n**Para 11 — the social argument, and the one detail people always miss.** Though the library was quiet, **whispered conversations** might start in the stacks — two readers, perhaps, searching for the same old book, the same **bound volumes of *Brain* from 1890** — and conversations could lead to **friendships**. Everyone was absorbed in their own world, and yet there was a sense of **community, even intimacy**. And then the pivotal claim: the **physicality of books** — along with their **places and their neighbours on the bookshelves** — was part of this camaraderie: handling books, sharing them, passing them between readers, QUOTE \"even seeing the names of previous readers and the dates they took books out.\"\n\n**Para 12 — the turn.** QUOTE \"But a shift was occurring by the 1990s.\" He kept visiting the library, sitting at a table with a **mountain of books** in front of him, but **students increasingly ignored the bookshelves, accessing what they needed with their computers**. Few went to the shelves any more. The books, so far as the students were concerned, were **unnecessary**. And because the majority of users were no longer using the books themselves, **the college decided, ultimately, to dispose of them**.\n\n> This is the answer to textbook question (h). Note the causal chain Sacks draws — students stop using shelves → the institution reads that as evidence the books are surplus → the institution discards them. The disposal is presented as an *institutional decision driven by usage statistics*, not as an inevitable consequence of technology.\n\n### Movement VI — The closing paragraph (para 13)\n\nThe final substantive paragraph is the complaint, and it is one paragraph, tightly built:\n\n- He **had no idea this was happening** — not only at the AECOM library but **in college and public libraries all over the country**.\n- He was **horrified** when he visited the library **a couple of months ago** and found the shelves, **once overflowing, sparsely occupied**.\n- Over the last few years **most of the books have been thrown out**, QUOTE \"with remarkably little objection from anyone.\"\n- The strongest sentence in the essay: he felt that QUOTE **\"a murder, a crime had been committed — the destruction of centuries of knowledge.\"**\n- **Seeing his distress, a librarian reassured him that everything \"of worth\" had been digitized.** Sacks puts QUOTE \"of worth\" in scare quotes — the quotation marks are doing the arguing.\n- His reply, in two parts: **he does not use a computer**; and he is **deeply saddened by the loss of books, even bound periodicals**, because there is something **irreplaceable about a physical book** — QUOTE \"its look, its smell, its heft.\"\n- He closes by circling back: he thought of how the library **once cherished \"old\" books** and **had a special room for old and rare books**; and how, **in 1967, rummaging through the stacks, he had found an 1873 book, Edward Liveing's *Megrim*, which inspired him to write his own first book.**\n\n**Para 14 — contributor note** (magazine apparatus, not the essay): identifies Sacks as a writer and neurologist and author of a dozen books including *Hallucinations*, *Musicophilia*, *Awakenings*, *The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat*, and *The Mind's Eye*.\n\n> **The closing detail is the load-bearing one and is easy to get wrong.** The book is **Edward Liveing's *Megrim* (1873)** — a Victorian monograph on migraine — found by **rummaging in the stacks in 1967**, and the \"own first book\" it inspired is **Sacks's *Migraine*** (published 1970). The rhetorical point is exact: the very kind of old, unrequested, apparently worthless volume that a digitisation-by-usage-statistics policy would discard first is the one that launched his entire writing career. Wikipedia independently corroborates the Liveing connection: it records that an epiphany while reading a book by the nineteenth-century migraine doctor **Edward Liveing** inspired Sacks to chronicle neurological disorders and to become QUOTE \"the 'Liveing of our Time'\" (`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Sacks`). Note also the neat internal circuit: *Migraine* is mentioned in para 10 as the book he wrote on top of a refrigerator, and in para 13 as the book a library discovery made possible.\n\n---\n\n## 3. HIS EXACT FINAL POSITION ON MODERN LIBRARIES AND DIGITISATION\n\nSacks's complaint is **not** anti-digital in the abstract. He never argues that digitisation is bad, never says text should not be scanned, and never claims screens cannot convey information. Precisely stated, his position has four components, all present in the last two paragraphs:\n\n1. **The object of his anger is disposal, not digitisation.** What horrified him was **empty shelves** — books physically **thrown out**. Digitisation is the *justification* offered for the discarding, and it is the justification he rejects, not the technology.\n\n2. **He rejects the librarian's premise that digitisation is substitution.** The librarian's reassurance that everything QUOTE \"of worth\" had been digitized contains two claims Sacks denies: that worth can be determined in advance (his own career refutes it — *Megrim*, 1873, unread in the stacks, would have failed any worth test), and that a digital surrogate is equivalent to the object.\n\n3. **Three things are lost that a scan cannot carry:**\n   - **The physical book itself** — QUOTE \"its look, its smell, its heft\" — which he calls **irreplaceable**.\n   - **Serendipity and adjacency.** A shelf lets your eye alight on what you did not know to ask for; a search box only returns what you already knew to type. This is why he stresses books' QUOTE \"places and their neighbors on the bookshelves.\"\n   - **Community and the traces of other readers.** Whispered conversations in the stacks becoming friendships; the names of previous borrowers and their dates written in the book. A library, for him, is a social and historical space, not a delivery mechanism.\n\n4. **The moral register is deliberately extreme, and the target is institutional complacency.** He calls it QUOTE \"a murder, a crime\" and QUOTE \"the destruction of centuries of knowledge,\" and he pointedly notes it happened QUOTE \"with remarkably little objection from anyone.\" The sharpest edge of the essay is aimed at that silence — an institution quietly destroying its holdings because a usage metric said nobody was looking, and nobody raising a hand.\n\nHe also states plainly, and without apology, that **he does not use a computer** — which is both a personal fact and a rhetorical position: he is refusing to accept the trade as a trade.\n\n---\n\n## 4. BIOGRAPHY OF OLIVER SACKS\n\nAll of the following is from the Wikipedia article, retrieved as raw wikitext on 27–28 September 2026: `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Sacks` (via `https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oliver_Sacks&action=raw`), plus his official site `https://oliversacks.com`.\n\n**Name and dates.** **Oliver Wolf Sacks, CBE, FRCP** — born **9 July 1933** in **Cricklewood, London, England**; died **30 August 2015** in **New York City, USA**, aged **82**.\n\n**Nationality and description.** **British** — a **neurologist, naturalist, historian of science, and writer**. He moved to the United States and spent most of his career there; Wikipedia categorises him as an English expatriate in the United States.\n\n**Family.** Youngest of **four children** of Jewish parents. Father **Samuel Sacks**, a Lithuanian Jewish physician and (per the essay) a Hebrew scholar. Mother **Muriel Elsie Landau** (d. 1972), **one of the first female surgeons in England**, and one of eighteen siblings; she would sometimes bring home deformed foetuses and dissect them with her son so he could learn anatomy. He had an extensive family of eminent scientists and physicians, and was first cousin to the Nobel laureate economist **Robert Aumann** and the Israeli statesman **Abba Eban**. (Note: contrary to a widespread claim, he was **not** related to Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.)\n\n**Early life.** In **December 1939**, aged six, he and his brother Michael were **evacuated from London to escape the Blitz**, sent to a boarding school in the English Midlands where he remained until **1943** — the experience recounted in *Uncle Tungsten*. From his return home at ten, under his Uncle Dave's tutelage, he became an intensely focused **amateur chemist**. He attended **The Hall School, Hampstead**, and then **St Paul's School, London**, where he formed lifelong friendships with **Jonathan Miller** and **Eric Korn**.\n\n**Medical training.** He entered **The Queen's College, Oxford, in 1951** to read medicine, and received his **medical degree in 1958** (BA, BM BCh, Oxford). He stayed an extra year to do research after being captivated by lectures on the history of medicine and nutrition by **Hugh Macdonald Sinclair**. He then began **pre-registration house officer rotations at Middlesex Hospital**, London — following his eldest brother Marcus. He subsequently moved to the United States: **internship at Mt. Zion Hospital, San Francisco**, and **residency in neurology and neuropathology at UCLA**. In San Francisco he became a lifelong friend of the poet **Thom Gunn**, and experimented heavily with recreational drugs — an episode he wrote about in a 2012 *New Yorker* piece and in *Hallucinations*.\n\n**Medical specialism.** **Neurology** (with **neuropathology** in his residency; later also appointed in psychiatry at Columbia). The infobox lists his specialism simply as neurology.\n\n**Where he worked.**\n- **Beth Abraham Hospital**, chronic-care facility in **the Bronx** — where he worked with survivors of the 1920s **encephalitis lethargica** (\"sleeping sickness\") epidemic who had been unable to move for decades. This became *Awakenings*. His work there also laid the foundation for the **Institute for Music and Neurologic Function**, to which he was honorary medical advisor; it gave him its first **Music Has Power Award** in 2000 and a second in 2006 marking his forty years at Beth Abraham.\n- **Albert Einstein College of Medicine** (Yeshiva University) — instructor, later **professor of clinical neurology, 1966–2007**. *This is the AECOM library of the essay's final movement.*\n- **New York University School of Medicine** — 1992–2007, and again from 2012 as professor of neurology and consulting neurologist in its epilepsy centre.\n- **Columbia University Medical Center** — from July 2007, professor of neurology and psychiatry.\n- Also **University of Warwick**, and the **Little Sisters of the Poor**. He served on the boards of **The Neurosciences Institute** and the **New York Botanical Garden**, and maintained a busy hospital-based practice in New York, accepting only a very limited number of private patients despite great demand.\n\n**Major books and what each is about** (from the Wikipedia bibliography, with subjects):\n- ***Migraine*** (1970) — his first book, on migraine; inspired by finding Liveing's *Megrim* (1873) in the Einstein stacks, and partly written on top of a refrigerator.\n- ***Awakenings*** (1973) — the Beth Abraham survivors of encephalitis lethargica and their response to L-DOPA. Adapted into the **Academy Award-nominated 1990 film** starring **Robin Williams** and **Robert De Niro**.\n- ***A Leg to Stand On*** (1984) — his own injury and the neurological experience of a limb becoming alien to its owner.\n- ***The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat*** (1985) — his most famous book; case histories of patients with neurological disorders. Became the basis of an **opera** of the same name.\n- ***Seeing Voices: A Journey Into the World of the Deaf*** (1989) — deaf culture and sign language.\n- ***An Anthropologist on Mars*** (1995) — seven longer case studies, including autism (the title comes from Temple Grandin).\n- ***The Island of the Colorblind*** (1997) — hereditary achromatopsia on Pingelap, and neurological disease in Guam.\n- ***Uncle Tungsten: Memories of a Chemical Boyhood*** (2001) — his **first autobiography**, on his wartime childhood and his chemistry obsession.\n- ***Oaxaca Journal*** (2002) — travelogue of a ten-day trip with the **American Fern Society** to Oaxaca, Mexico, in 2000.\n- ***Musicophilia: Tales of Music and the Brain*** (2007) — music and the nervous system.\n- ***The Mind's Eye*** (2010) — vision, and his own loss of stereoscopic vision.\n- ***Hallucinations*** (2012) — hallucination across conditions, including his own drug experiences.\n- ***On the Move: A Life*** (2015) — his **second autobiography**, published months before his death.\n- ***Gratitude*** (2015, posthumous) — the four late essays written as he was dying.\n- ***The River of Consciousness*** (2017, posthumous) — essays on evolution, creativity, memory, time.\n- ***Everything in Its Place: First Loves and Last Tales*** (2019, posthumous) — **the collection containing this essay**; ferns, swimming, horsetails, gardens, asylums, schizophrenia, dementia, Alzheimer's, Robin Williams, Spalding Gray, social media, climate change, and libraries.\n- ***Letters*** (2024, posthumous), edited by Kate Edgar.\n- He also wrote the **foreword to Steve Silberman's *NeuroTribes*** (2015).\n\n**Standing and honours.** **Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE)** and **Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians (FRCP)**. A **member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters**. **Fellow of the Queen's College, Oxford.** The **minor planet 84928 Oliversacks**, discovered 2003, was named in his honour. He published hundreds of articles, both peer-reviewed and for general audiences. His books were adapted into plays, feature films, animated shorts, opera, dance, fine art, and classical music.
