So the essay is the **third essay in Literature Unit Three**, pp. 257–260, not Unit 15. (The other essays in that unit: 1. \"On Libraries\" – Oliver Sacks; 2. \"Marriage as a Social Institution\" – Stephen L. Nock; 4. \"Humility\" – Yuval Noah Harari; 5. \"Human Rights and the Age of Inequality\" – Samuel Moyn.)\n\n---\n\n## 2. SOURCE — verified, and your hypothesis is right but incomplete\n\n**The book.** *Portraits from Memory, and Other Essays*, **1956**, published simultaneously in London by **George Allen & Unwin** (227 pp., LCCN 56058977, OCLC 425363) and in New York by **Simon and Schuster** (246 pp., LCCN 56011187, OCLC 783853). Verified via Open Library edition records https://openlibrary.org/books/OL6215616M.json and https://openlibrary.org/books/OL6201682M.json, and against the Simon & Schuster title page in the scan itself, which reads \"SIMON AND SCHUSTER / NEW YORK / 1956\". \"Knowledge and Wisdom\" appears in the contents of both editions (contents page of the US scan; and the Allen & Unwin contents listing at https://www.russell-j.com/cool/48E-IDX.HTM). It is now Chapter 23 of the Routledge Classics reissue (ISBN 9780367540845), per https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/mono/10.4324/9781003090359-23/knowledge-wisdom-bertrand-russell.\n\n**It did appear first elsewhere — twice over.** This is the part worth having:\n\n- It was **first printed in *The Listener*, vol. 52, no. 1332 (9 September 1954), p. 390**, under the magazine's \"PHILOSOPHY\" heading as \"Knowledge and Wisdom (Bertrand Russell, O.M.)\". Verified two independent ways: the Bertrand Russell Society's bibliography of Russell's articles, which is based on Blackwell/Ruja/Turcon's *A Bibliography of Bertrand Russell* — entry reads `\"Knowledge and Wisdom,\" The Listener 52 (Sep 9 1954), 390 Repr. PfM` (https://users.drew.edu/jlenz/br-bib-articles3.html) — **and** the scanned issue itself, whose contents page and body text I located (the article opens \"MOST people would agree that, although our age far surpasses all previous ages in knowledge…\").\n- *The Listener* was the BBC's print organ for broadcast talks, and the editorial headnote to the piece as reprinted in ***The Collected Papers of Bertrand Russell*** states it **\"had been broadcast over the BBC on 22 August 1954\"** and that \"Russell reprinted it in *Portraits from Memory* (1956). Nine additional reprintings have been recorded; they are listed in Volume 11 of *A Bibliography of Bertrand Russell*.\" Chapter 76, \"Knowledge and Wisdom [1954]\", eds. John Slater and Peter Köllner: https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/mono/10.4324/9781003557357-76/knowledge-wisdom-1954-bertrand-russell-john-slater-peter-köllner — **partial verification only**: Taylor & Francis returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so I have this sentence from the indexed page abstract rather than from the page itself. Treat \"broadcast 22 August 1954\" as high-confidence-but-second-hand; the 9 Sept 1954 *Listener* printing is fully verified.\n\nSo the accurate citation chain is: **BBC talk (Aug 1954) → *The Listener*, 9 Sept 1954, p. 390 → *Portraits from Memory and Other Essays*, 1956 → Nepal CDC *English Grade 12*, 2021, pp. 257–260.**\n\n---\n\n## 3. THE FULL CONTENT AND ARGUMENT, paragraph by paragraph\n\nThe original essay is **eight paragraphs**, roughly 1,500 words. The CDC textbook prints it as eleven blocks because its typesetting breaks three of Russell's paragraphs mid-stream (at \"'You will be surprised to learn…\", at \"But perhaps, if you have sufficient patience…\", and at \"It might be objected that it is right to hate…\"). I give Russell's real paragraphing.\n\n**¶1 — The problem stated.** Russell opens with a concession most readers will grant: our age \"far surpasses all previous ages in knowledge\" but there has been \"no correlative increase in wisdom.\" Agreement stops the moment you try to define wisdom or say how to promote it. He sets his two-part agenda explicitly: \"I want to ask first what wisdom is, and then what can be done to teach it.\" Note the structure — the essay is a definition followed by a pedagogy, and Russell keeps that promise exactly.\n\n**¶2 — Factor one: a sense of proportion.** \"There are, I think, several factors that contribute to wisdom. Of these I should put first a sense of proportion: the capacity to take account of all the important factors in a problem and to attach to each its due weight.\" (In the 1954 *Listener* version this sentence lacks the hedge: \"There are several factors that contribute to wisdom.\") He immediately says why this is harder now than it used to be — \"the extent and complexity of the specialized knowledge required of various kinds of technicians.\" Then the two illustrations (see §4 below): the medical researcher, and the atomic physicist. The paragraph's conclusion is the essay's load-bearing claim: \"the pursuit of knowledge may become harmful unless it is combined with wisdom; and wisdom in the sense of comprehensive vision is not necessarily present in specialists in the pursuit of knowledge.\"\n\n**¶3 — Factor two: awareness of the ends of human life; and feeling.** \"Comprehensiveness alone, however, is not enough to constitute wisdom. There must be, also, a certain awareness of the ends of human life.\" He illustrates from historiography: \"Many eminent historians have done more harm than good because they viewed facts through the distorting medium of their own passions,\" and gives Hegel as the case (see §4). He then proposes an enlargement of the term: \"Perhaps one could stretch the comprehensiveness that constitutes wisdom to include not only intellect but also feeling.\" And the sentence you were half-remembering: \"It is by no means uncommon to find men whose knowledge is wide but whose feelings are narrow. Such men lack what I am calling wisdom.\" (CDC text: \"what I call wisdom.\") **So your item (iv) is right in substance — comprehensiveness without feeling is not wisdom — but it belongs here, not as a separate fourth factor.**\n\n**¶4 — Factor three: choice of ends and emancipation from personal prejudice; wisdom in private life.** \"It is not only in public ways, but in private life equally, that wisdom is needed. It is needed in the choice of ends to be pursued and in emancipation from personal prejudice.\" Two illustrations: the alchemists chasing the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life (an end noble if attainable, but \"inherently impossible of achievement,\" so \"their lives were wasted\"); and, \"to descend to less heroic matters,\" the Mr A / Mr B parable of mutual hatred (see §4). The payoff: if you can persuade each that the other \"has only the normal share of human wickedness,\" \"you will have instilled some fragment of wisdom.\"\n\n**¶5 — The essence of wisdom.** This is the definitional climax: \"I think the essence of wisdom is emancipation, as far as possible, from the tyranny of the here and the now.\" (CDC prints \"as **fat** as possible\" — a typo — and drops the second \"the\": \"the tyranny of the here and now.\") He grounds this developmentally rather than morally: we cannot help \"the egoism of our senses\"; sight, sound and touch are bound up with our bodies \"and cannot be made impersonal\"; our emotions likewise start from ourselves. An infant \"feels hunger or discomfort, and is unaffected except by his own physical condition\"; \"gradually with the years, his horizon widens,\" and in proportion as thought and feeling become \"less personal and less concerned with his own physical states, he achieves growing wisdom.\" He then puts in the crucial qualification: \"No one can view the world with complete impartiality; and if anyone could, he would hardly be able to remain alive.\" Impartiality is an asymptote approached by two distinct means — \"on the one hand, by knowing things somewhat remote in time or space, and, on the other hand, by giving to such things their due weight in our feelings.\" Closing sentence: \"It is this approach toward impartiality that constitutes growth in wisdom.\" **This confirms your item (iii) verbatim and shows that \"impartiality\" (your item iv) is not a separate listed factor but the name Russell gives to the direction of growth itself.**\n\n**¶6 — Can wisdom be taught? Yes; and the hatred problem.** \"Can wisdom in this sense be taught? And, if it can, should the teaching of it be one of the aims of education? I should answer both these questions in the affirmative.\" Then the Good Samaritan argument (see §4), and the objection-and-reply on hating the harmful: \"If you hate them, it is only too likely that you will become equally harmful; and it is very unlikely that you will induce them to abandon their evil ways. Hatred of evil is itself a kind of bondage to evil. The way out is through understanding, not through hate.\" He then guards his flank against a pacifist misreading: \"I am not advocating non-resistance. But I am saying that resistance, if it is to be effective in preventing the spread of evil, should be combined with the greatest degree of understanding and the smallest degree of force that is compatible with the survival of the good things that we wish to preserve.\"\n\n**¶7 — The objection from effectiveness.** \"It is commonly urged that a point of view such as I have been advocating is incompatible with vigor in action. I do not think history bears out this view.\" Then Elizabeth I, Henri IV, Lincoln (see §4).\n\n**¶8 — How to teach it, and the conclusion.** The teaching of wisdom \"should have a larger intellectual element than has been customary in what has been thought of as moral instruction.\" The mechanism is indirect and cognitive: \"the disastrous results of hatred and narrow-mindedness to those who feel them can be pointed out **incidentally in the course of giving knowledge**.\" Hence: \"I do not think that knowledge and morals ought to be too much separated.\" Specialized skill-knowledge \"has very little to do with wisdom,\" but \"it should be supplemented in education by wider surveys calculated to put it in its place in the total of human activities.\" Then the cosmopolitan sting: \"Even the best technicians should also be good citizens; and when I say 'citizens,' I mean citizens of the world and not of this or that sect or nation.\"\n\n### How Russell distinguishes knowledge from wisdom\n\nPrecisely and only functionally. He never gives a dictionary definition of knowledge. Knowledge is treated as **content and capacity** — data, specialized technique, \"skill\"; it is cumulative, it is what our age has more of than any previous age, and it is morally inert. Wisdom is treated as **the governance of that capacity**: a sense of proportion over the whole field of consequences, an awareness of the ends toward which capacity is directed, feeling proportioned to knowledge, and emancipation from the egoism of the immediately present self. The relation is asymmetric and dangerous: knowledge is neutral amplification, so the more of it you have the more wisdom you need. His own formulation of the mechanism, in ¶8, is the sharpest statement of the distinction anywhere in the essay: \"every such increase augments our capacity of realizing our purposes, and therefore augments our capacity for evil, if our purposes are unwise.\"\n\nA caution for teaching: the CDC textbook's own editorial headnote (p. 257) glosses the distinction as \"knowledge is … the acquisition of data and information, while wisdom is … the practical application and use of the knowledge to create value. Wisdom is gained through learning and practical experience, not just memorization.\" **That is the textbook's paraphrase, not Russell's — and it is a poor fit.** Russell nowhere defines wisdom as the application of knowledge; for him the wise application of knowledge is a *consequence* of wisdom, and wisdom itself is comprehensiveness plus awareness of ends plus impartiality of feeling. Nepali answer keys frequently reproduce the headnote as if it were Russell's position.\n\n### The factors — the verified list\n\nRussell says \"several factors\" and never numbers them, which is why answer keys disagree. Read strictly from the text there are **three** introduced as factors, plus one enlargement and one summative name:\n\n1. **\"a sense of proportion: the capacity to take account of all the important factors in a problem and to attach to each its due weight\"** — explicitly ranked first (\"Of these I should put first…\"). Also called \"comprehensiveness\" and \"comprehensive vision.\"\n2. **\"a certain awareness of the ends of human life\"** — introduced as what comprehensiveness alone lacks.\n3. **\"the choice of ends to be pursued and … emancipation from personal prejudice\"** — the private-life factor.\n4. *Enlargement of (1), not a new item:* comprehensiveness \"to include not only intellect but also feeling\" — hence \"men whose knowledge is wide but whose feelings are narrow\" lack wisdom.\n5. *The summative essence:* **\"emancipation, as far as possible, from the tyranny of the here and the now\"**, whose measure is \"a continual approach toward impartiality.\"\n\nYour four-item list is therefore substantively right; the only corrections are that (iv) \"impartiality\" is the *criterion of growth* rather than a listed factor, and that the feeling point is an extension of the sense-of-proportion factor. The five-item lists on Nepali sites (sense of proportion / awareness of ends / emancipation from prejudice / impartiality / \"intellectual element\") are defensible as exam answers but the fifth item, \"intellectual element\", is drawn from ¶8's remark about *teaching* wisdom, not from Russell's account of what wisdom *is*.\n\n---\n\n## 4. EVERY example and illustration — with your list audited\n\n**Actually in the essay (five, in order):**\n\n1. **The medical researcher.** Correct in outline, but two details of your version are wrong. Russell does **not** say \"a cure for a disease\" and does **not** name a tropical country. He says: suppose you are \"engaged in research in scientific medicine\"; the work \"is likely to absorb the whole of your intellectual energy\"; you have no time to consider effects outside medicine; \"You succeed (let us say), as modern medicine has succeeded, in enormously lowering the **infant death rate**, not only in Europe and America, but also in **Asia and Africa**. This has the entirely unintended result of making the food supply inadequate and lowering the standard of life in the most populous parts of the world.\" So: lowered infant mortality, worldwide rather than one tropical country, and the consequence is stated as inadequate food supply and a lowered standard of life — the words \"population growth\" and \"suffering\" are yours, not his.\n2. **The atom.** Introduced as \"an even more spectacular example, which is in everybody's mind at the present time\": \"You study the composition of the atom from a disinterested desire for knowledge, and incidentally place in the hands of **powerful lunatics** the means of destroying the human race.\" Note: Russell never uses the words \"atomic bomb\" or \"hydrogen bomb\" in this essay. The phrase \"powerful lunatics\" is the one to quote.\n3. **Hegel.** Correct that Hegel is present, wrong about which Hegel anecdote. Russell's point is about the ends-blindness of an otherwise comprehensive historian: Hegel \"had a philosophy of history which did not suffer from any lack of comprehensiveness, since it started from the earliest times and continued into an indefinite future. But the chief lesson of history which he sought to inculcate was that from the year A.D. 400 down to his own time **Germany had been the most important nation and the standard bearer of progress in the world**.\" (CDC prints \"400AD\".) **There is no remark about America and no anecdote about Herr Krug's pen** — see the disconfirmations below.\n4. **The alchemists.** \"Many men in past ages devoted their lives to a search for the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life. No doubt, if they could have found them, they would have conferred great benefits upon mankind, but as it was their lives were wasted.\" This is the example of an end noble in itself but \"inherently impossible of achievement.\" **This is the one you missed, and it is the one your \"scholar who devotes his whole life to one narrow subject\" is probably a distorted memory of.** There is no Empedocles.\n5. **Mr A and Mr B.** The extended parable of mutual hatred: each gives \"an appalling list\" of the other's vices, \"partly true, partly false,\" with \"an equal admixture of truth and falsehood\"; you report each to the other; \"the first effect, no doubt, will be to increase their mutual hatred, since each will be so horrified by the other's injustice\"; but with patience and persuasiveness each may be convinced that the other \"has only the normal share of human wickedness, and that their enmity is harmful to both.\" **Also missed in your list, and it is the essay's longest single illustration.**\n6. **The Good Samaritan.** Used in the teaching section: \"We are told on Sundays that we should love our neighbor as ourselves. On the other six days of the week, we are exhorted to hate him.\" Russell notes that because \"we no longer have any wish to hate Samaritans … we are apt to miss the point of the parable,\" and gives the updating instruction: \"If you want to get its point, you should **substitute Communist or anti-Communist**, as the case may be, for Samaritan.\" **Also missed in your list; it is the essay's most-quoted passage after \"the tyranny of the here and now.\"** (The CDC textbook silently deletes Russell's self-interrupting sentence here — see §5.)\n7. **Elizabeth I, Henri IV, Lincoln.** Your version is close but the framing is not \"waged wars without hatred,\" it is *freedom from the fanaticism of one's own age is compatible with vigour in action.* \"Queen Elizabeth I in England and **Henri** IV in France lived in a world where almost everybody was fanatical, either on the Protestant or on the Catholic side. Both remained free from the errors of their time and both, by remaining free, were beneficent and certainly not ineffective. Abraham Lincoln conducted a great war without ever departing from what I have been calling wisdom.\" Only Lincoln is connected to war-waging; Elizabeth and Henri are examples of resisting sectarian fanaticism. CDC anglicises \"Henri IV\" to \"Henry IV\" and prints \"what I have called wisdom\".\n\n**NOT in the essay — and not anywhere in the book.** I grepped the complete OCR of the 1956 Simon & Schuster edition (all 246 pp., every essay) for each of these. Hit counts: `Xerxes` 0, `Alcibiades` 0, `Krug` 0, `Empedocles` 0, `sinned` 0, `Copernic` 0, `heliocentric` 0. So the following are **disconfirmed for this essay and for the whole of *Portraits from Memory***:\n\n- Hegel's remark about America — absent.\n- The Hegel / Herr Krug's pen anecdote — absent. (Russell does discuss Hegel's challenge to Krug elsewhere in his corpus, but not here.)\n- Empedocles, and the scholar devoted to one narrow subject — absent. Nearest thing is the alchemists.\n- King Lear, \"I am a man more sinned against than sinning\" — absent.\n- Xerxes — absent.\n- The sun-centred vs earth-centred lesson in escaping self-centredness — absent. Russell's escape-from-egoism argument in ¶5 is developmental (the infant) and epistemic (\"knowing things somewhat remote in time or space\"), never astronomical. *(Sidenote that may explain the cross-wiring: the very next essay in the CDC textbook, Harari's \"Humility\" at p. 261, opens with the section heading \"You are not the centre of the world\" and works through rival nations each believing itself \"the linchpin of human history.\" That is almost certainly the source of the conflation, since the two texts sit back to back.)*\n- Alcibiades — absent.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Can wisdom be taught, and how\n\nRussell answers **yes to both of his questions** — it can be taught, and teaching it should be one of the aims of education — and his account of the *how* has three parts, all of them in ¶6 and ¶8:\n\n1. **Make it intellectual, not exhortatory.** \"I think that this teaching should have a larger intellectual element than has been customary in what has been thought of as moral instruction.\" Wisdom is taught by argument and information, not by preaching.\n2. **Teach it incidentally, inside the teaching of knowledge.** \"the disastrous results of hatred and narrow-mindedness to those who feel them can be pointed out **incidentally in the course of giving knowledge**. I do not think that knowledge and morals ought to be too much separated.\" Note the specific psychological claim: what should be pointed out is the harm hatred does **to those who feel it**, not to its objects.\n3. **Supplement specialism with breadth, and aim at world citizenship.** Specialized skill-knowledge \"has very little to do with wisdom,\" \"but it should be supplemented in education by **wider surveys calculated to put it in its place in the total of human activities**. Even the best technicians should also be good citizens; and when I say 'citizens,' I mean **citizens of the world and not of this or that sect or nation**.\"\n\n**On how history should be taught, and one's own nation vs. others — you need to drop this.** There is no such passage in this essay. What Russell says about history is confined to ¶3 and is a warning about *historians*, not a prescription for curricula: eminent historians \"have done more harm than good because they viewed facts through the distorting medium of their own passions,\" with Hegel's German exceptionalism as the instance. The only curricular prescriptions are the three above. (Russell does argue at length for teaching world history rather than national history in other works — notably in his education writings — but if you attribute it to \"Knowledge and Wisdom\" you will be wrong, and the *Portraits from Memory* grep confirms it is not smuggled in from a neighbouring essay in the same volume.)\n\nThe essay's other teaching-adjacent argument is the Samaritan passage plus the reply to the \"but it is right to hate the harmful\" objection, culminating in \"Hatred of evil is itself a kind of bondage to evil. The way out is through understanding, not through hate,\" fenced by the explicit disclaimer \"I am not advocating non-resistance.\"\n\n### His concluding claim\n\nThe last two sentences, verbatim: **\"The world needs wisdom as it has never needed it before; and if knowledge continues to increase, the world will need wisdom in the future even more than it does now.\"** The premise licensing it is the immediately preceding sentence: \"With every increase of knowledge and skill, wisdom becomes more necessary, for every such increase augments our capacity of realizing our purposes, and therefore augments our capacity for evil, if our purposes are unwise.\" The logical shape is worth flagging for students: the need for wisdom scales with the power of knowledge, so the conclusion is *conditional and escalating*, not a lament about the present.\n\n### Textual differences between the 1956 original and the CDC 2021 text\n\nI collated them line by line. No paragraph of argument is cut, but there are errors worth knowing about if you are teaching from the textbook:\n\n- **One sentence is silently deleted.** Original ¶6: \"…we should love our neighbor as ourselves. On the other six days of the week, we are exhorted to hate **him. You may say that this is nonsense, since it is not our neighbor whom we are exhorted to hate.** But you will remember…\" The CDC text runs \"…we are exhorted to hate. But you will remember…\", removing Russell's own anticipated objection and leaving \"hate\" without an object.\n- **Typos in the CDC text:** \"as **fat** as possible\" (for \"as far as possible\"); \"complexity **for** the specialized knowledge\" (for \"of\"); \"Suppose you go to **the** Mr A\"; glossary entry \"inculcate (v.): **inplant**, infuse, instil\" (for \"implant\").\n- **Silent alterations:** \"Henri IV\" → \"Henry IV\"; \"A.D. 400\" → \"400AD\"; \"cannot be made impersonal\" → \"cannot be impersonal\"; \"what I am calling wisdom\" → \"what I call wisdom\" (twice); \"the here and the now\" → \"the here and now\"; US spellings \"vigor\"/\"toward\" → \"vigour\"/\"towards\" (but \"neighbors\" left American).\n- The 1954 *Listener* text differs from the 1956 book text in at least one place: \"There are several factors…\" (book adds \"I think\").\n\n---\n\n## 6. The CDC textbook apparatus — verbatim from the PDF\n\nThese are transcribed from pp. 257 and 260 of the official PDF, not from a study site. I then cross-checked them against two Nepali solution sites (https://www.skultech.com/summary-of-knowledge-and-wisdom-exercise/ and https://iswori.com.np/knowledge-and-wisdom-essay-exercise-class-12-english/) and they match word for word, so this **is** the version that recurs across sites.\n\n**Before reading** (p. 257) — *Discuss the following questions.*\na. What are the differences between a learned man and a wise man?\nb. Why do you think some knowledgeable people are not wise?\n\n**Glossary** (p. 260) — proportion (n.): a part or share of a whole / absorb (v.): to take, draw or suck something in / distorting (v.): pull or twist out of shape / inculcate (v.): inplant, infuse, instil / bound up (v.): to limit something / fanatical (adj.): a person who is too enthusiastic about something\n\n**Understanding the text** — *Answer the following questions.*\na. What are the factors that contribute to wisdom?\nb. What message does the writer try to convey with the example of technicians?\nc. Which leaders does Russell say were able to mix knowledge and wisdom soundly?\nd. Why is wisdom needed not only in public ways, but in private life equally?\ne. What, according to Russell, is the true aim of education?\nf. Can wisdom be taught? If so, how?\ng. Why does the world need more wisdom in the future?\n\n**Reference to the context**\na. According to Russel, \"The pursuit of knowledge may become harmful unless it is combined with wisdom.\" Justify this statement.\nb. What, according to Russell, is the essence of wisdom? And how can one acquire the very essence?\n\n**Reference beyond the text**\na. Why is wisdom necessary in education? Discuss.\nb. How can you become wise? Do you think what you are doing in college contributes to wisdom?\n\nTwo notes. The textbook prints \"Russel\" (one *l*) in *Reference to the context* (a) — study sites faithfully reproduce the misspelling, which is a useful fingerprint for telling genuine reproductions from rewrites. And *Understanding the text* (b) is singular, \"the example of technicians\"; several sites render it \"the examples of technicians\" (plural), so if a student's book and a website disagree there, the book above is authoritative.\n\n---\n\n## 7. BIOGRAPHY — verified\n\n**Name and title.** Bertrand Arthur William Russell, **3rd Earl Russell**. He succeeded to the earldom in **1931**, on the death of his elder brother Frank, becoming 3rd Earl Russell of Kingston Russell with the subsidiary title Viscount Amberley; he held the title and the accompanying seat in the House of Lords until his death. The Nobel Foundation styles him \"Earl (Bertrand Arthur William) Russell.\" He was also awarded the **Order of Merit** in the King's Birthday Honours of 9 June 1949 — hence \"Bertrand Russell, O.M.\" in the 1954 *Listener* byline. (Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_Russell; https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1950/russell/facts/)\n\n**Dates and nationality.** Born **18 May 1872** at Ravenscroft, Trellech, Monmouthshire (Wales), into the liberal British aristocracy; died **2 February 1970** at Penrhyndeudraeth, Wales. **British/English** — Wikipedia's lead says \"English philosopher, logician, mathematician, and social reformer\"; the CDC textbook's own headnote says \"a British philosopher, logician, essayist and social critic.\" His grandfather was Lord John Russell, 1st Earl Russell, twice Prime Minister; John Stuart Mill was his secular godfather (Mill died the year after Russell's birth). Orphaned by four, raised by his grandmother Frances, Countess Russell, at Pembroke Lodge; educated at home by tutors; scholarship to Trinity College, Cambridge; first-class degree in mathematics, 1893.\n\n**Mathematics and logic.** *An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry* (1897). Met Peano at the first International Congress of Philosophy, Paris, 1900, and mastered his symbolism. ***The Principles of Mathematics*** (Cambridge University Press, **1903**) — advances **logicism**, the thesis \"that mathematics and logic are one and the same\"; its appendix sets out what became **Russell's paradox** and his first attempt at a resolution, developed later into the **theory of types**. ***Principia Mathematica*** with his former teacher **Alfred North Whitehead**, three volumes, **1910–1913** — \"a milestone in the development of classical logic and a major attempt to reduce the whole of mathematics to logic.\" Elected FRS 1908. De Morgan Medal 1932; Sylvester Medal 1934.\n\n**Philosophy.** A founder of **analytic philosophy**, alongside Frege, G. E. Moore and his student Wittgenstein; with Moore he led the British **\"revolt against idealism,\"** rejecting dialectic, monism and idealism for logical analysis and pluralism. **Theory of descriptions**: set out in **\"On Denoting\"** (*Mind*, **1905**), which Frank Ramsey called \"a paradigm of philosophy\" — the theory of definite descriptions lets \"The present King of France is bald\" come out meaningful but false, without ontological commitment to a present King of France, against Meinong and against Frege's sense/reference treatment. **Logical atomism**: delivered as the lecture series \"The Philosophy of Logical Atomism\" in **1918** — an ideal isomorphic language mirroring the world, knowledge reducible to atomic propositions and their truth-functional compounds, the world consisting of \"logically independent facts, a plurality of facts.\" He also championed **neutral monism** (the CDC headnote correctly names this, along with his refinement of Frege's predicate calculus, logicism, definite descriptions, logical atomism and logical types). Later doubted parts of atomism, especially the isomorphism principle.\n\n**The popular books.** ***The Problems of Philosophy*** (London: Williams and Norgate, **1912**). ***Marriage and Morals*** (George Allen & Unwin, **1929**) — argued that sex outside marriage is not necessarily immoral between people who genuinely love each other, advocated \"trial marriage\"/companionate marriage, open sex education, access to contraception and easier divorce; it provoked denunciations in the United States and was the specific ground on which a New York court in **1940** annulled his City College of New York professorship as \"morally unfit,\" a judgment protested by John Dewey among many others (Einstein's line about \"great spirits\" encountering \"violent opposition from mediocre minds\" comes from his 19 March 1940 open letter in Russell's support). ***Why I Am Not a Christian*** — the title essay was a **talk given on 6 March 1927 at Battersea Town Hall** for the South London Branch of the National Secular Society, published as a pamphlet that year (Watts); the collection *Why I Am Not a Christian and Other Essays on Religion and Related Subjects*, ed. Paul Edwards, Allen & Unwin, 1957, addresses the first cause, natural-law, design and moral arguments for God. ***A History of Western Philosophy*** (**1945**; Simon and Schuster, New York — UK edition 1946) grew out of lectures he gave at the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia after the CCNY affair; it became a best-seller, \"provided Russell with a steady income for the remainder of his life,\" and **was cited as one of the books that won him the Nobel Prize**. Criticised for overgeneralisation and omissions, especially post-Cartesian. He wrote more than sixty books and over two thousand articles.\n\n**Nobel Prize.** The **Nobel Prize in Literature, 1950** — not Peace, which is the usual error given his activism. Prize share 1/1. Citation, verbatim from the Nobel Foundation: **\"in recognition of his varied and significant writings in which he champions humanitarian ideals and freedom of thought.\"** The Foundation's own summary of the work notes that his \"writing is characterized by levity and humor\" and that he \"extended knowledge about science and philosophy to a wide circle of readers,\" describing him as \"an advocate for reason and humanism and a dedicated defender of freedom of speech and freedom of thought.\" Other honours: Kalinga Prize 1957, Jerusalem Prize 1963. (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1950/russell/facts/)\n\n**Pacifism and imprisonments — three distinct episodes, often muddled.**\n1. **1916:** convicted for his anti-conscription activity and **fined £100**, which he refused to pay hoping to be jailed; his books were auctioned to raise the money and bought by friends. He later treasured the copy of the King James Bible stamped \"Confiscated by Cambridge Police.\" His activism also cost him travel freedom within Britain and the non-renewal of his Trinity College fellowship.\n2. **1918:** convicted under the **Defence of the Realm Act** for publicly lecturing against inviting the United States into the war (he had argued British workers should be wary of the US Army, experienced as it was in strike-breaking), and sentenced to **six months in Brixton Prison**. He found it \"in many ways quite agreeable\": \"I had no engagements, no difficult decisions to make, no fear of callers, no interruptions to my work. I read enormously; I wrote a book, 'Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy'… and began the work for 'The Analysis of Mind.'\" He was released after serving the sentence but remained closely supervised until the war's end.\n3. **September 1961:** aged 89, **imprisoned for a week under the Justices of the Peace Act 1361**, serving the sentence **in the hospital wing of Brixton Prison**, for refusing to call off a mass ban-the-bomb demonstration at the Ministry of Defence organised by the Committee of 100.\n\nHis pacifism was not absolute. He chaired the England-based India League and championed anti-imperialism; he initially favoured appeasing Nazi Germany but changed his view in **1943**, describing war as a necessary \"lesser of two evils\"; after 1945 he preferred American to Soviet hegemony; he later condemned Stalinist totalitarianism and US involvement in Vietnam. The stance in \"Knowledge and Wisdom\" — \"I am not advocating non-resistance… the smallest degree of force that is compatible with the survival of the good things that we wish to preserve\" — is exactly this qualified position, written in 1954.\n\n**Nuclear disarmament.** The **Russell–Einstein Manifesto**, issued in **London on 9 July 1955**, warning of the dangers of nuclear weapons and calling on world leaders to seek peaceful resolution of conflict; signed by eleven pre-eminent scientists and intellectuals including **Einstein, who signed shortly before his death on 18 April 1955**. Cyrus S. Eaton then sponsored the conference the manifesto had called for, held in **Pugwash, Nova Scotia, in July 1957** — the first of the **Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs**. In **1957–58** Russell became the **first president of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament**, which pressed for unilateral British nuclear disarmament; he **resigned two years later when CND would not support civil disobedience** and formed the **Committee of 100** — set up in 1960 with a hundred public signatories by Russell, Ralph Schoenman, Michael Scott and others, using mass non-violent resistance and civil disobedience, and, per the historian Martin Shaw, \"the driving force of the mass movement against nuclear weapons in 1961-63.\" Related: his 1954 BBC broadcast \"Man's Peril\" is reprinted in the same volume as \"Knowledge and Wisdom.\"\n\n**Prose style — from primary evidence.** *Portraits from Memory* contains an essay, \"How I Write\" (pp. 210 ff.), two chapters after \"Knowledge and Wisdom,\" in which Russell describes his own practice. Until he was twenty-one he wanted to write \"in the style of John Stuart Mill,\" liking \"the structure of his sentences and his manner of developing a subject,\" but already held a rival ideal \"derived, I suppose, from mathematics: I wished to say everything in the smallest number of words in which it could be said clearly. Perhaps, I thought, one should imitate **Baedeker** rather than any more literary model. I would spend hours trying to find the shortest way of saying something without ambiguity, and to this aim I was willing to sacrifice all attempts at aesthetic excellence.\" At twenty-one Logan Pearsall Smith (his future brother-in-law), a devotee of Flaubert and Pater, gave him rules he remembered as \"Put a comma every four words\" and \"never use 'and' except at the beginning of a sentence,\" and pressed him always to rewrite — advice Russell tried and abandoned, finding \"that my first draft was almost always better than my second… I do not, of course, apply it to the substance, but only to the form.\" He also describes needing \"a period of subconscious incubation\" before writing.\n\nThat is the style visible in \"Knowledge and Wisdom\" itself, and it is worth pointing out to students as the reason the essay is set: extreme economy (the whole argument in ~1,500 words and eight paragraphs); short declarative sentences carrying the load; abstractions immediately cashed out in a concrete case (\"Suppose, for example, that you are engaged in research in scientific medicine…\"); the direct second person \"you\" drawing the reader into the thought-experiments; scrupulous self-qualification (\"This is of course a matter of degree\"; \"I am not advocating non-resistance\"); anticipation and rebuttal of objections in Russell's own voice (\"It might be objected…\"; \"It is commonly urged…\"); dry understatement and irony as the chief ornament (\"powerful lunatics\"; \"We are told on Sundays that we should love our neighbor as ourselves. On the other six days of the week, we are exhorted to hate him\"; \"to descend to less heroic matters\"); and the epigram reserved for the turn of the argument (\"Hatred of evil is itself a kind of bondage to evil\").\n\n---\n\n## 8. What I could NOT verify, and what I disproved\n\n**Disproved (high confidence, by exhaustive grep of the complete 1956 book text):** Hegel on America; the Herr Krug's pen anecdote; Empedocles; the narrow-subject scholar; King Lear / \"more sinned against than sinning\"; Xerxes; Alcibiades; the sun-centred vs earth-centred illustration; and any discussion of how history should be taught or of studying one's own nation vs. others. ELI JENKINS:** *Every morning when I wake, …*\n\nCorroborated independently by **Wikipedia, \"Under Milk Wood\"** (three separate confirmations):\n- \"He stayed with the comedian Harry Locke, and worked on the play, re-writing parts of the first half, and writing **Eli Jenkins' sunset poem** and Waldo's chimney sweep song for the second half.\" (New York, autumn 1953 — i.e. this poem was among the very last things Thomas wrote, weeks before his death.)\n- \"**As night begins, Reverend Jenkins recites another poem.**\"\n- \"The prayer recited by Reverend Eli Jenkins in the play, known as the **'Sunset Poem'**…\"; and the Bryn Terfel recording is listed as \"**Eli Jenkins's Sunset Poem**.\"\n- Also listed among the play's famous lines: \"*We are not wholly bad or good, who live our lives under Milk Wood* – **prayer of the Reverend Eli Jenkins**.\"\n\n### The speaker\n**Rev. Eli Jenkins** — VERIFIED. Wikipedia character list: \"Rev. Eli Jenkins – The reverend, poet and preacher, dreams of Eisteddfodau. Author of the **White Book of Llareggub**.\" He lives at **Bethesda House** and speaks both poems from its doorway.\n\n### The OTHER poem — Eli Jenkins's MORNING poem (VERIFIED, full text located)\nAt dawn, Eli Jenkins \"gropes out of bed into his preacher's black, combs back his bard's white hair, forgets to wash, pads barefoot downstairs, opens the front door, stands in the doorway and… remembers his own verses and tells them softly to empty Coronation Street.\" He then recites:\n\n> **\"Dear Gwalia! I know there are / Towns lovelier than ours, / And fairer hills and loftier far, / And groves more full of flowers,\"**\n\nIt runs **nine quatrains (36 lines)**, catalogues Welsh mountains and rivers (Cader Idris, Moel yr Wyddfa, Carnedd Llewelyn, Plinlimmon, Penmaenmawr; Sawdde, Senny, Dovey, Dee, Taff, Towy, Claerwen, Cleddau…), and ends \"…And hear the Dewi sing all day, / And never, never leave the town.\" It contains the lines \"**Llaregyb Hill a molehill seems, / A pygmy to a giant**\" and \"**A tiny dingle is Milk Wood**.\" It closes with the stage direction: \"**The Reverend Jenkins closes the front door. His morning service is over.**\"\n\nSo the pairing is:\n- **Morning poem / \"morning service\"** = *\"Dear Gwalia! I know there are…\"* — a hymn of love for the town, 36 lines.\n- **Sunset poem** = *\"Every morning when I wake…\"* — the prayer set as the CDC textbook's Unit 9, 16 lines.\n\n**Important nuance for the guide:** the *content* of the sunset poem covers the whole diurnal round — it looks back at the morning prayer (\"Every morning when I wake\") and forward through the night (\"Bless us all this night, I pray\"). That is exactly why Thomas gives it at sundown: it is a summing-up of the day. Saying \"it is a morning prayer\" is a factual error about the play, even though the poem's first line says \"every morning.\"\n\n### Llareggub\n**VERIFIED (Wikipedia, \"Under Milk Wood\"):**\n- \"the fictional small Welsh fishing town, **Llareggub, (buggerall spelt backwards)**.\"\n- \"The fictional name **Llareggub was derived by reversing the phrase 'bugger all'**. In some published editions of the play, it is often rendered (**contrary to Thomas's own use**) as **Llaregyb** or similar. It is pronounced **[ɬaˈrɛɡɪb]**. The name bears some resemblance to many actual Welsh place names, which often begin with *Llan*, meaning church or, more correctly, sanctified enclosure, although a double *g* is not used in written Welsh.\"\n- Thomas first used the name in two 1936 short stories, \"The Orchards\" and \"The Burning Baby.\" Working titles for the play included *The Village of the Mad*, *The Town that was Mad*, *Llareggub Hill*, and *Llareggub. A Piece for Radio Perhaps*; retitled *Under Milk Wood* in summer 1952 because John Brinnin thought \"Llareggub Hill\" too forbidding for American audiences.\n- The town is modelled chiefly on **New Quay, Cardiganshire**, with elements of **Laugharne**.\n\n**Spelling caution (VERIFIED):** the Gutenberg Australia, coldreads and Crescent Theatre scripts all print **\"Llaregyb\"** (the bowdlerised Dent/BBC spelling) in the sunset-poem stage direction. The Crescent copy uses yet another form, \"Llarregub.\" Thomas's own spelling was **Llareggub**. The CDC textbook uses **\"Llareggub\"** in the author note — correct — but **misspells it as \"Llaggerub\" in the glossary** (see B.4 below).\n\n## B.2 Text, form, and phrase-by-phrase verification\n\n### B.2.a Text as printed in the CDC textbook (VERIFIED, p. 234–235)\nStanza structure confirmed from PDF line coordinates (16.8 pt within stanza, 22.5 pt between): **4 stanzas × 4 lines = 16 lines.** Stanza 2 ends p. 234; stanzas 3–4 on p. 235.\n\n- **First line:** `Every morning when I wake,`\n- **Last line:** `And say, good-bye – but just for now!`\n\n### B.2.b Your list of candidate phrases — adjudicated\n\n| Phrase you asked about | Verdict | Position / correction |\n|---|---|---|\n| **\"Every morning when I wake\"** | **GENUINE** | **Line 1**, stanza 1. There is no \"a little more\" anywhere in the poem, in the sunset poem, or in the play text (searched full script: 0 occurrences). |\n| **\"Bless us all this night, I pray\"** | **GENUINE** | **Line 14**, stanza 4 line 2. Exact. |\n| **Milk Wood reference** | **GENUINE, once** | **Line 10: \"Who live our lives under Milk Wood,\"** — this is the poem's only Milk Wood reference, and it is also the phrase that gave the play its title. |\n| **Llareggub reference** | **NOT in the poem** | Llareggub/Llaregyb appears **only in the stage direction** (\"recites to Llaregyb Hill his sunset poem\"), never inside the poem. Wikipedia lists it among the play's most quoted lines. |\n| **\"Thou knowest we are but as young\"** | **NOT GENUINE** | Searched the complete play text: **\"Thou knowest\" occurs 0 times.** This phrase is not in the poem and not in *Under Milk Wood* at all. The poem's only \"Thou\" is line 11, **\"And Thou, I know, wilt be the first\"**. It looks like a confusion with that line. |\n\n### B.2.c A textual variant in line 3 you should know about — IMPORTANT\n\nThe CDC textbook prints line 3 as:\n> `O please do keep Thy loving eye`\n\nAll three **full play scripts** I checked print:\n> `O please **to** keep Thy **lovely** eye`\n\n(Gutenberg Australia; Crescent Theatre reading copy p. 82; coldreads.org PDF — identical in all three.)\n\nTwo other circulating readings: oatridge.co.uk has \"O please **do** keep Thy **lovely** eye\"; the Bryn Terfel sung lyric (elyrics.net) has \"O please **to** keep Thy **loving** eye.\" So *both* words vary across secondary web sources, but the three **full scripts** agree on **\"to … lovely.\"**\n\n**Verdict: the best-attested reading in full play texts is \"O please to keep Thy lovely eye\"; the CDC textbook's \"O please do keep Thy loving eye\" appears to be a corruption.** I could **NOT** verify this against the authoritative Dent/Everyman definitive edition (ed. Walford Davies & Ralph Maud), which is not accessible online — so treat this as *strongly probable*, not certain. For exam purposes students must of course quote the textbook's wording; but the guide could carry a footnote.\n\nMinor punctuation differences from the play text: the play has the em dash in the last line as `good-bye--but just for now!`; the textbook uses a spaced en dash, `good-bye – but just for now!`. The play's line 4 has no terminal period (\"On all poor creatures born to die\"); the textbook likewise has none.\n\n### B.2.d Rhyme scheme — exact\n\n**Rhyming couplets throughout — every stanza is two couplets.** Full scheme: **aabb ccdd eeff gghh**.\n\n| Stanza | Rhyme pairs | Letters | Quality |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | wake / make; eye / die | **aabb** | both perfect |\n| 2 | sun-down / town; no / touch-and-go | **ccdd** | both perfect |\n| 3 | good / Wood; first / worst | **eeff** | both perfect (good/Wood = /ɡʊd/ /wʊd/; first/worst = /fɜːst/ /wɜːst/) |\n| 4 | day / pray; bow / now | **gghh** | both perfect |\n\nThere are **no slant rhymes** in this poem — a deliberate contrast with the Dickinson. The unbroken couplets are what make it sound like a hymn or a child's bedtime prayer, and this is the answer the textbook's RTC question (d) — \"How does the rhyme scheme of the poem reinforce its message?\" — is fishing for. (Analysis: the good/Wood couplet at lines 9–10 binds human moral frailty to the place itself, which is the poem's whole argument.)\n\n### B.2.e Metre\n\n**ANALYSIS, not from a source — flagged as such.** Syllable counts per line of the textbook text: 8(or 7), 8, 8, 8 / 8, 8, **9**, 8 / 8, 8, 8, 8 / 8, **7**, 8, 8.\n\nThe poem is in **iambic tetrameter rhyming couplets** — the \"long metre\"/hymn-quatrain shape, which is exactly right for a preacher's prayer. Two regular departures:\n- **Line 14, \"Bless us all this night, I pray,\" = 7 syllables** — a headless/catalectic line with a trochaic opening (\"BLESS us | ALL this | NIGHT, I | PRAY\"), which lands the imperative hard.\n- **Line 7, \"For whether we last the night or no\" = 9 syllables** — an anapaestic substitution, loosening the line where the sense is most colloquial (\"touch-and-go\").\n- Line 1 is 7 or 8 depending on whether \"Every\" is elided to \"Ev'ry.\"\n\nSo: \"predominantly iambic tetrameter in rhyming couplets, with occasional seven- and nine-syllable variation.\" Do not write \"strict iambic tetrameter throughout.\"\n\n## B.3 Dylan Thomas — biography\n\nSource unless noted: **Wikipedia, \"Dylan Thomas\"** and **Wikipedia, \"Under Milk Wood.\"**\n\n**VERIFIED:**\n- **Dylan Marlais Thomas, 27 October 1914 – 9 November 1953**, Welsh poet and writer. **Born in Swansea**, Wales.\n- Left school 1932 to become a reporter for the *South Wales Daily Post*. Produced some 200 poems 1931–35. **\"And Death Shall Have No Dominion\" was the first poem he published in a national journal, in May 1933**, while still a teenager.\n- Married **Caitlin Macnamara** — met in London, married at the register office in **Penzance, Cornwall, 11 July 1937**; three children, Llewelyn, Aeronwy and Colm.\n- **Works named in your brief, all verified as his:** *Under Milk Wood* (the \"play for voices\"); **\"Do not go gentle into that good night\"** — \"an ode, in the form of a **villanelle**, to his dying father\"; **\"Fern Hill\"** — the **1945** lyric evoking **Fernhill**, \"a dilapidated 15-acre farm rented by his maternal aunt, Ann Jones\"; **\"And death shall have no dominion.\"** Also *A Child's Christmas in Wales*, *Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog*, \"In Country Sleep,\" \"Ballad of the Long-legged Bait,\" \"Ceremony After a Fire Raid,\" \"A Refusal to Mourn the Death, by Fire, of a Child in London.\"\n- **BBC / radio work:** Wikipedia has a section headed \"**Broadcasting years 1945–1949**.\" \"**On 31 August 1945, the BBC Home Service broadcast *Quite Early One Morning* and, in the three years beginning in October 1945, Thomas made over a hundred broadcasts for the corporation.**\" In December 1944 he recorded *Quite Early One Morning* for the Welsh BBC (producer Aneirin Talfan Davies) but BBC London initially rejected it for national broadcast. From the second half of 1945 he read for the BBC radio programme *Book of Verse*. *Quite Early One Morning*, a walk around New Quay, is described by Prof. Walford Davies as \"a **veritable storehouse of phrases, rhythms and details later resurrected or modified for *Under Milk Wood***\" — i.e. it is the direct precursor of the play.\n- **Death in New York, 1953:** on his **fourth** American trip he checked into the **Chelsea Hotel**, took the first rehearsal of *Under Milk Wood*, drank at the **White Horse Tavern** in Greenwich Village, was admitted to **St Vincent's Hospital at 1:58 am**, fell into a coma and **died at noon on 9 November 1953**, aged **39**. Later assessment: he had been suffering from bronchitis, pneumonia, emphysema and asthma before admission. His body was returned to Wales; **interred 25 November 1953 at St Martin's churchyard, Laugharne, Carmarthenshire**.\n- ***Under Milk Wood* dates — note the textbook is wrong here.** First **public reading**: **14 May 1953, The Poetry Center at the 92nd Street Y, New York**; Thomas himself read First Voice and **the Reverend Eli Jenkins**. That is the only recorded performance with Thomas in the cast (issued by Caedmon Records). The **BBC first broadcast** it, \"described as 'a new Play for Voices'\", on the **Third Programme on 25 January 1954, two months after Thomas's death**, produced by **Douglas Cleverdon** with an all-Welsh cast and **Richard Burton as First Voice**; several sections were omitted. Cleverdon recorded the complete text in 1963 (broadcast 11 October 1963).\n\n**COULD NOT VERIFY:** that Thomas's first BBC broadcast was in 1937 (\"Life and the Modern Poet\") — the Wikipedia extract does not mention it and I did not find a second source, so I am not asserting it. The safe, sourced statement is: **\"his BBC broadcasting career took off from 1945, with over a hundred broadcasts in the three years from October 1945.\"** The textbook's \"He started working for BBC in 1945\" is therefore defensible as written.\n\n## B.4 Errors in the CDC textbook's own Unit 9 material — flag these to students\n\nAll VERIFIED by direct reading of pp. 234–235 of the PDF:\n\n1. **\"Under Milk Wood (1953), a radio play\"** — the date is wrong for the broadcast. It was **first broadcast 25 January 1954** and published in 1954. 1953 is the year of the first public *reading* (14 May) and of Thomas's death. Suggest phrasing it as \"written 1953, first broadcast 1954.\"\n2. **\"'Every Morning I Wake' is an extract from *Under the Milk Wood*\"** — the play's title has **no \"the.\"** It is *Under Milk Wood*. (The book gets it right twice elsewhere on the same page.)\n3. **Glossary reads: \"Milk Wood (adj.): a wooded area in the hills above a Welsh seaside village of *Llaggerub* in Dylan Thomas' play Under Milk Wood.\"** Two errors: **\"Llaggerub\" is a misspelling of Llareggub**, and **\"Milk Wood\" is a noun, not an adjective** — the \"(adj.)\" tag is wrong.\n4. **\"Romanticism, that flourished in the nineteenth century *Englnad*\"** — typo for *England*, in the printed book.\n5. The author note says the play \"**is set in a small Welsh town called Llareggub**\" — correct spelling here, contradicting the glossary two pages later.\n6. The introductory blurb says \"**Thomas prays to the magnificent God to have mercy on ordinary inhabitants living under the Milk Wood**\" — but it is not Thomas praying; it is the dramatic character **Rev. Eli Jenkins**, and it is his **sunset** poem. Worth a note.\n\n## B.5 CDC exercise questions — EXACT wording (VERIFIED from the textbook PDF, p. 234–235)\n\n> ### Before reading\n> Answer the following questions.\n> a. Why do people offer prayers to the God?\n> b. What do you feel when you visit the mosque, temple, or church? How does the rhyme scheme of the poem reinforce its message?\n\n> ### Reference beyond the text\n> a. Does the God exist? Give your opinion.\n> b. In his Epistle to the author of the book, The Three Impostors (1768), Voltaire says, \"Even if the God didn't exist, it would be necessary to invent him.\" Write an essay highlighting the importance of the God in the society.\n\nCounts: Understanding the text = **5 (a–e)**; Reference to the context = **4 (a–d)**; Reference beyond the text = **2 (a–b)**. Note this unit has **only four** RTC questions, unlike \"A Day\" which has five.\n\n**Three wording points that matter a great deal, all verified against the book:**\n\n1. **The textbook writes \"the God,\" not \"God,\" in six places** — Before reading (a); RTC (a), (b), (c); RBT (a), (b) — plus \"the society\" in RBT (b). This is non-standard English but it is what the book prints. This inconsistency is in the printed book. It is also the giveaway that the CDC compilers were working from a source that titled it from the poem's actual first line. This is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence — settling it would need AustLit, Trove, or the acknowledgements page of a *Scission* edition, none of which I could reach.\n\n**⚠️ IMPORTANT FOR THE STUDY GUIDE — the \"Migrants of Australia\" problem.** Essentially every Nepali study site states that the textbook's version of \"Neighbours\" was \"taken from *Migrants of Australia*, edited by **Harwood Lawler**.\" This appears on acharyar.com.np, ezilearning.com, subodhbhattarai.com, arjundauliya.com.np, kalawati175.com.np and rigidbhanu.blogspot.com in near-identical wording — a pattern consistent with all of them copying a source-note in the CDC textbook itself. **I could find no library catalogue, publisher, or bibliographic record for any book called *Migrants of Australia* edited by Harwood Lawler — treat its existence as UNVERIFIED.** A study guide should say: *the CDC textbook credits \"Migrants of Australia\" ed. Harwood Lawler, but the story's original publication is Winton's collection Scission (1985).*\n\n---\n\n## 3. FULL PLOT, IN ORDER (verified against the full text)\n\nSource of full text: **https://xpressenglish.com/our-stories/neighbours/**\n\n1. **Arrival.** A young married couple move into a small house on an old inner-suburb street. Opening line: *\"When they first moved in, the young couple were wary of the neighbourhood.\"* The house is small, but *\"high ceilings and paned windows\"* give it the feel of an elegant cottage. They had come from the expansive outer suburbs, where good neighbours were *\"seldom seen and never heard.\"* The street is full of **European migrants**, which makes the couple feel foreign in their own city.\n\n2. **The neighbours as the story names them.** Only three nationalities are attached to specific neighbours:\n   - **A Macedonian family on one side (the left)** — including a big woman with \"butcher's arms\" and a small boy with cobalt-blue eyes who watches over the fence.\n   - **A Polish widower on the other side (the right).**\n   - Later, during the pregnancy, **Italian** women (suggesting names) and **Greek** women (in the street) appear.\n   - ✅ **There is no Greek *neighbour* household and no Italian *neighbour* household** — those nationalities only appear as women in the street during the pregnancy. Get this right: it is commonly garbled.\n\n3. **The husband's occupation.** He does **not** have a job; he stays home writing an **academic thesis** while his wife earns the money. His thesis subject is **\"the development of the twentieth-century novel.\"** This is load-bearing for the ending.\n\n4. **The wife's job.** ⚠️ **Never stated as a title.** The text says only that she \"worked\" while he wrote, and that he listened to \"her tales of eccentric patients and hospital incompetence.\" **She works in a hospital**; whether she is a nurse is an inference, not a statement. She later takes maternity leave. A study guide should say \"works at a hospital,\" not \"is a nurse.\"\n\n5. **The noises that disturb them.** *\"The sounds of spitting and washing and daybreak watering came as a shock.\"* Plus: the Macedonians' shouting, ranting and screaming — which the couple took **about six months** to recognise as ordinary conversation, not violence; the Polish widower's constant hammering; and roosters crowing at dusk.\n\n6. **The kitchen garden.** In **autumn** the couple clear rubbish, turn and manure the soil, and plant **leeks, onions, cabbage, brussels sprouts and broad beans**, watched by the neighbours. The neighbours then come to the fence with **unsolicited advice** on spacing, hilling and mulching. The young man is irritated but absorbs the advice anyway. The **Macedonian woman gives the wife garlic cloves** to plant. Later the couple **give away cabbage heads**, receiving **grappa and firewood** in return.\n\n7. **The Muscovy ducks — NOT a pig.** The couple keep **Muscovy ducks** (\"big, silent muscovies\") over winter. In spring the **Macedonian family teaches them to kill, pluck and dress** the birds. Everyone sits on chopping blocks and upturned buckets, swapping stories they barely understand — men butchering, women plucking — amid down and steam. The couple feel \"intoxicated.\" The cat plays with the severed heads while the child pulls its tail. The newcomers find themselves shouting too. **There is no pig and no pig slaughter anywhere in the story.**\n\n8. **The Polish widower's building.** He has no car. He hammers nails into timber and pulls them out again, and hoards salvaged lumber without building anything. He silently **slips through the fence uninvited and rebuilds the couple's collapsed henhouse**. Then in late spring he starts actually constructing — sinking posts, pouring cement — a **two-car garage**, though he has no car. The noise infuriates the couple, who suspect deliberate provocation. He later brings them **barrowfuls of woodscraps** for their fire. They never understand a word he says.\n\n9. **The pregnancy.** It is **unplanned** and shocks them, arriving earlier than their friends' children. The whole street soon knows. People smile constantly; **the deli man gives her chocolates and him cigarettes** (he doesn't smoke and stores them). **Italian women suggest names. Greek women lift her skirt in the street to feel her belly and predict a boy. The woman next door knits a complete baby outfit with booties and beanie.** Her own reaction is mixed — flattered and grateful, but also claustrophobic and peeved.\n\n10. **The ending, exactly.** Labour comes on suddenly. The husband **drops his thesis** to phone for help; the wife starts blacking the stove; the **midwife** arrives and helps her finish it. He runs about uselessly while she directs him. **Going out for firewood at dusk, he sees faces along both fences — he counts twelve** — the Macedonians waving and shouting what he takes to be good wishes. Through the night she dozes between contractions, walks, shouts, bathes, eats ice, asks for liverwurst; the midwife croons; he rubs her back and oils her lips. She gives birth **in a squat, by firelight**, the floor shaking; he is struck by \"the power of her, the sophistication of her.\" **A boy is born**, lifted to the breast trailing cord and vernix, one eye on his father. The baby briefly loses the nipple and cries. Hearing shouting, the husband goes to the back door: *\"On the Macedonian side of the fence, a small queue of bleary faces looked up, cheering, and the young man began to weep.\"* Final line: **\"The twentieth-century novel had not prepared him for this.\"**\n    - **Who weeps: the young man (the husband).** Not the wife, not the neighbours.\n    - **Who cheers: the Macedonian neighbours**, in a queue along the fence.\n\n11. **Named characters: NONE. ✅ Your belief is correct.** No character in the story has a proper name. Everyone is \"the young man,\" \"the young woman,\" \"the Polish widower,\" \"the midwife,\" \"the child,\" \"the Macedonian woman.\" The only proper nouns are places and nationalities (Moreton Bay figs; Macedonian, Polish, Italian, Greek).\n\n---\n\n## 4. CONCRETE DETAILS A STUDY GUIDE MUST GET RIGHT\n\n| Detail | Verdict |\n|---|---|\n| **Pig slaughter** | ❌ **FALSE.** The word \"pig\" does not appear. It is **Muscovy ducks**, killed and plucked in spring, taught by the Macedonian family. |\n| **Chopping of wood (with an axe)** | ❌ **NOT IN THE STORY.** No axe, no wood-chopping scene. Wood features constantly — the widower's salvaged lumber, his hammering nails in and out, gifts of firewood and \"barrowfuls of woodscraps,\" woodsmoke, and the husband fetching wood during labour — but nobody chops wood. (Note: *chopping blocks* are sat on during the duck-plucking. And \"My Father's Axe\" is a *different* story in *Scission* — a likely source of the confusion.) |\n| **The fence** | ✅ **REAL and central.** A recurring boundary-symbol: the Macedonian boy peers over it with only his eyes showing; neighbours lean on it to give garden advice; the Polish widower slips **through** it uninvited to rebuild the henhouse; **twelve faces** line both fences during the birth; the cheering queue at the end is \"on the Macedonian side of the fence.\" |\n| **\"Hawking and spitting\"** | ⚠️ **HALF FALSE.** **Spitting is real** — *\"The sounds of spitting and washing and daybreak watering came as a shock.\"* But the word **\"hawking\" does not appear in the text.** Do not use the phrase \"hawking and spitting.\" |\n| **Polish widower's habits** | ✅ **REAL.** Widower, no car; hammers nails into timber and pulls them out again; stockpiles salvaged wood without building; silently rebuilds the couple's collapsed henhouse without being asked; then builds a **two-car garage** (infuriating noise); brings them firewood scraps; his speech is never understood. |\n| **The young man's thesis subject** | ✅ **REAL and exact: \"the development of the twentieth-century novel.\"** He is a house-husband supported by his wife. |\n| **The wife's job** | ⚠️ Hospital work — **never given a title.** Say \"works at a hospital,\" not \"nurse.\" |\n| **The dog** | ✅ **REAL.** The couple own *\"a docile, moulting collie\"* which they walk in the park; the neighbours are initially wary of it. Frequently omitted from summaries. |\n| **The word \"wondering\"** | ❌ **NOT IN THE STORY.** Neither \"wonder\" nor \"wondering\" appears. There is no passage where the man \"realises something about his wondering.\" The closest real material: he looks out of his **study window** over rooftops toward the fig trees early in the story, and **separately and much later**, outdoors while fetching firewood during labour, **\"He counted twelve faces.\"** These are two distinct moments — do not merge them. |\n| **The garlic** | ✅ Real — the Macedonian woman gives the wife **garlic cloves** to plant. |\n| **The chocolates and cigarettes** | ✅ Real — from the **deli man**; the husband doesn't smoke and stores them. |\n| **Six months** | ✅ Real — roughly how long it took the couple to realise the shouting was ordinary conversation. |\n\n---\n\n## 5. THEMES AND CRITICAL POINTS\n\nSource: https://litbug.com/neighbours-summary-and-analysis/ (plus the text itself)\n\n- **Multiculturalism.** A street where Anglo-Australians and European migrants coexist. Lacking a shared language, they communicate through **gestures and selfless actions** — garlic cloves, grappa, a rebuilt henhouse, knitted booties, woodscraps. Winton's claim is that harmony across cultural difference is achievable without shared language.\n- **Prejudice, and that it runs both ways.** This is the most-missed critical point. The couple are repelled by the Macedonian boy urinating outdoors and by the noise; **but the Macedonians equally disapprove** — of the couple's late rising and of the \"gender imbalance\" of a wife who works while the husband stays home. Assumptions are mutual, and both sides are wrong.\n- **Postcolonial reading.** Litbug frames the story as a corrective to colonial writing that painted other peoples as \"uncultured who need to be civilised.\" The migrants turn out to be the more generous, more communal party.\n- **Community vs. privacy / Anglo-Australian reserve.** The couple come from suburbs where neighbours were \"seldom seen and never heard.\" Privacy is their default value; the street's default is involvement. The widower crossing the fence uninvited first reads as **violation**, then as **gift** — this reversal is the story's structural pivot. Litbug does not use the phrase \"Anglo-Australian reserve\" but describes exactly this.\n- **Belonging is earned, not inherited.** Australian identity is grounded in \"fellow feeling and humanity\" rather than nativity — a \"welcoming smile\" can suffice.\n- **Books vs. life — the central irony.** The husband's thesis on the twentieth-century novel is the engine of the ending. Twentieth-century fiction (with its alienation, its stereotypes of Europe, its isolated modern individual) **schooled him in exactly the wrong expectations**. His tears are the collapse of a literary framework against lived experience. The thesis is literally abandoned mid-sentence when labour starts.\n- **Winton's style.** Terse, spare, pared-back prose; third-person omniscient (read by Litbug as a deliberate refusal to grant authority to any one culture); heavy reliance on sensory detail and sound; **seasonal structure** — autumn → winter → spring — tracking the couple's thaw, with winter cold paradoxically generating communal warmth and the spring births (ducks, then the baby) closing the cycle; a biblical register (the couple as \"sojourners in a foreign land\"); contrast as the governing device.\n- **Anonymity as technique.** No character is named — universalising the situation and forcing the reader to see people as types first, then as individuals, mirroring the couple's own arc.\n\n---\n\n## 6. THE CDC TEXTBOOK EXERCISE QUESTIONS (VERBATIM)\n\n**Primary source used:** https://www.acharyar.com.np/2023/01/neighbors-summary-exercise-grade-12.html\n**Cross-checked against:**\n- https://nebenglishguide.acharyar.com.np/2023/01/neighbors-grade-12.html\n- https://iswori.com.np/neighbours-exercise-question-answers-class-12-english/\n- https://www.ezilearning.com/neighbours-by-tim-winton-summary-question-answer.html\n- https://www.skl.com.np/2021/08/neighbours-by-tim-winton-exercise.html\n\nI could not obtain the official CDC PDF (https://moecdc.gov.np/content/26/english-grade-12/ renders its download link via script; no direct PDF URL was retrievable). The text below is what four independent Nepali sites agree on.\n\n### Understanding the text\n*(Preceded in the textbook by the instruction: \"Answer the following questions.\")*\n\na. Describe how the young couple's house looked like.\nb. How did the young couple identify their neighbours at the beginning of their arrival?\nc. How did the neighbours help the young couple in the kitchen garden?\nd. Why were the people in the neighbourhood surprised at the role of the young man and his wife in their family?\ne. How did the neighbours respond to the woman's pregnancy?\nf. Why did the young man begin to weep at the end of the story?\ng. Why do you think the author did not characterize the persons in the story with proper names?\n\n### Reference to the context\n\na. The story shows that linguistic and cultural barriers do not create any obstacle in human relationship. Cite some examples from the story where the neighbours have transcended such barriers.\nb. The last sentence of the story reads \"The twentieth-century novel had not prepared him for this.\" In your view, what differences did the young man find between twentieth-century novels and human relations?\nc. A Nepali proverb says \"Neighbors are companions for wedding procession as well as for funeral procession.\" Does this proverb apply in the story? Justify.\nd. The author has dealt with an issue of multiculturalism in the story. Why do you think multiculturalism has become a major issue in the present world?\n\n### Reference beyond the text\n\na. Write an essay on Celebration of Childbirth in my Community.\nb. Do the people in your community respond with similar reactions upon the pregnancy and childbirth as depicted in the story? Give a couple of examples.\n\n### Where sources disagree\n\n1. **Understanding the text (b)** — acharyar, nebenglishguide and iswori all give **\"identify their neighbours at the beginning of their arrival.\"** ezilearning gives \"…**in** the beginning of their arrival.\" skl.com.np renders it \"How did the young couple **recognize** their neighbours **in** the beginning of their arrival?\" — a paraphrase, and the clear outlier. **Use the 3-source majority: \"identify … at the beginning.\"**\n2. **Understanding the text (d)** — ezilearning spells it \"neighborhood\" (US), others \"neighbourhood\" (UK). The textbook uses UK spelling throughout, so \"neighbourhood.\"\n3. **Reference to the context (c)** — the proverb is quoted with the **US spelling \"Neighbors\"** in acharyar and iswori, but **\"Neighbours\"** in ezilearning. The inconsistency (US spelling inside a UK-spelling textbook) is odd but is reproduced by the two most reliable sources, suggesting it is a genuine typo in the CDC textbook. Flag it rather than silently correcting it.\n4. **Numbering** — ezilearning presents the questions unlettered as 1–7 and omits \"Reference beyond the text\" entirely. All other sources use **a–g / a–d / a–b**, which matches CDC house style across the book. Use letters.\n5. **Counts are consistent across all sources:** Understanding the text = **7 (a–g)**; Reference to the context = **4 (a–d)**; Reference beyond the text = **2 (a–b)**.\n\n---\n\n## SUMMARY OF CORRECTIONS TO YOUR ASSUMPTIONS\n\n1. ❌ **\"Minimum of Two, 1987\" is wrong.** \"Neighbours\" is in **Scission (1985)**.\n2. ❌ **No pig slaughter.** It is **Muscovy ducks**.\n3. ❌ **No wood-chopping / axe.**\n4. ❌ **No \"hawking.\"** Spitting only.\n5. ❌ **No \"wondering.\"** That word never appears; there is no realisation about \"his wondering.\"\n6. ❌ **No Greek or Italian neighbours.** Macedonian family + Polish widower only; Greek and Italian women appear briefly during the pregnancy.\n7. ✅ **Fence — correct and central.**\n8. ✅ **Thesis on the twentieth-century novel — correct.**\n9. ✅ **No named characters — correct.**\n10. ⚠️ **Wife's job is \"hospital,\" not \"nurse.\"**\n11. ⚠️ **New finding:** the textbook credits \"*Migrants of Australia*, ed. Harwood Lawler\" — a book I could not verify exists.\n12. ✅ **A free CC BY-SA 3.0 photo of Winton exists on Wikimedia Commons.** agentId: ae1e47f48692053e1 (use SendMessage with to: 'ae1e47f48692053e1', summary: '<5-10 word recap>' to continue this agent)\n<usage>subagent_tokens: 66069\ntool_uses: 50\nduration_ms: 640820</usage>"}
