AUTHOR FACTS**\n\n- Born Catherine (\"Kate\") O'Flaherty, St. Louis, Missouri, 8 February 1850. Second child of Thomas O'Flaherty (Co. Galway, Ireland) and Eliza Faris of St. Louis; mother's family French-descended, so Chopin grew up bilingual/bicultural. Educated at the St. Louis Academy of the Sacred Heart, 1855–1868. Father killed in a railroad accident, 1855.\n- Married Oscar Chopin of Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, 1870. Settled in New Orleans, where he was a cotton factor. Six children (five sons, one daughter) 1871–1879. Moved to Cloutierville, Natchitoches Parish, 1879 after his business failed. This is the Creole/Cajun Louisiana world of her fiction.\n- Oscar died of malaria, 1882; widowed at 32 with six children; never remarried. (Biographer Emily Toth records an affair with a local planter, 1883–84.) Returned to St. Louis; mother died 1885. Her physician-friend Dr. Frederick Kolbenheyer urged her to write. Strongly influenced by Maupassant. First story published in the *St. Louis Post-Dispatch*, 1889; first novel *At Fault*, privately printed, 1890.\n- *Bayou Folk* (Houghton Mifflin, 1894), 23 stories — a success, c. 100 press notices, praised for dialect. *A Night in Acadie* (Way and Williams, 1897), 21 stories. *The Awakening* (Herbert S. Stone, 1899; completed 1898).\n- *The Awakening*'s reception was hostile: reviewers called it \"morbid,\" \"unhealthy,\" \"poison\"; Willa Cather dismissed it. The often-repeated claim that the St. Louis library banned it is UNVERIFIED (katechopin.org says so explicitly); the Evanston, Illinois public library did remove it from open shelves in 1902. Her planned third collection *A Vocation and a Voice* was cancelled and not published separately until 1991.\n- Died 22 August 1904, St. Louis (cerebral hemorrhage after a hot day at the 1904 World's Fair); buried Calvary Cemetery.\n- Revival: Cyrille Arnavon in the 1940s–50s (French translation of *The Awakening* as *Edna*); Kenneth Eble's 1956 article and 1964 paperback introduction; the decisive turn was 1969, when Per Seyersted published his critical biography plus *The Complete Works of Kate Chopin*. Feminist criticism dominated thereafter.\n- Style: local colour / regionalism of Creole and Cajun Louisiana; French-inflected dialect and vocabulary; compressed Maupassant-like form; restrained irony; proto-feminist interest in female desire and autonomy; and famously open, withheld endings — katechopin.org groups \"A Respectable Woman\" with \"The Storm,\" \"The Story of an Hour,\" \"Fedora\" and \"Désirée's Baby\" as stories readers argue about because of their last lines.\n\n**2. PUBLICATION CONTEXT of \"A Respectable Woman\"**\n\n- Written: 20 January 1894.\n- First published: *Vogue*, 15 February 1894. (*Vogue* published nineteen Chopin stories in all.)\n- Reprinted in her collection *A Night in Acadie* (1897) — CONFIRMED. (Not *Bayou Folk*, which appeared in 1894 but was already set.)\n- Setting: Gaston Baroda's Louisiana sugar plantation, \"apparently in the 1880s or early 1890s.\"\n- Note for teaching: the Nepali textbook's headnote says the story is \"taken out from her collection The Awakening and Other Short Stories (2005).\" That is a modern reprint anthology, not a Chopin collection. The textbook statement is misleading.\n\n**3. FULL PLOT, in order**\n\n1. Mrs. Baroda is \"a little provoked\" to learn Gaston has invited his college friend Gouvernail, now a journalist, to the plantation for a week or two. They had entertained heavily all winter and spent time in New Orleans; she wanted \"unbroken rest\" and an undisturbed tête-à-tête with her husband.\n2. She has never met Gouvernail but has formed an image: she \"pictured him tall, slim, cynical; with eyeglasses, and his hands in his pockets\" — and she did not like that image.\n3. The real man contradicts it: \"slim enough, but he wasn't very tall nor very cynical,\" no eyeglasses, hands not in pockets. She rather likes him on sight, and cannot explain why.\n4. She can find none of the \"brilliant and promising traits\" Gaston had promised. He sits \"mute and receptive\" against her chatty eagerness; courteous, but makes \"no direct appeal to her approval or even esteem.\"\n5. At the plantation he likes to sit on the wide portico in the shade of a big Corinthian pillar, smoking a cigar, listening to Gaston on sugar planting. \"This is what I call living,\" he says. He befriends the dogs, declines to fish, shows no eagerness to shoot grosbecs.\n6. His self-sufficiency puzzles then irritates her: she \"gave over being puzzled and remained piqued.\" First she leaves the two men alone; when he takes no exception to that either, she imposes her company — walks to the mill, along the batture — \"persistently sought to penetrate the reserve.\"\n7. She asks Gaston \"When is he going—your friend?\" and says \"he tires me frightfully\"; she would like him better if he gave trouble. Gaston, in her dressing-room, calls her \"full of surprises, ma belle,\" says she is making a \"commotion\" over him, and explains Gouvernail is \"run down by overwork.\" She retorts that Gaston had called him \"a man of ideas,\" announces she is going to the city in the morning to have her spring gowns fitted, and will be at her Aunt Octavie's until Gouvernail is gone.\n8. NIGHT SCENE: she sits alone on a bench beneath a live oak at the edge of the gravel walk, thoughts \"so confused,\" feeling only \"a distinct necessity to quit her home in the morning.\" She hears footsteps and sees only \"the approaching red point of a lighted cigar\" — she knows it is Gouvernail because her husband does not smoke. Her white gown gives her away. He throws away the cigar, sits beside her, and hands her the filmy white scarf Gaston sent out. He makes a commonplace remark about the night air, then murmurs, half to himself, the Whitman lines (see §6). \"She made no reply to this apostrophe to the night, which, indeed, was not addressed to her.\"\n9. His reserve melts. In \"a low, hesitating drawl\" he speaks of the old college days with Gaston, of \"keen and blind ambitions,\" and of what is left now: \"a philosophic acquiescence to the existing order\" — only a wish to exist with \"now and then a little whiff of genuine life.\"\n10. THE TURN: \"Her mind only vaguely grasped what he was saying. Her physical being was for the moment predominant.\" She is \"not thinking of his words, only drinking in the tones of his voice.\" She wanted to reach out in the darkness and touch him \"upon the face or the lips\"; she wanted to draw close and whisper against his cheek — \"she did not care what\" — \"as she might have done if she had not been a respectable woman.\"\n11. WHAT SHE DOES NOT DO: \"The stronger the impulse grew to bring herself near him, the further, in fact, did she draw away from him.\" She rises and leaves as soon as she can without rudeness. Before she reaches the house he has lit a fresh cigar and \"ended his apostrophe to the night.\"\n12. She is greatly tempted to tell her husband — \"who was also her friend\" — of \"this folly,\" but does not: \"Besides being a respectable woman she was a very sensible one; and she knew there are some battles in life which a human being must fight alone.\"\n13. FLIGHT: she takes an early morning train to the city before Gaston is up, and does not return until Gouvernail has left. When Gaston wants him back that summer, his desire \"yielded to his wife's strenuous opposition.\"\n14. CLOSING: before the year ends she herself proposes inviting Gouvernail again. Gaston is \"surprised and delighted\": \"I am glad, chere amie, to know that you have finally overcome your dislike for him; truly he did not deserve it.\" Her reply — the last line, after \"pressing a long, tender kiss upon his lips,\" laughingly: \"I have overcome everything! You will see. This time I shall be very nice to him.\"\n  - Textual note: Wikisource/Chopin's text reads \"I have overcome everything! you will see.\" (lowercase \"you\"); the Nepali textbook capitalises it. Same wording otherwise.\n  - AMBIGUITY: \"overcome everything\" is deliberately unresolved. Reading A: she has mastered the attraction and can now be a gracious hostess. Reading B: she has overcome the scruple — i.e. respectability itself — and intends to act on the desire. Reading C (weakest but arguable): she has overcome only her self-deception. katechopin.org states the ending \"has several possible meanings\" and does not adjudicate. Chopin supplies no narratorial gloss after that line; the story simply stops. Do not teach Reading B as the \"correct answer.\"\n\n**4. CHARACTERS**\n\n- **Mrs. Baroda** — no first name is ever given in the story (worth noting: she exists textually as a wife). Wealthy plantation mistress, sociable, talkative, used to managing people; \"provoked\" and then \"piqued\" by a guest she cannot manage. Both respectable and, Chopin insists, \"a very sensible one.\"\n- **Gaston Baroda** — her husband, a sugar planter; \"frank and wordy hospitality,\" affectionate, uses French endearments to her (\"ma belle,\" \"chère amie\"); admires Gouvernail as clever and \"a man of ideas.\" He is trusting to the point of obtuseness — his misreading of her final line is the mechanism of the irony.\n- **Gouvernail** — Gaston's old college friend, now a journalist; \"in no sense a society man or 'a man about town'\"; run down by overwork. Quiet, \"mute and receptive,\" self-sufficient, unselfconscious, a cigar-smoker, reads/quotes Whitman. Not diffident — his reserve is \"the result of moods,\" not constitution. \"A lovable, inoffensive fellow.\"\n- **Other Chopin works featuring Gouvernail** (CONFIRMED by katechopin.org): \"Athénaïse\" (written 10–28 April 1895; published in *Atlantic Monthly*, August and September 1896, in two instalments; collected in *A Night in Acadie*), where he is a journalist and long-term lodger at Sylvie's New Orleans boarding house; and *The Awakening* (1899), a cameo at Edna Pontellier's dinner party in Chapter XXX, where he again quotes poetry. katechopin.org calls him one of Chopin's rare male \"sensitive, intelligent, insightful characters\"; cf. Joyce Dyer's essay \"Gouvernail, Kate Chopin's Sensitive Bachelor.\"\n  - The specific lines he quotes at Edna's party are from Swinburne (\"There was a graven image of Desire...\") — UNVERIFIED in this session; I could not confirm it from a fetched source, only that he quotes poetry there.\n  - The description of Gouvernail as holding \"advanced opinions\" is attributed by katechopin.org's \"A Respectable Woman\" page to \"Athénaïse\" (and the page links it to *Vogue*'s readership under editor Josephine Redding). The \"Athénaïse\" page does not contain the phrase, so the exact wording is only single-sourced.\n- **NAME MEANING**: *gouvernail* is French for a rudder or tiller (a helm). katechopin.org glosses it as suggesting someone \"who knows the direction, who understands where things are headed.\" Why it matters: the passive, seemingly directionless guest is the one who steers — he alters the course of Mrs. Baroda's inner life without intending or noticing anything. The irony is that the rudder is unaware it is steering. Also note \"Aunt Octavie\" and \"batture\" as the same Louisiana-French texture.\n\n**5. THEMES AND CRITICAL READINGS**\n\n- **Desire vs. respectability.** The story's engine is not adultery but the *thought* of it. Chopin locates the transgression entirely in an unacted impulse, and stages the conflict physically: attraction expressed as recoil (\"the stronger the impulse... the further... did she draw away\").\n- **The title.** \"Respectable\" is a social label, not a moral description. The phrase appears inside the narration as the sole thing preventing her — \"as she might have done if she had not been a respectable woman\" — so respectability functions as external constraint rather than internal virtue. The title is therefore ironic: it names what she is called, and the story shows what that label suppresses.\n- **The double meaning of \"I have overcome everything.\"** Gaston supplies one antecedent (\"your dislike for him\"); her \"everything\" exceeds it. Read against §12 (\"some battles... must fight alone\"), \"overcome\" can mean either *conquered the desire* or *conquered the inhibition*. \"This time I shall be very nice to him\" is equally double: hostessly courtesy, or something more. Chopin's refusal to resolve it is the point; the pleasure of the ending is that both readings are fully supported by the text.\n- **Marriage and female autonomy.** Her marriage is affectionate and companionate — Gaston is \"also her friend\" — yet she cannot speak to him. The nameless \"Mrs. Baroda\" claims her interiority precisely by withholding it. Her flight to the city under the pretext of \"spring gowns\" is a woman using a permitted social movement to accomplish a forbidden private one.\n- **The Whitman allusion's erotic charge.** The quoted passage is from an ecstatic, frankly sensual apostrophe (\"Press close bare-bosom'd night—press close magnetic nourishing night!... mad naked summer night\"). Gouvernail quotes the *middle* of it and later \"ended his apostrophe to the night\" offstage — so the erotic content is simultaneously introduced and deflected. The narrator's insistence that it \"was not addressed to her\" invites the reader to notice that she received it anyway. Choosing Whitman, the period's byword for sexual candour, marks the story's stance as much as its content; note also that the story appeared in *Vogue*, a magazine of \"advanced opinions.\"\n- **Irony.** Situational (the boring guest becomes the dangerous one); dramatic (Gaston celebrates the very reversal that threatens him); and structural (the \"respectable woman\" of the title is defined by what she nearly did).\n- Recent criticism listed by katechopin.org for this story: Ailee Cho, \"Chopin and the Desire of Flight,\" *Nineteenth Century Literature in English* 7 (2003): 119–134.\n\n**6. THE WHITMAN LINES**\n\nAs printed in the story (and in the Nepali textbook, p. 186):\n\n  \"'Night of south winds—night of the large few stars! Still nodding night—'\"\n\nSource: Walt Whitman, \"Song of Myself,\" **section 21**, in *Leaves of Grass* (1891–92, the \"deathbed\" edition; katechopin.org says the 1892 edition). Verified against Project Gutenberg's *Leaves of Grass*. The full passage reads:\n\n  \"Press close bare-bosom'd night--press close magnetic nourishing night! / Night of south winds--night of the large few stars! / Still nodding night--mad naked summer night.\"\n\nSo Gouvernail begins mid-apostrophe and breaks off before \"mad naked summer night\" — Chopin cuts exactly where the eroticism becomes explicit.\n\n**7. THEMES AND CRITICAL POINTS**\nFrom the EBSCO/Magill's article (Sahni & Lutz) plus the text itself:\n- **Irony of the title**: the story \"looks at the problem of old age from two different angles\"; the father's \"final act of rebellion makes the reader wonder whether the son's almost tyrannical control… is justified in the name of filial devotion. Viewed in this light, the title of the story becomes ironic.\"\n- **Filial duty inverted / the tyranny of care**: the narrator's own pivot is explicit — \"his masterly efficiency was nothing but cold heartlessness, his authority was only tyranny in disguise.\" Rakesh's justification is duty (\"I have my duty to you papa\"); the effect is deprivation.\n- **Old age and loss of autonomy**: food, betel, movement, posture and speech are all decided for him; his name disappears from the gate; medicine \"became his diet\".\n- **Modern medicine vs. traditional life**: hygiene and epidemiology (cholera, typhoid, gastroenteritis), weighed aata, pills and tonics, the stomach pump — set against halwa, jalebis, betel, brass tumbler, the string-bed under the stars.\n- **Generational conflict and the Indian joint family**: three generations under one roof; the daughter-in-law as the regime's smirking instrument; the grandchild as the old man's only conduit to pleasure; feet-touching as the story's recurring index of respect — and the closing refusal of it (feet tucked away) as the reversal.\n- **Class mobility and its costs**: illiterate, kerosene-depot/vegetable-market origins to \"the richest doctor in town\"; neighbours' envy; parental ambition realised and then turning on the parent.\n- **Note**: this story is unusual in Desai's output for being centred on male characters, per the Magill's article.\n\n**6. She extends her arms: **\"Give me back my husband!\"**\n4. The Actress stares in \"speechless bewilderment\"; the wife identifies him unprompted: blond, not tall, spectacles, a lawyer, her manager's lawyer, **Alfred**.\n5. Actress: \"Oh! She weeps.\n9. **The wife's big aria** (the play's best set-piece, and the \"ordinary woman vs actress\" question in the exercise): \"One night you dress like a royal princess, and the next night you undress like a Greek goddess. You blacken your eyebrows and redden your lips and wax your lashes and paint your face. You have cosmetics and bright lights to make you seem beautiful. An author's lines to make you seem witty and wise… What chance have I against you in my cheap little frock, my own lips and eyebrows, my own unstudied ways? … I haven't got Mr. Shakespeare to write beautiful speeches for me. In reality you may be more stupid than I am, but I admit that when it comes to alluring men I am no match for you.\"\n10. **The pivot.** The Actress, \"[Without anger, slowly, regards her appraisingly]\": \"This is a very interesting case.\" — \"Yours.\"\n11. **The diagnostic cross-examination** (four quick leading questions): haven't you and your husband been getting on badly of late? / you used to be very affectionate? / and of late you have been quite cold? — all answered \"Yes.\"\n12. **The fabricated explanation:** \"Of course! A typical case…. It is perfectly clear that your husband has been **playing a little comedy to make you jealous, to revive your interest in him**.\" Asked whether this has happened before: \"**Endless times.** It happens to every actress who is moderately pretty and successful… There is scarcely a man connected with the theater who doesn't make use of us in that way… authors, composers, scene designers, lawyers, orchestra leaders, even the managers themselves. To regain a wife or sweetheart's affections all they need to do is invent a love affair with one of us. The wife is always so ready to believe it… At least we have the consolation of knowing that we are the means of making many a marriage happy which might otherwise have ended in the divorce court.\"\n13. **She then demolishes each piece of evidence in turn** — and, crucially, **volunteers items the wife had not mentioned**: he left the letter on the desk deliberately (\"Trust a lawyer never to do that unintentionally\"); he phones in a flower order in the morning and cancels it on reaching his office; and then, unprompted, **\"By the way, hasn't he a lock of my hair?\"** — Wife: \"Yes. In his desk drawer. I brought it with me.\" Actress: \"They bribe my hair-dresser to steal from me. It is a wonder I have any hair left at all.\" Then: \"hasn't he left any of my love letters lying around?\" Wife, in alarm: \"No.\" Actress: \"Don't be alarmed. I haven't written him any.\"\n14. She goes further, offering the counterfactual: had Alfred asked her frankly (\"I say, Sara, will you do something for me?…\") she would gladly have written him \"a letter that would have made you weep into your pillow for a fortnight. I wrote ten like that for a very eminent playwright once. But he had no luck with them. His wife was such a proper person she returned them all to him unread.\"\n15. Wife: \"How clever you are! How good!\" Actress: \"I'm neither better nor worse than any other girl in the theater. Even though you do consider us such monsters.\" Wife, contritely: \"I have been a perfect fool.\"\n16. **The closest line to your remembered \"he is a silly little man\" — and it is NOT that.** The exact text is: \"Well, **you do look a bit silly**, standing there with tears in your eyes, and your face flushed with happiness because you have discovered that **a little blond man with spectacles** loves you, after all. NO — none found.** I checked Yang & Yang (*Selected Stories of Lu Hsun*, FLP Beijing 1960; reissued 2007 as *Lu Xun Selected Works*; also the 4-vol 1980 *Selected Works*), Lyell (*Diary of a Madman and Other Stories*, Hawaii 1990), Lovell (*The Real Story of Ah-Q and Other Tales of China*, Penguin 2009), Wang Chi-chen (*Ah Q and Others*, Columbia 1941), George Kin Leung (1926), Snow & Wales (*Living China*, 1936), Kowallis (*The Lyrical Lu Xun*, 1996), Cheng (*Jottings under Lamplight*, 2017). **No collection in any of these is called \"Hometown\" or \"My Old Home.\"** One near-miss to avoid: archive.org holds \"Gu xiang: Lu Xun zhuan ji\" (2010) — that is a **Chinese-language** volume, not an English collection.\n\n**The accurate statement for your purposes:** *\"My Old Home\" (故鄉, \"Guxiang,\" also translated \"Hometown\") was written in January 1921, first published in New Youth (新青年) vol. 9, no. 1, on 1 May 1921, and collected in Nahan (吶喊, variously translated Call to Arms / Outcry / Cheering from the Sidelines), published 1923.* The Nepali textbook has mistaken the **story** title for a **collection** title.\n\n**Which translation the textbook is using.** The wording is diagnostic, and it points to **Yang Xianyi & Gladys Yang**, but in a **later, pinyin-revised printing**, not the 1960 original. Evidence:\n\n- The 1960/1972 Yang & Yang text (on marxists.org) uses **Wade-Giles**: \"Jun-tu\" (glossed \"Intercalary Earth\"), \"Hung-erh,\" \"Shui-sheng,\" and the singular **\"the Compass\"**; it renders the official's post not as \"Daotai\" but as **\"intendant of a circuit\"**; and Mrs. Yang is \"Beancurd Beauty\" / \"the Compass.\" It does use **\"zha\"**.\n- Your textbook has **pinyin** \"Runtu,\" \"Hong'er,\" \"Shuisheng,\" plus \"Compasses\" (plural) and \"Daotai\" (untranslated).\n\nSo: the **\"zha\"** romanisation, the \"Compass(es)\" nickname and the melon-guarding scene are unmistakably the **Yang & Yang** lineage — but the pinyin names and retained \"Daotai\" indicate a **revised/reprinted Yang & Yang** (e.g. the 1980 four-volume *Lu Xun: Selected Works* or the 2007 *Lu Xun Selected Works*, both FLP, which convert to pinyin), or a textbook editor's light re-romanisation of it. It is **not** Lyell and **not** Lovell. **UNVERIFIED:** \"busy-monther\" — I could not locate this word in any edition; it is very likely a **typo or OCR corruption in the Nepali textbook**, most plausibly for \"busybody\" (or a garbling of a phrase about Mrs. Yang). Recommend you treat it as a textbook error rather than a translator's choice.\n\nFor completeness, Wang Chi-chen (1941) renders 故鄉 as **\"My native heath\"** (confirmed from the edition's contents note) — so the user's alternative \"My Native Land\" matches no standard translator exactly. Lyell's and Lovell's renderings of the story title are **UNVERIFIED** (no table of contents obtainable); both are commonly cited as \"Hometown,\" and English Wikipedia's Lu Xun bibliography does read 'My Old Home, also translated as \"Hometown\" (故鄉)' — but attributes \"Hometown\" to no translator.\n\n---\n\n## 3. CRITICAL / CONTEXTUAL POINTS\n\n### Autobiographical basis — now VERIFIED to the day, from Lu Xun's own diary\n\nThis was the strongest find. Lu Xun's 1919 diary (己未日記, Chinese Wikisource) confirms:\n\n- **10 July 1919** — first viewed the Badaowan house; **23 July** — agreed to buy the Luo family's property; **4 November** — paid 1,350 and completed the handover; **21 November 1919** — 「上午與二弟眷屬俱移入八道彎宅」, moved in with Zhou Zuoren's household.\n- **1 December 1919** — left Beijing: 「晨至前門乘京奉車，午抵天津換津浦車。」 (Qianmen, Peking–Mukden train; Tianjin at noon, changed to the Tianjin–Pukou line). 2 Dec Shanghai, 3 Dec Hangzhou.\n- **4 December 1919** — 「上午渡錢江，乘越安輪，晚抵紹興城，即乘轎回家。」 Crossed the Qiantang River, took the SS Yue'an, reached Shaoxing city that evening, sedan chair home.\n- **23 December 1919** — 「午後畫售屋押。」 Signed/sealed the deed for the **sold house** that afternoon.\n- **24 December 1919** — 「下午以舟二艘奉母偕三弟及眷屬攜行李發紹興…」 Left Shaoxing in **two boats** with his mother, third brother Zhou Jianren and dependents and the baggage. (That night a lantern caught fire and he burned a finger smothering it.)\n- **29 December 1919** — 「晨發天津，午抵前門站…下午俱到家。」 Reached Qianmen station at noon, met by Zhou Zuoren; all home that afternoon.\n\nSo **yes, 1–29 December 1919, and the story's frame — the return, the sale of the old house, the departure by boat with the family — maps directly onto this trip.** Two refinements: (i) the purchase of the Beijing house was **completed before** the Shaoxing sale, not after, so Chinese Wikipedia's compressed \"1919年11月…賣掉紹興的老宅，合力購置\" has the sequence backwards; (ii) the diary spells it **八道彎**, not 八道灣/八道湾. Note also the story was written **thirteen months after** the trip, and the trip fell in the May Fourth year itself.\n\n**UNVERIFIED:** no source I reached *explicitly states* \"故鄉 is based on the December 1919 journey.\" The correspondence is universally assumed and the diary makes it near-certain, but if you need a citation for the claim itself, cite the diary and the story side by side rather than an authority.\n\n### Runtu's real-life model — VERIFIED, with a name correction\n\n**章運水 / Zhang Yunshui** was his real name; **Lu Xun altered it to 章閏水 (Zhang Runshui)**, whence the character 閏土 (Runtu). Chinese Wikipedia's article is titled 章闰水. Details:\n\n- Born **1879**, Duputsun village, Shangyu county, Shaoxing prefecture (now Daoxu, Shangyu district).\n- The families were already acquainted: 「章家和鲁迅的周家原为熟识」. His father **章福慶 (Zhang Fuqing)** was a **bamboo craftsman** who did bamboo work for the Zhou family; his mother **阿長 (A Chang)** was the Zhou family's **nanny** — i.e. the \"Chang Mama\" (長媽媽) of Lu Xun's memoirs. Zhang lived in the Zhou household as a boy; the two called each other 「阿水」 and 「大阿官」.\n- He is described as 「质朴老实」 (plain and honest) and taught Lu Xun **bird-trapping** and told him about the sandy shore's animals and plants and the **jumping fish** (跳魚) — all of which appear in the story.\n- **Shuisheng in the story corresponds to Zhang's eldest son, 章啟生 (Zhang Qisheng).**\n- His later life confirms the story's economics: after his father died in **1903** he supported the family alone on **six mu of thin sandy land**; 「收获粮食缴完租税后所剩不多」 — after paying rent and taxes little remained — and 「起早摸黑地干，还是养不活一家人」. In the **1934 Shaoxing drought** the harvest failed, creditors forced him to **sell the six mu**, and he fell back on rented land and wage labour, dying in poverty and illness aged 55.\n- **Date-of-death discrepancy:** the article's infobox says **1936** and its text says 「1936年，章運水在贫病交加中去世，终年55岁」, while the opening template and the drought narrative point to **1934**. Given birth in 1879, age 55 fits **1934**. Flag as inconsistent; **1934** is the more internally coherent.\n- His grandson **章貴 (Zhang Gui)** served as deputy director of the Shaoxing Lu Xun Memorial Museum, retiring in 1993 — a neat historical coda worth mentioning in teaching notes.\n\n### The silver neck ring and the Buddha vow — CONFIRMED (Yang & Yang text)\n\nYoung Runtu wears \"a gleaming silver necklet round his neck,\" because his father \"had made a pledge with the gods and buddhas, using the necklet as a talisman.\" The point for annotation: it is an **apotropaic charm** — a vow made to the gods and Buddha to protect a child (typically an only or precious son) from early death, the ring symbolically \"tethering\" the child to life. It marks Runtu in boyhood as cherished and protected; its absence from the middle-aged Runtu, who appears with a ragged felt hat and thin cotton clothes in bitter cold, measures the loss. Note the irony available here: the charm belongs to exactly the \"superstitious\" folk religion Lu Xun's New Culture circle attacked, yet in the story it is rendered with tenderness, not scorn.\n\n### Runtu calling the narrator \"Master\" — text CONFIRMED, criticism UNVERIFIED\n\nIn the Yang & Yang text Runtu struggles to speak, then adopts a deferential manner and says **\"Master! . . .\"** The narrator's reaction is immediate: **\"I felt a shiver run through me; for I knew then what a lamentably thick wall had grown up between us.\"**\n\nThe structurally important point: **the wall image is triggered by the honorific itself.** The class barrier registers *linguistically* — in a single word of address — before it is ever stated as a proposition. In boyhood the two used given names; the adult Runtu now uses 老爺 (*laoye*, \"master/His Honour\"), the address of a tenant or servant to gentry. The narrator's horror is not at Runtu's poverty but at Runtu's **internalisation** of hierarchy — he has become the willing subject of a system that has ruined him. This is the same diagnosis as *Ah Q*: the oppressed reproducing their own oppression.\n\nCaveats: I could **not** verify 老爺, 厚障壁 or 高牆 in the **original Chinese** — Chinese Wikisource's 故鄉 page only transcludes scanned pages of the 1948 *魯迅全集* (`<pages index=\"魯迅全集01_(1948).pdf\" from=\"365\" to=\"379\" />`), which would not resolve. And **no published criticism specifically on *laoye*'s class significance was reachable — UNVERIFIED.** The reading above is the standard one but I am giving it to you as inference from the text, not as a sourced citation.\n\n### The \"high invisible wall\" — CONFIRMED\n\nTwo wall images, and they are distinct — worth keeping separate in teaching:\n\n1. **\"a lamentably thick wall\"** (厚障壁), at the moment Runtu says \"Master\" — a barrier between **two individuals**, made of class deference. (Yang & Yang 1960 edn., p. 60.)\n2. **\"an invisible high wall, cutting me off from my fellows, and this depressed me thoroughly\"** — as the boat pulls away at the end: a barrier between the returning **intellectual** and the **people** as a whole. (p. 63.)\n\nEnglish Wikipedia's *Selected Stories of Lu Hsun* article cites both with page references and glosses the story's themes as: **\"divisions created artificially by class difference\"**, the persistence of memory, a place being made of its people as much as its geography, the pain of being cut off from one's past, and intellectuals having to stop looking backward toward history and face the present. It also groups \"My Old Home\" with \"Kong Yiji,\" \"In the Wine Shop\" and \"Regret for the Past\" under **\"the problem of how members of the intellectual class are to live their lives\"** — the most useful single critical frame available for the story.\n\n### The closing image of hope — text CONFIRMED, critics' readings UNVERIFIED\n\nYang & Yang: dozing on the boat, the narrator pictures the moonlit green shore again and reflects that **\"hope cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist. It is just like roads across the earth\"** — the ground held no roads originally, **\"but when many men pass one way, a road is made.\"**\n\n**I found no published criticism or encyclopaedia commentary on how critics read this ending — mark \"critics read it as Lu Xun's ambivalence\" as UNVERIFIED.** However, the two comparanda you wanted are solidly confirmed and can carry the argument without needing a secondary citation:\n\n- **The iron house parable** (*Nahan* preface, quoted on English Wikipedia): \"an iron house without windows, absolutely indestructible, with many people fast asleep inside\"; since they \"will die in their sleep, they will not feel the pain of death,\" so rousing \"a few of the lighter sleepers\" only inflicts \"the agony of irrevocable death.\" **Qian Xuantong's reply supplies the counter-move: \"But if a few awake, you can't say that there is no hope of destroying the iron house.\"** The parallel to the roads passage is exact — hope as neither existent nor non-existent, contingent on **collective** movement. This is the strongest available anchor for the standard reading, and it is Lu Xun's own framing.\n- **Britannica** on his general position: his writing was \"marked by sensitivity and pessimism,\" and he held that darkness could be resisted only from a stance of pessimism — a **\"resistance of despair\"**, which Britannica calls \"a core concept of his thought.\" His late Shanghai position was *hengzhan* (\"horizontal stand\"), fighting both \"cultural conservatism and mechanical evolution,\" emblematic of the modern intellectual's \"complex and tragic predicament.\"\n- **Yecao** (野草, **1927**) is the prose-poem collection where the hope/despair dialectic is most explicit.\n\nTwo teaching points the text itself supports. First, the hope is **not** placed in the narrator or in Runtu but in **Hong'er and Shuisheng** — the next generation, cousins across the class line who play as the narrator and Runtu once did; the wish is that they should *not* repeat the pattern. Second, the grammar of the closing image is **conditional and collective**: no road exists in advance, and no individual makes one. This is why the ending reads as neither optimism nor despair but as a refusal of both — and why it was so readily absorbed into later revolutionary rhetoric, a reception Lu Xun himself resisted (recall that in 1935 he **declined** the CCP's request for a rural revolutionary novel).\n\n### Late-Qing / early-Republican rural context — CONFIRMED\n\n**1911 Revolution** (English Wikipedia; note \"Xinhai Revolution\" is now only a redirect): **10 October 1911 – 12 February 1912**; the Wuchang Uprising as trigger, \"an armed rebellion by members of the New Army\"; ROC declared **1 January 1912** under Sun Yat-sen; the abdication edict of the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor \"was promulgated on 12 February 1912\"; Yuan Shikai sworn in as president **10 March 1912**. It ended \"the 267-year reign of the Qing, over two millennia of imperial rule in China.\" On the gentry: \"The gentry's strength in local politics became apparent,\" and \"the upper strata of local Chinese society were supporters of the constitutionalists\" protecting \"the interests they had already gained.\" The **Chinese famine of 1906–1907 \"was also a major contributor to the revolution.\"**\n\n**CAVEAT:** that article carries **no substantive material on land reform, tenancy, or village-level change**, so the familiar claim that 1911 changed the dynasty while leaving the **gentry-peasant structure intact** is **UNVERIFIED from the sources I reached** — though the story itself, and Zhang Yunshui's biography (rent and taxes eating a six-mu holding, 1903–1934), are themselves evidence for it.\n\n**Warlord Era** (**6 June 1916 – 29 December 1928**) — this is where the rural-immiseration evidence actually lives, and it is abundant. \"Following Yuan's death on 6 June 1916, a power vacuum was established and quickly filled by military strongmen.\"\n\n- **Taxation:** *lijin* transit levies \"often confiscatory and inflicted much economic harm\"; Sichuan had **27 separate salt taxes**; a paper shipment down the Yangtze to Shanghai was taxed **11 times, totalling \"160% of its value\"**; one warlord set a **100% tax on rail freight including food \"even though there was a famine in his province\"**; Zhang Zuolin raised **land taxes 12% between 1922 and 1928**.\n- **Hyperinflation:** Hunan's warlord printed 22 million Chinese dollars against a one-million silver reserve in a single year; Zhang Zongchang in Shandong, 55 million against 1.5 million.\n- **Conscription:** \"the rank-and-file of the warlord armies tended to be **village conscripts**,\" often captured and re-enlisted repeatedly; Wu Peifu absorbed at least 200,000 prisoners; troop numbers rose from about half a million in 1916 to roughly **nine times that by 1924**; a 1924 survey found 90% of one garrison illiterate; Stilwell in 1926 saw a unit of average age **14**.\n- **Banditry:** \"when the war ended, the soldiers became bandits\"; looting \"was institutionalized, as many warlords lacked the money to pay their troops\"; kidnappers sometimes mailed \"a hostage's severed fingers\"; in 1921 the *North China Daily News* reported Shaanxi crime \"frightened the farmers.\" Peasants formed secret-society militias (the Red Spear Society's \"supposedly bulletproof red clay\"), many turning millenarian, hoping a Ming emperor would restore \"a reign of happiness and justice for all.\"\n\nThis is precisely the world of Runtu's complaint in the story — bad harvests, extortionate levies, soldiers, bandits, officials, and gentry all taking their cut.\n\n**New Culture / May Fourth.** New Culture Movement: \"a progressive sociopolitical movement in China during the 1910s and 1920s,\" beginning with Chen Duxiu's *Youth Magazine* (1915, later *New Youth*); Chen \"called for 'Mr. Confucius' to be replaced by 'Mr. Science'\" and \"Mr. Democracy\"; Hu Shih's vernacular programme — \"Speak in the language of the time in which you live,\" \"Do not imitate the ancients\" (1917), \"a dead language cannot produce a living literature.\" Lu Xun's stories \"created a sensation with their condemnation of Confucian culture,\" and \"A Madman's Diary\" (2 April 1918) \"directly implied that China's traditional culture was mentally cannibalistic.\" The movement \"was the progenitor of the May Fourth Movement\"; the **4 May 1919** Beijing student protests over Jiaozhou Bay \"transform[ed] what had been a cultural movement into a political one.\"\n\n---\n\n## 4. WHAT IS \"ZHA\" (猹)? — FULLY RESOLVED, with Lu Xun's own answer\n\nThis is the cleanest result of the research: **Lu Xun invented the character, and later admitted he did not know what the animal was.**\n\n- **The character.** 猹 is a **phono-semantic compound Lu Xun coined in January 1921** for this story: the dog radical 犬/犭 as semantic element plus 查 as phonetic. It was **not a pre-existing word.**\n- **Pronunciation.** *zhā* or *chá*. Early dictionaries prescribed **zhā** (Shu Xincheng's 1936 《辭海》; Wei Jiangong's 1954 《新華字典》) — which is exactly why your textbook's Yang & Yang text romanises it **\"zha.\"** The 1973 《現代漢語詞典》 switched to **chá** (homophone of 查), and the 1985 《普通話異讀詞審音表》 confirmed *chá*, which most later sources follow. So \"zha\" is the older, and historically correct-to-Lu-Xun, reading.\n- **Lu Xun's own explanation**, in a **1929 letter to Shu Xincheng** (the 辭海 editor, who had written to ask):\n\n  > 「猹」字是我據鄉下人所說的聲音，生造出來的，讀如「查」。但我自己也不知道究竟是怎樣的動物，因為這乃是閏土所說，別人不知其詳。現在想起來，也許是獾罷。\n\n  In paraphrase: he **made the character up** from a sound he had heard **country people** say; it is read like 查; he **does not himself know what kind of animal it is**, because it came from what **Runtu** said and nobody else knows the details; and — \"thinking about it now, perhaps it was a **badger** (獾).\"\n\n  This is the key find for your annotation: the narrator's confession in the story (\"I had no idea then what this thing called zha was—and I am not much clearer now for that matter\") is **not a literary device — it is literally true of the author.** The gap in the text is a real gap in Lu Xun's knowledge, preserved deliberately.\n- **In the story.** The narrator says he \"並不知道這所謂猹的是怎麼一件東西\" — only vaguely imagining it as dog-like in shape but fierce. Elsewhere Runtu lists it **alongside** badgers, boars and hedgehogs as melon-field pests — which, note, slightly cuts against Lu Xun's own later \"perhaps a badger\" guess, since the story treats 猹 and 獾 as different creatures.\n- **What annotators say.** **Chinese Wikipedia redirects 猹 straight to 獾 (badger)** — but that is an editorial decision, not a sourced identification. Modern reference works generally gloss it as a badger or badger-like animal, following Lu Xun's own guess. **One 2016 source proposes 獐 (river deer / Chinese water deer)** instead. The honest summary: **it is not a real, identified species** — it is a dialect sound Lu Xun transcribed into an invented character, most often taken to be a badger, possibly a raccoon dog or water deer, and strictly speaking unidentifiable.\n\n**Suggested gloss for the textbook:** *zha (猹) — a character Lu Xun invented for this story from a Shaoxing country word for a melon-raiding animal. Lu Xun himself wrote in 1929 that he did not know what animal it was and guessed \"perhaps a badger.\" No species has ever been firmly identified.*\n\n---\n\n## 5. Note `File:Lu_Xun_1930.jpg` (with underscores/spaces as written) **404s** — the correct name is `File:LuXun1930.jpg`.\n\n**(b) Shaoxing / Lu Xun's former residence — licence verified:**\n\n- **`File:Former Residence of Lu Xun in Shaoxing 01 2018-09.jpg`** — 4,912 × 3,264 px, ~5 MB. The **乌篷船**, the black-awning boat of Shaoxing's canals — thematically ideal, since the family leaves Shaoxing **by boat** in the story and in the diary (\"以舟二艘\").\n- `File:浙江绍兴三味书屋.jpg` — the **Sanwei Study (三味書屋)**, Lu Xun's childhood schoolroom; 1,920 × 872.\n- `File:浙江绍兴咸亨酒店.jpg` — the **Xianheng Tavern**, the setting of \"Kong Yiji\"; 1,920 × 874.\n- `File:Anchang Town (61724297).jpeg`, `File:Anchang Town (61727079).jpeg`, `File:Anchang Town (81146085).jpeg` — **Anchang**, a Shaoxing canal/old-street water town; the closest match to \"a Chinese water-town village.\"\n- `File:Shusheng Cultural Street.jpg`, `File:Shen's Garden.jpg`, `File:Shaoxing Cityscape.jpg`, `File:Lu Xun Cultural Festival.jpg`.\n- For more canal/bridge photographs, the subcategories **`Category:Buildings in Shaoxing`** (46 subcats, 113 files) and **`Category:Geography of Shaoxing`** are the places to look — `Category:Shaoxing` itself holds only 19 files.\n\n**Search note:** Commons `Special:MediaSearch` with multi-word queries like \"Shaoxing canal water town\" returns **zero results**; browsing `Category:Shaoxing` worked far better. Use category browsing, not media search, for follow-ups.\n\n---\n\n## SUMMARY OF CORRECTIONS TO YOUR WORKING ASSUMPTIONS\n\n1. **First publication is 1 May 1921, New Youth vol. 9 no. 1** — not January 1921. January 1921 is the **composition** date printed in English editions.\n2. **The exam-bribery culprit was the father, Zhou Boyi (1893)**; the grandfather Zhou Fuqing was imprisoned as an implicated party, sentenced to beheading then commuted, released 1901.\n3. **The textbook's \"collection Hometown\" is an error** — no English edition titles any collection \"Hometown.\" The collection is **Nahan (吶喊), 1923**.\n4. **Runtu's model was 章運水 / Zhang Yunshui**, whom Lu Xun renamed 章閏水 — your \"Zhang Yunshui\" guess was right. Sources: Michael Hutt, *Himalayan Voices* (full text, UC Press CDL archive); en/ne/es Wikipedia raw wikitext; Britannica; Open Library; Wikimedia Commons API.\n\n=====================================================\nPART A — SHANKAR LAMICHHANE / \"THE HALF-CLOSED EYES OF THE BUDDHA AND THE SLOWLY SINKING SUN\"\n=====================================================\n\nA1. BIOGRAPHY\n- Born 17 March 1928 (5 Chaitra 1984 BS), Jaisidewal, Kathmandu. Parents Hari Prasad (Harihar) Lamichhane and Raj Kumari.\n- DEATH DATE CONFLICT: Hutt (1991) gives \"Shankar Lamichhane (1928-1975)\". en/ne Wikipedia give 24 January 1976 (10 Magh 2032 BS), aged 47. Nepali Wikipedia: died of a brain tumour. Both dates circulate; the Magh 2032 BS date straddles the Gregorian year boundary, which is the likely origin of \"1975\". Report as 1928-1975/76.\n- BANARAS: Hutt says he \"lived with an uncle in Banaras until he was eleven.\" Nepali/English Wikipedia instead say his MOTHER took him and his brother to Banaras (the brother died there; the mother taught school and died about a decade later). The uncle detail is Hutt's alone — treat the guardian's identity as UNVERIFIED, but the Banaras childhood to age ~11 is solid.\n- Education: Tri-Chandra College, Kathmandu (I.Sc.; Hutt: \"some basic education at Trichandra College\"). ne.wikipedia: science to roughly class 12. No degree completed.\n- Jobs: first job at 22 — kharidar (खरदार, junior clerk) at the Guthi Adda at the end of the Rana period; then head of the library of the Nepal–India Cultural Centre; Hutt: \"worked for a number of governmental and cultural institutions in Kathmandu. In his later years he became the manager of a handicrafts store.\" Also member-secretary of Kavya Pratishthan (at Devkota's urging), editor of *Indreni*, editor of the 8-volume children's series *Hamro Sahitya*.\n- FOREIGN VISITORS — confirmed and stronger than the brief assumed: Hutt says he \"frequently mixed with foreign visitors to Nepal\"; ne.wikipedia says he actually WORKED AS A TOURIST GUIDE, and drew Devkota into guiding too. This is directly germane to the story's guide-narrator.\n- American fiction: confirmed. Hutt: \"an admirer of modern American fiction.\"\n- MOVEMENT — the brief's guess needs correcting. Lamichhane was NOT a member of Tesro Aayam (तेस्रो आयाम, \"Third Dimension\", founded 1960 by Ishwar Ballav, Bairagi Kainla and Indra Bahadur Rai). Hutt groups him WITH that generation without making him of it: \"the clearest signs of a radical change in Nepali fiction at this time are to be found in the works of Indra Bahadur Rai, his ayameli colleague Ishwar Ballabh, and Shankar Lamichhane\" — note \"ayameli\" attaches to Ballabh, not to Lamichhane. Safe formulation: a leading figure of the post-1950 Nepali modernist generation, contemporary with and parallel to the Aayamik writers but not affiliated. He is also credited by ne.wikipedia with introducing stream-of-consciousness (चेतनप्रवाह शैली) into the Nepali essay.\n- MADAN PURASKAR: YES — won 2024 BS (1967) for *Abstract Chintan: Pyaj*.\n- Also: published his first piece in *Sahitya Srot* before age 15; close to Devkota; called Parijat \"sister\"; two marriages (Ratna Rai, Subarna Shrestha). He stopped writing before his death, discouraged by an anonymous plagiarism accusation which he accepted (en.wikipedia).\n- BEST KNOWN AS: essayist, not short-story writer. ne.wikipedia is explicit — everyone interested in Nepali literature knows Shankar as a NIBANDHAKAR (essayist). Hutt corroborates from the fiction side: his stories are \"heavy with symbolism, often lacking a conventional plot and more closely resembling essays, but his prose is rich, fluent, and mature.\" So: a major essayist whose single most famous work is a short story.\n\nA2. WORKS (BS dates from ne.wikipedia, Gregorian in brackets)\n- एब्स्ट्राक्ट चिन्तन : प्याज / *Abstract Chintan: Pyaj* (Abstract Thought: Onion) — essays, Sajha Prakashan, 1967 (2024 BS), 84 pp. WON THE MADAN PURASKAR 2024 BS. Title essay uses the onion (peel away layer after layer, find no core) as its metaphor. Date and prize both CONFIRMED.\n- गौँथलीको गुँड / *Gaunthaliko Gunda* (Swallow's Nest) — short stories, 2025 BS [1968]. Hutt: \"Most of Lamichhane's stories are collected in Gaunthaliko Gund (Swallow's Nest, 1968).\"\n- गोधूलि संसार / *Godhuli Sansar* (Twilight World) — essays, 2027 BS [1970/71].\n- बिम्ब प्रतिबिम्ब / *Bimba Pratibimba* (Image, Reflection) — literary essays, 2028 BS [1971/72].\n- शङ्कर लामिछाने — 2032 BS [1975/76].\n- Also listed: *Shankar Lamichhane ka Nibandhaharu* (collected essays), *Shankar Lamichhane Aatmakatha* (autobiography) — dates UNVERIFIED, likely posthumous compilations.\n\nA3. THE STORY — publication facts\n- Nepali title (Hutt's romanisation): *Ardhamudit Nayan ra Dubna Lageko Gham*. Devanagari form UNVERIFIED — I could not retrieve a Devanagari source; the expected form is अर्धमुदित नयन र डुब्न लागेको घाम but do not print it as verified.\n- FIRST PUBLISHED IN NEPALI: 1962. Hutt's end-of-story note: \"(first published 1962; from Sajha Katha [1968] 1979; also included in Nepali Katha Sangraha [1973] 1988, vol. 2)\". Hutt's essay confirms: it \"made an enormous impact on Nepali fiction when it was published in 1962.\" NOT 1968 — 1968 is the *Gaunthaliko Gunda* / *Sajha Katha* collection year. Original 1962 magazine venue not identified in Hutt; UNVERIFIED.\n- ANTHOLOGY CONFIRMED: *Himalayan Voices: An Introduction to Modern Nepali Literature*, translated and edited by Michael Hutt, University of California Press, Berkeley, 1991 (Voices from Asia series). ISBNs 0520070461 / 0520070488. Story at pp. 253-259; Lamichhane headnote p. 253; discussed pp. 176, 187-188. Full free text at publishing.cdlib.org (ark:/13030/ft729007x1). The 1991 year in the brief is CORRECT.\n- TRANSLATOR: Michael Hutt himself. The volume is \"Translated and Edited by\" Hutt throughout, and his endnote 1 to this story reads \"An abridged version of this translation was published in Bazaar South Asian Arts Magazine (London), Spring 1988.\" No separate translator is credited. (The CDL title page shows \"Michael James Hurt\" — an OCR error for Hutt.)\n- TITLE WORDING: Hutt's chapter heading reads \"The Half-Closed Eyes of the Buddha and the Slowly SETTING Sun\"; his index entry reads \"Slowly SINKING Sun\". Both are Hutt's; \"Sinking\" (the textbook's form) is defensible.\n\nA4. CRITICAL POINTS (Hutt's own reading, quoted short)\n- STRUCTURE: \"This famous story is composed of two monologues.\" Monologue 1 = the Western tourist, pre-dinner at his hotel, giving \"a rapturous description of all he hopes to see\"; monologue 2 = the Nepali guide. The guide's voice answers and dismantles the tourist's.\n- ORIENTALISM: the tourist \"brings with him his notions of the culture and history of Nepal, acquired from books published in the West.\" Hutt frames the whole against the tourist myth: \"Since foreign tourists began to visit Nepal during the 1950s, the popular Western view of Nepal has been of an idyllic Shangri-la.\" (Hutt returned to exactly this in a 1996 chapter, \"Looking for Shangri-la, from Hilton to Lamicchane,\" in *The Tourist Image: Myths and Myth-Making in Tourism*, Wiley, pp. 49-60 — useful corroboration that the Shangri-la reading is the scholarly consensus, not an invention.)\n- STATUS: \"is regarded as a classic of modern Nepali literature.\"\n- THEME per Hutt: it \"turned away from the internal concerns of the writer's own society to consider a foreigner's perception of Nepal.\"\n- THE CHILD: Hutt's summary — \"the guide shows the tourist an aspect of contemporary Nepal of which he is unaware by taking him to visit a farmer whose son is completely paralyzed.\" Note: Hutt says \"completely paralyzed,\" not \"polio-stricken.\" Polio is a common gloss but is an inference; mark the specific diagnosis UNVERIFIED unless the text names it.\n- SAMYAK GAZE: in-text definition — \"It is called the samyak gaze. Do you know what that means? It is perception, pure and without contamination; sight that perceives everything in its true form.\" The Buddhist link is made explicit in the story itself: \"(Perhaps I have begun to speak unwittingly in the terms of the Aryan eightfold path, which will either be your influence or a virtue bestowed upon me by the child.)\" Sanskrit samyak-dṛṣṭi = \"right view,\" the FIRST limb of the Noble Eightfold Path (Pali sammā-diṭṭhi). So the title's half-closed eyes, the stupa's painted eyes, and the paralysed child's eyes are all measured against a Buddhist standard of true seeing. Closing line of that thread: \"I don't know whether his eyes have the samyak gaze or not.\"\n- THE DOCTOR LIE: \"I have lied to his parents; I have told them that you are a doctor.\" The irony: the tourist who came to consume Nepal as spectacle is handed, without his knowledge, the role of healer — and can heal nothing. The parents' hope is manufactured by the guide.\n- EYES MOTIF: \"This is a land of eyes, a land guarded by the half-closed eyes of the Lord Buddha.\" And the closing turn onto the child's eyes: \"Look! They are just as beautiful as the setting sun's reflection in the eyes of the Buddha!\" Hutt's endnote on the stupas: \"Onto many of these monuments there are painted a pair of enigmatic eyes.\"\n- \"Om mani padme hum\" — Hutt glosses: \"'Hail to the jewel in the lotus' (a famous Tibetan Buddhist mantra).\"\n- CHAR BHANJYANG: Hutt — \"The Four Passes (Char Bhanjyang) is a name for the Kathmandu Valley.\"\n- KASTHAMANDAP: Hutt — \"reputed to be the oldest building in Kathmandu; the city itself was probably named after this temple, which is said to have been built from the wood of a single tree.\"\n- Mo-mos: Hutt — \"steamed meat dumplings, a Tibetan delicacy.\"\n\nMANJUSHRI LEGEND — VERIFIED (and the Chobhar link is the point)\nHutt's endnote: \"In the remote geological past, the Kathmandu Valley was filled by a lake. A famous Buddhist legend says that a miraculous flame became manifest upon the surface of this lake, above the present site of Swyambhu hill. The Bodhisattva Manjushri came down from the north to see this miracle and declared that it was a sign that the lake should be drained so that human beings could inhabit the valley. He struck with his sword at Chobhar, cleaving the hills to the south of the valley to let the waters escape.\"\nCorroboration: the *Swayambhu Purana* has the lotus/flame of the Buddha Vipassi on the lake and Manjushri draining it \"by cutting the mountains with his indestructible sword\" at Kacchapala Giri (Chobhar hill). Manjushri is the bodhisattva of prajñā (transcendent wisdom); his standard attributes are the flaming sword of wisdom and the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra — so the sword that opens the valley is literally the sword of wisdom, which rhymes with samyak-dṛṣṭi. The Chobhar gorge is the real geological outlet of the Bagmati.\nADINATH: Hutt's glossary — \"Adinath a name of Shiva, or of an aspect of the Buddha worshipped at a particular temple in Chobhar village to the south of Kathmandu\"; his endnote adds it is \"an epithet meaning 'primordial lord'.\" Properly the Anandadi Lokeshwar Mandir, Chobhar: 15th century, rebuilt 1640, famous as the \"pots and pans\" temple (metal vessels nailed to the facade by newly-married couples). In local tradition Manjushri (as Manjudeva) cut the hills here and became known as Adinath (Locke, *Karunamaya*, 1980, pp. 350-351). The Hindu/Buddhist double identity of Adinath is itself thematic — syncretism the tourist cannot see.\nSWAYAMBHUNATH: the eyes-on-the-stupa referent; UNESCO World Heritage 1979 as part of the Kathmandu Valley property; popularly \"the Monkey Temple\"; re-gilded 2010 with ~20 kg of gold.\n\nBHRIKUTI / AMSHUVARMA — the brief's framing needs care\n- Hutt's endnote (the version the textbook follows): \"The Tibetan king Songsten Gampo (r. 627-650), who established Buddhism in Tibet, took two wives. One was a Chinese princess; the other was Bhrikuti, daughter of the Nepalese king Amshuvarman. Both of these princesses have been credited by various scholars with the king's conversion to Buddhism.\"\n- So: the NEPALI princess Bhrikuti was sent TO TIBET, to marry SONGTSEN GAMPO (Tibetan king, r. 627-650). The Chinese co-wife is Princess Wencheng (married 641). Bhrikuti is traditionally said to have brought the Jowo Mikyo Dorje (Akshobhya) image and Newar craftsmen; the Jokhang in Lhasa is associated with her. She is identified with Green Tara.\n- CHRONOLOGY PROBLEM — flag it. Amshuverma (Licchavi, builder of Kailashkut Bhawan) reigned c. 605-621 CE, i.e. he DIED BEFORE Songtsen Gampo's reign began. If Bhrikuti was his daughter the marriage must predate c. 624; one source (Kirti Tulku Lobsang Tenzin) dates it 632. Other scholarship makes her the daughter of Udayadeva (\"Udayavarman\"), sister of Narendradeva, arguing an Amshuverma daughter would have been too old. Her historicity is genuinely disputed — she is absent from the Dunhuang Tibetan annals. Verdict: the Amshuvarma-father version is the TRADITIONAL account that Hutt and the textbook transmit, but it is chronologically strained and Bhrikuti's existence is UNVERIFIED as history. Present it as legend/tradition, which suits the story — the tourist is quoting exactly this kind of guidebook history.\n\nA5. AUTHOR FACTS\n- Full name: Gabriel José García Márquez. Nickname \"Gabo\" (also \"Gabito\").\n- BIRTH YEAR CONFLICT — UNVERIFIED, report both. Born 6 March in Aracataca, Magdalena, Colombia; the YEAR is disputed in the sources available here. Britannica says 1927 (and gives age at death 87, consistent with 1927). en.wikipedia says 1928, citing Gerald Martin, *Gabriel García Márquez: A Life* (2008), p. 27: \"On Sunday 6 March 1928, at 9am, in the midst of an unseasonal rainstorm, a baby boy, Gabriel José García Márquez, was born.\" The nobelprize.org biographical page returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked. 1927 is the long-standing traditional date; 1928 is the date modern biography favours. Safest for a textbook: \"6 March 1927 (some sources 1928)\".\n- Died 17 April 2014, Mexico City.\n- GRANDPARENTS' HOUSE, Aracataca — the single most important biographical fact for this story. Raised by his maternal grandparents. Grandfather Col. Nicolás Ricardo Márquez Mejía (\"Papalelo\"), a Thousand Days War veteran, whom GGM called his \"umbilical cord with history and reality.\" Grandmother Doña Tranquilina Iguarán Cotes \"treated the extraordinary as something perfectly natural\" and was \"the source of the magical, superstitious and supernatural view of reality.\" GGM himself credited her deadpan delivery — her \"brick face\" — as the narrative voice of his magical realism (Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 69, 1981), alongside the shock of reading Kafka's \"The Metamorphosis.\" That grandmother's unastonished tone IS the narrator of \"A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.\"\n- JOURNALISM: first published story \"La tercera resignación,\" *El Espectador*, 13 September 1947. Reporter at *El Universal* (Cartagena) 1948-49; *El Heraldo* (Barranquilla) 1950-52, writing a column under the pen name \"Septimus\"; member of the Barranquilla Group; *El Espectador* 1954-55. His 14-part 1955 series on a naval shipwreck (later *The Story of a Shipwrecked Sailor*) embarrassed the Rojas Pinilla government and led to his being posted to Europe.\n- EXILE / MEXICO: lived in Europe from 1955; married Mercedes Barcha 1958; settled in Mexico City in 1961, wrote *One Hundred Years of Solitude* there; lived in Spain 1967-1975; a committed leftist, friend of Fidel Castro, long barred from the USA. Died in Mexico City.\n- PRIZES: Neustadt International Prize 1972; NOBEL PRIZE IN LITERATURE 1982, citation \"for his novels and short stories, in which the fantastic and the realistic are combined in a richly composed world of imagination, reflecting a continent's life and conflicts.\" Nobel lecture: \"The Solitude of Latin America.\"\n- WORKS — all dates in the brief CONFIRMED against Britannica:\n  *La hojarasca* / Leaf Storm — 1955\n  *El coronel no tiene quien le escriba* / No One Writes to the Colonel — 1961\n  *La mala hora* / In Evil Hour — 1962\n  *Los funerales de la Mamá Grande* / Big Mama's Funeral — 1962\n  *Cien años de soledad* / One Hundred Years of Solitude — 1967\n  *El otoño del patriarca* / The Autumn of the Patriarch — 1975\n  *Crónica de una muerte anunciada* / Chronicle of a Death Foretold — 1981\n  *El amor en los tiempos del cólera* / Love in the Time of Cholera — 1985\n  *El general en su laberinto* / The General in His Labyrinth — 1989\n  *Del amor y otros demonios* / Of Love and Other Demons — 1994\n  *Noticia de un secuestro* / News of a Kidnapping — 1996\n  *Vivir para contarla* / Living to Tell the Tale — 2002 (memoir)\n  *Memoria de mis putas tristes* / Memories of My Melancholy Whores — 2004\n- MAGICAL REALISM, accurate genealogy: the term descends from art criticism, not literature. Franz Roh coined *magischer Realismus* in 1925 for post-Expressionist painting (Neue Sachlichkeit); translated into Spanish by *Revista de Occidente* in 1927. Arturo Uslar Pietri first applied *realismo mágico* to literature in 1948. Alejo Carpentier \"rejected Roh's magic realism as tiresome pretension\" and developed the related but distinct *lo real maravilloso* (\"the marvellous real\") in 1949, in the prologue to *El reino de este mundo* — his claim being that the marvellous is not a technique but a property of American reality itself. Angel Flores's 1955 essay \"Magical Realism in Spanish American Fiction\" fixed the English term. *One Hundred Years of Solitude* (1967) is its canonical incarnation.\n- LATIN AMERICAN BOOM: 1960s-70s internationalisation of Latin American fiction — García Márquez, Julio Cortázar, Carlos Fuentes, Mario Vargas Llosa; publisher Seix Barral (Barcelona) as the commercial engine; the 1959 Cuban Revolution as political catalyst; the 1971 Padilla affair as the point where the writers' political unity broke.\n\nB2. THE CRITICAL POINT — SETTLED. THE TEXTBOOK'S \"1955\" IS WRONG.\n- WRITTEN: 1968 (Gerald Martin, *Gabriel García Márquez: A Life*, Bloomsbury 2008, p. 275).\n- FIRST PUBLICATION, Spanish: the journal *CASA DE LAS AMÉRICAS* (Havana), May-June 1968 issue, vol. VIII no. 48. Source: Don Klein, *Gabriel García Márquez: una bibliografía descriptiva*, vol. 2, Grupo Editorial Norma, 2003, p. 578. es.wikipedia's article likewise states it \"es un cuento de 1968,\" cites Klein p. 578, and files it under \"Cuentos de 1968.\"\n- FIRST ENGLISH PUBLICATION: *New American Review* 13, 1971, pp. 70-77.\n- ENGLISH TRANSLATOR: GREGORY RABASSA. Confirmed.\n- BOOK COLLECTIONS, both 1972: in Spanish, *La increíble y triste historia de la cándida Eréndira y de su abuela desalmada* (Sudamericana, 1972, 155 pp.) — the story stands FIRST in that volume's contents. In English, *Leaf Storm and Other Stories* (Harper & Row, 1972), alongside \"The Handsomest Drowned Man in the World,\" \"Blacamán the Good, Vendor of Miracles,\" \"The Last Voyage of the Ghost Ship,\" \"The Monologue of Isabel Watching It Rain in Macondo,\" and \"Nabo.\"\n- So the brief's belief was right on every point: 1968 origin, 1972 Spanish collection, Rabassa, *Leaf Storm and Other Stories* 1972 — with the added precision that the true first appearance was the Havana journal in May-June 1968, and the first English was 1971 in *New American Review*, a year before the book.\n- SOURCE OF THE \"1955\" ERROR — found, and it is concrete. THE SPANISH WIKIPEDIA DISAMBIGUATION PAGE for \"Un señor muy viejo con unas alas enormes\" literally reads: \"Un señor muy viejo con unas alas enormes (cuento) (1955), cuento de Gabriel García Márquez.\" That erroneous 1955 sits on the disambiguation page even though the linked article itself correctly says 1968. Anyone compiling a textbook note from a quick look-up would copy 1955 straight off it. Two further factors reinforce the mistake: (i) *La hojarasca* / *Leaf Storm* genuinely IS 1955, and the story's English home is the volume TITLED *Leaf Storm and Other Stories*, so the collection's title date gets misattributed to its contents; (ii) 1955 is also the year of Angel Flores's famous magical-realism essay, which co-occurs with the story in teaching materials. Recommend correcting the textbook to 1968.\n\nB3. CRITICAL POINTS ON THE STORY\n- MAGICAL REALISM AS TECHNIQUE: the impossible is reported in the register of the mundane and the mundane in the register of the marvellous. The winged man is described with flat, degrading physical detail — few teeth, parasites in his feathers, a dialect nobody knows, a \"strong sailor's voice,\" eyes described as \"antiquarian\" — while the narrator reserves no astonishment for the wings at all. The prose treats a fallen angel as a weather event and treats a woman turned into a spider as a ticketed attraction. Grandmother Tranquilina's unblinking tone (B1) is the direct source.\n- THE CROWD: curiosity without compassion, quickly exhausted. Pelayo and Elisenda cage him in the chicken coop and charge admission. Onlookers throw food, pluck feathers for relics, and finally prod him with a branding iron to make him react — he is burned awake. The crowd's imagination is small: the \"consolation miracles\" attributed to him are absurd anticlimaxes (the blind man who grows new teeth instead of regaining sight; the paralytic who nearly wins the lottery; the leper whose sores sprout sunflowers). Grace arrives, and it arrives wrong, because the recipients' desires are trivial.\n- THE CHURCH: Father Gonzaga, \"before becoming a priest... had been a robust woodcutter,\" tests the captive by addressing him in LATIN; the old man does not respond, so the priest judges him not to be an angel, warns the faithful that the devil often uses \"carnival tricks,\" and refers the matter to his bishop, who refers it to the primate, who refers it to Rome. The letters to Rome ask questions of pure scholastic uselessness — whether the prisoner had a navel, whether his dialect had any relation to Aramaic, how many times he could fit on the head of a pin. Satire of institutional religion: confronted with the numinous, the Church files paperwork and awaits a \"final verdict\" that never comes. The narrator notes the correspondence \"might have come and gone until the end of time\" had an event not settled it.\n- THE SPIDER WOMAN as rival spectacle, and WHY SHE WINS: a travelling fair arrives with a woman who has been turned into a tarantula the size of a ram with a maiden's head, for having disobeyed her parents and gone dancing. Admission to see her costs less than admission to see the angel, and she ANSWERS QUESTIONS about her condition — the crowd deserts the angel instantly. This is the story's sharpest point about narrative and audience: her tale has a legible moral structure (transgression, punishment, lesson) and she speaks; the angel offers no explanation, no doctrine, no interaction, no meaning. The crowd does not want the sacred, it wants a story with a moral and a ticket price. \"A spectacle... full of so much human truth\" outcompetes an actual miracle, because the miracle is mute.\n- COMMODIFICATION / EXPLOITATION: the admission money builds Pelayo and Elisenda a two-storey mansion with balconies and gardens; Elisenda buys satin pumps and \"many changes of those iridescent silk dresses\"; Pelayo quits his job as a bailiff and sets up a rabbit warren. The family's entire prosperity is extracted from a caged being they never once address as a person. After the spider woman ruins the trade, the coop is abandoned and the angel is left to drag himself around the house, an intruder Elisenda finds unbearable — her closing complaint is that it is \"hell full of angels.\"\n- CRUELTY TO THE DIFFERENT: he is caged with the hens, poked, burned, laughed at, thought a \"circus animal\" and a possible \"mayor of the world\" or \"five-star general\" who might \"win all wars,\" and finally resented as household vermin. His only defence is patience. The crowning cruelty is casual: the child and the old man contract CHICKENPOX at the same time, and the doctor who examines the angel is astonished less by the wings than by how NATURAL they are — \"so natural on that completely human organism that he couldn't understand why other men didn't have them too.\" The wings are not the anomaly; the treatment of their bearer is.\n- AMBIGUITY: never resolved. Evidence for: wings, immunity to time, the \"unbearable smell of the outdoors,\" the mysterious patience, the eventual healing of his feathers, flight. Evidence against: parasites, decrepitude, incomprehensible speech, no Latin, no message, no miracle that works as intended. The neighbour woman who \"knew everything about life and death\" pronounces him an angel come for the sick child; Father Gonzaga denies it; the narrator declines to arbitrate. The text's own framing question — \"How many angels can fit on the head of a pin?\" — mocks the demand for a definite answer.\n- THE ENDING: his feathers return, he practises flight in secret, and one morning Elisenda, cutting onions, sees him lurching off over the last houses; she watches \"until it was no longer possible for her to see him, because then he was no longer an annoyance in her life but an imaginary dot on the horizon of the sea.\" Reading: no redemption, no revelation, no gratitude, no punishment. The marvellous departs and the household is merely RELIEVED — the free indirect style pins the callousness on Elisenda, not the narrator. \"Imaginary dot\" is the crucial phrase: as he recedes he is reclassified from nuisance to fiction, which is exactly what her indifference had always made of him. A cure for her annoyance, not a miracle for anyone.\n- SUBTITLE \"A TALE FOR CHILDREN\" — UNVERIFIED, use with hedging. en.wikipedia states the story is \"subtitled 'A Tale for Children',\" and the subtitle (*Un cuento para niños*) is widely reproduced in English editions and anthologies. However the Spanish text I checked (ciudadseva) carries NO subtitle and cites only the 1972 *Eréndira* collection. I could not confirm it against the 1968 *Casa de las Américas* printing or a scholarly bibliography. Treat as: commonly and probably correctly attached in English editions, origin in the Spanish original unconfirmed. If used in teaching, the ironic force is worth noting either way — a \"tale for children\" whose subject is adult greed.\n\nB4.
